At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles . But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common. As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025. It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come. Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy. When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them. Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup. “This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation. Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says. Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says. The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.) Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives. Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources. BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report . That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands. And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices. There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data. Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky. While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study , his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels. “These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.” These scientists hope that fire-spotting satellites, AI tools and ancient land practices could preserve the world’s vulnerable permafrost—and the vast carbon it stores. New technology could help cut power losses and reinvent a staple of the grid. Batteries that swap liquid electrolytes for solid materials promise to charge faster, last longer, and (crucially) run cooler.

extraction.body: Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox. Counterintuitively, it is data centers’ independence from the grid and use of natural gas that will hike energy costs for homes and businesses, write experts from Energy Innovation. Jeffrey Rissman is a senior director at at Energy Innovation, where he works on technologies and policies to eliminate industrial greenhouse gas emissions. Eric Gimon is a senior fellow and consults as a technical expert, research scholar and policy adviser with Energy Innovation. A colossal data center is rising amidst the farmlands of Richland Parish, Louisiana. It will guzzle 2.2 GW of power , about twice as much as the entire city of New Orleans on a peak summer day. Near Cheyenne, Wyoming, an even larger data center looms on the horizon. While its first phase requires only 1.8 GW, it is ultimately designed to scale to 10 GW , as much power as all of New York City draws at its peak. Aside from their ravenous power demand, these behemoths share one crucial trait: They will be fed by on-site power plants burning natural gas, not by the electric grid. Counterintuitively, it is data centers’ independence from the grid — coupled with their use of natural gas — that will hike energy costs for American homes and small businesses. To date, most data centers have been powered by the electric grid, but this is changing fast. Facing pressure from policymakers to supply their own power, as well as multi-year delays getting permission to connect to the grid, data center projects increasingly plan to build their own on-site generation capacity, mostly powered by natural gas . A recent Bloomberg New Energy Finance analysis finds 100 GW of on-site gas-burning capacity are planned to power data centers across America. That’s equivalent to 18% of the total existing capacity of all U.S. natural gas power plants , a staggering amount. Building your own natural gas power plant might appear to protect other energy customers by reducing new demand on the grid, but that’s not the case. Natural gas is a market-traded commodity, meaning data centers that gobble up lots of natural gas will naturally compete with other gas customers, increasing prices. That does more than just worsen home heating costs. Since natural gas supplies 43% of U.S. electricity and gas-fired generators set the price of electricity in most hours, higher natural gas prices also raise electricity costs. In fact, data centers with on-site gas plants could spike American energy bills more than connecting those data centers to the grid. That’s because policymakers and regulators can require utilities to charge grid-connected data centers sufficiently high rates to cover their full costs or even enough to help modernize the grid and lower costs for other ratepayers . However, a data center with its own gas power plant signs a contract with a gas supplier, not with a utility, putting its gas rates outside the jurisdiction of state utility regulators. Data centers can buy gas in bulk and sign long-term contracts (as we’ve seen in Texas , Pennsylvania and New Mexico ) , giving them access to cheap gas, even if this unfairly drives up prices for everyone else. Since the most efficient combined-cycle turbines that burn natural gas for electricity are back-ordered for five to seven years , tech firms are relying on inefficient equipment that requires even more gas and creates more pollution. This is creating conflicts across the country, such as in Southaven, Mississippi, where xAI is being sued for violating the Clean Air Act and operating inefficient, polluting gas turbines without a permit. For tech companies, on-site gas plants might seem like a “hack” to speed up power access for data centers, but they’re only exchanging one dependency for another: As tech firms disconnect from the electric grid, they become hooked on the gas grid, where their immense new demand will run into supply bottlenecks, especially during extreme weather like Winter Storm Fern . Meanwhile, their on-site gas strategy will likely come under political pressure as residents demand solutions to rising energy bills and air pollution. Fortunately, there’s a solution that protects data center operators and the public: clean energy. Policymakers should ensure that data centers not simply bring their own electricity — but bring their own clean electricity. Wind and solar backed by batteries, along with enhanced geothermal systems, can be deployed quickly to provide the firm power data centers crave. These energy sources don’t require fuel, so they don’t increase gas or electricity costs for existing customers. And they are affordable — onshore wind and solar are the cheapest forms of generation in America, and they remain cost-competitive with natural gas even when including the cost of batteries. Some tech firms already recognize this opportunity. Google’s upcoming Minnesota data center will be powered by 1.6 GW of wind and solar with 300 MW of battery storage. And Amazon recently outbid a local utility to purchase 1.2 GW of solar capacity and an equal amount of battery storage to supply its Oregon data centers. While clean energy is already an affordable and reliable solution, policy can help make it standard for data centers. State policymakers can use siting and zoning requirements, air quality regulations, or new legislation to require that data centers build enough pollution-free capacity to supply their electricity needs, protecting communities and electric ratepayers. This must be accompanied by permitting, siting and interconnection support that allows clean energy to quickly meet new demand. For instance, states can adopt “permit-by-rule” to automatically permit renewable energy projects that comply with standardized regulations. States should also pre-authorize zones where renewables and transmission can connect without extensive permits or impact assessments such as Texas’ Competitive Renewable Energy Zones , Nevada’s Solar Energy Zones , and Arizona’s Renewable Energy Incentive Districts . Simultaneously, they should set standards that harmonize local permitting requirements and prevent localities from enforcing onerous rules intended to block renewables. Smart examples include Michigan’s HB 5120 and Illinois’s HB 4412 , both enacted in 2023. Public support for data center development is at an all-time low. Most U.S. voters now oppose data centers out of concern for their impacts on home energy costs, the environment and the quality of life of nearby residents, which can be harmed by constant noise and soot from gas turbines. A “bring your own clean energy” mandate can help address all three concerns, ensuring the data centers powering the AI revolution don’t come at the expense of Americans’ wallets, health and well-being. coreStoryFacts.text: Now, exempting data-center power plants from complying with the acid rain regulations may jeopardize how much information regulators eventually get about data center emissions—including CO2 emissions, Goffman says.

But in its official letter on the rule recommendations, the EPA used an example provided by an unnamed company that is building a planned 500-megawatt power plant of simple-cycle natural gas engines “to exclusively power an adjacent, third-party-owned data center.” Williams’ project in Utah and two of its projects in Ohio to power Meta data centers are around 500 megawatts each.

In the testimony, Gebbia made several suggestions as to how EPA should change or clarify the implementation of the Clean Air Act, including exempting behind-the-meter data centers from Acid Rain Program requirements.
However, data center developers are also increasingly turning to private power because it’s often quicker to build their own infrastructure than wait for a grid connection.

The program, they say, was explicitly intended to apply only to power plants that sold power to the grid. (Some environmental groups disagree with Goffman and Jenks: Earthjustice and the NRDC sent a letter to the EPA in September challenging the agency’s interpretation of the law in its July recommendation.) When the program was created in 1990, though, wealthy tech companies weren’t rushing to build hundreds of megawatts of private fossil-fuel power that may not ever be connected to the grid.
These private power plants often create more emissions than many of their on-grid counterparts.
Williams’ materials submitted to regulators did not specifically reference its relationship with Meta.
Natural gas plants emit lower levels of these pollutants than traditional coal-fired power plants.
BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US.
One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade.
Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.
“These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says.
That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.
In fact, data centers with on-site gas plants could spike American energy bills more than connecting those data centers to the grid.
However, a data center with its own gas power plant signs a contract with a gas supplier, not with a utility, putting its gas rates outside the jurisdiction of state utility regulators.
That’s equivalent to 18% of the total existing capacity of all U.S. natural gas power plants , a staggering amount.
Google’s upcoming Minnesota data center will be powered by 1.6 GW of wind and solar with 300 MW of battery storage.

extraction.body: The oil and gas infrastructure company’s private discussions with the agency come as the Trump administration loosens a number of environmental requirements for data centers and the natural gas plants being built to power them. “The administration is trying to relax, if not suspend for all intents and purposes, a range of regulatory requirements for these data centers,” says Joseph Goffman, the former assistant administrator at the EPA’s Office of Air and Radiation. “What this administration is trying to do, either explicitly or de facto, is take layers [of regulatory protections] away.” In response to a list of questions from WIRED, Williams spokesperson Alex Schott said in an emailed statement that the company “is committed to developing energy solutions to enhance America’s position in the global competition for AI, while prioritizing environmental protection—including addressing legislation and regulations to modernize construction and implementation timelines.” Meta declined to comment. In July, the EPA announced new federal guidance for states around participation in the Acid Rain Program, following inquiries from “companies and States.” The decades-old program was designed to reduce harmful emissions of chemicals that cause acid rain. Power plants that fall under the program need to submit a permit application two years before a facility comes online, and then regularly monitor emissions to ensure compliance. That month, the EPA said that it recommends that “islanded” power plants—which are increasingly being adopted by data centers across the country—be exempt from the program. Because the program was designed for facilities that sell electricity to the grid, the EPA said, power plants that exclusively power data centers wouldn’t need to comply. Documents obtained by WIRED from the EPA show that Williams was one of three private companies that asked regulators for guidance on the program. In a February letter sent to the Utah Department of Environmental Quality and obtained by WIRED, Williams director of permitting Steve Hall wrote that the “current regulatory uncertainty” around power plants being built solely to power data centers has created “obstacles … for data center development in the United States.” The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams sent the agency this letter. Hall wrote that the company believed its power plants “are not subject to the Acid Rain Permit program requirements, as this program was never intended to apply to sources that do not sell power to the public grid.” Getting federal guidance, he wrote, would “accelerate deployment of critical infrastructure” and “support national goals for digital infrastructure and energy reliability in the global AI race.” The EPA said in its July announcement that the new guidance was in keeping with orders from the White House to encourage data center developers to build their own power, in order to avoid increasing utility rates for consumers. However, data center developers are also increasingly turning to private power because it’s often quicker to build their own infrastructure than wait for a grid connection. These private power plants often create more emissions than many of their on-grid counterparts. Williams, one of the top oil and gas infrastructure companies in the country, has emerged in recent years as a power provider for data centers. As of November, Williams had at least six data-center power plant projects in states across the country. Meta is the client for at least four of those projects: four in Ohio, and one in Utah. Calendar invites provided by EPA show that Hall and other executives were invited to at least two meetings with EPA officials, including at least one with Aaron Szabo, then the chief of the agency’s Air office, earlier this year. In an external meeting request form filed with the agency in April, Williams indicated that its request to discuss projects in Ohio and Utah—sites where it is building power plants for Meta—was “urgent.” The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams “requested regulatory guidance for both projects” in Ohio and Utah, and that the meetings “broadly discussed air regulations.” “EPA program offices regularly meet with stakeholders in their areas of jurisdiction,” the agency added. Williams’ materials submitted to regulators did not specifically reference its relationship with Meta. But in its official letter on the rule recommendations, the EPA used an example provided by an unnamed company that is building a planned 500-megawatt power plant of simple-cycle natural gas engines “to exclusively power an adjacent, third-party-owned data center.” Williams’ project in Utah and two of its projects in Ohio to power Meta data centers are around 500 megawatts each. Williams first publicly proposed the exemption to the Acid Rain Program in September 2025 in testimony to the House of Representatives from Mark Gebbia, then the company’s vice president of environmental, permitting, and regulatory affairs. In the testimony, Gebbia made several suggestions as to how EPA should change or clarify the implementation of the Clean Air Act, including exempting behind-the-meter data centers from Acid Rain Program requirements. He noted that the long timelines for the permits are “not feasible given the urgent need to install and operate gas-fired generation for AI data centers.” The Acid Rain Program has long been considered a regulatory success that’s ensured coal plants reduce emissions of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, pollutants that help create acid rain. The law created a cap-and-trade program for power plants, allowing them to buy and sell credits for emissions to keep national levels of the pollutants low. Natural gas plants emit lower levels of these pollutants than traditional coal-fired power plants. The permit application for Williams’ facility to power Meta’s data center in Utah, for example, shows that it could emit a maximum of around 100 tons of nitrogen oxide and 11 tons of sulfur dioxide each year. Other local and national restrictions may limit how much of these pollutants come from natural gas plants. But Acid Rain Program regulations also created crucial reporting requirements that are now in jeopardy for data-center power plants. In the early 1990s, Congress passed an amendment to the Clean Air Act mandating that power facilities monitor and report various emissions in order to establish the program. Now, exempting data-center power plants from complying with the acid rain regulations may jeopardize how much information regulators eventually get about data center emissions—including CO2 emissions, Goffman says. “If the Trump administration was not deranged, and the greenhouse gas reporting program was operating, I think the EPA would be either interpreting that program’s existing requirements to cover these gas plants, or they would be promulgating new regulations to ensure these new gas plants were reporting their greenhouse gas emissions,” he says. Both Goffman and Carrie Jenks, who directs the Environmental and Energy Law Program at Harvard Law School, agree that the EPA’s guidance on the Acid Rain Program for data centers seems to stick to the letter of the law. The program, they say, was explicitly intended to apply only to power plants that sold power to the grid. (Some environmental groups disagree with Goffman and Jenks: Earthjustice and the NRDC sent a letter to the EPA in September challenging the agency’s interpretation of the law in its July recommendation.) When the program was created in 1990, though, wealthy tech companies weren’t rushing to build hundreds of megawatts of private fossil-fuel power that may not ever be connected to the grid. “No one expected it to be economical to develop a bunch of power plants that wouldn’t sell the product they were creating. The program “was never designed to address behind-the-meter generation,” she says. Some estimates show that there’s more than 110 gigawatts of planned behind-the-meter gas projects in the US, with some facilities—like Amazon’s 7-gigawatt facility in Texas, and SoftBank’s 9.2-gigawatt project in Ohio—on track to be some of the largest natural gas plants in the world. Even if those facilities don’t technically qualify for the Acid Rain Program because they’re not on the grid, lawmakers could move to change requirements to make sure that these massive facilities are covered by the program.

extraction.body: The numbers behind the off-grid gas power boom. One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom. xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles . But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common. As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025. It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come. Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy. When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them. Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup. “This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation. Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says. Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says. The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.) Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives. Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources. BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report . That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands. And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices. There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data. Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky. While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study , his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels. “These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.” These scientists hope that fire-spotting satellites, AI tools and ancient land practices could preserve the world’s vulnerable permafrost—and the vast carbon it stores. New technology could help cut power losses and reinvent a staple of the grid. Batteries that swap liquid electrolytes for solid materials promise to charge faster, last longer, and (crucially) run cooler.

And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices.

There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data.

Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.

While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study , his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels.

“These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.”

Counterintuitively, it is data centers’ independence from the grid and use of natural gas that will hike energy costs for homes and businesses, write experts from Energy Innovation. Jeffrey Rissman is a senior director at at Energy Innovation, where he works on technologies and policies to eliminate industrial greenhouse gas emissions. Eric Gimon is a senior fellow and consults as a technical expert, research scholar and policy adviser with Energy Innovation. A colossal data center is rising amidst the farmlands of Richland Parish, Louisiana. It will guzzle 2.2 GW of power , about twice as much as the entire city of New Orleans on a peak summer day. Near Cheyenne, Wyoming, an even larger data center looms on the horizon. While its first phase requires only 1.8 GW, it is ultimately designed to scale to 10 GW , as much power as all of New York City draws at its peak. Aside from their ravenous power demand, these behemoths share one crucial trait: They will be fed by on-site power plants burning natural gas, not by the electric grid. Counterintuitively, it is data centers’ independence from the grid — coupled with their use of natural gas — that will hike energy costs for American homes and small businesses. To date, most data centers have been powered by the electric grid, but this is changing fast. Facing pressure from policymakers to supply their own power, as well as multi-year delays getting permission to connect to the grid, data center projects increasingly plan to build their own on-site generation capacity, mostly powered by natural gas . A recent Bloomberg New Energy Finance analysis finds 100 GW of on-site gas-burning capacity are planned to power data centers across America. That’s equivalent to 18% of the total existing capacity of all U.S. natural gas power plants , a staggering amount. Building your own natural gas power plant might appear to protect other energy customers by reducing new demand on the grid, but that’s not the case. Natural gas is a market-traded commodity, meaning data centers that gobble up lots of natural gas will naturally compete with other gas customers, increasing prices. That does more than just worsen home heating costs. Since natural gas supplies 43% of U.S. electricity and gas-fired generators set the price of electricity in most hours, higher natural gas prices also raise electricity costs. In fact, data centers with on-site gas plants could spike American energy bills more than connecting those data centers to the grid. That’s because policymakers and regulators can require utilities to charge grid-connected data centers sufficiently high rates to cover their full costs or even enough to help modernize the grid and lower costs for other ratepayers . However, a data center with its own gas power plant signs a contract with a gas supplier, not with a utility, putting its gas rates outside the jurisdiction of state utility regulators. Data centers can buy gas in bulk and sign long-term contracts (as we’ve seen in Texas , Pennsylvania and New Mexico ) , giving them access to cheap gas, even if this unfairly drives up prices for everyone else. Since the most efficient combined-cycle turbines that burn natural gas for electricity are back-ordered for five to seven years , tech firms are relying on inefficient equipment that requires even more gas and creates more pollution. This is creating conflicts across the country, such as in Southaven, Mississippi, where xAI is being sued for violating the Clean Air Act and operating inefficient, polluting gas turbines without a permit. For tech companies, on-site gas plants might seem like a “hack” to speed up power access for data centers, but they’re only exchanging one dependency for another: As tech firms disconnect from the electric grid, they become hooked on the gas grid, where their immense new demand will run into supply bottlenecks, especially during extreme weather like Winter Storm Fern . Meanwhile, their on-site gas strategy will likely come under political pressure as residents demand solutions to rising energy bills and air pollution. Fortunately, there’s a solution that protects data center operators and the public: clean energy. Policymakers should ensure that data centers not simply bring their own electricity — but bring their own clean electricity. Wind and solar backed by batteries, along with enhanced geothermal systems, can be deployed quickly to provide the firm power data centers crave. These energy sources don’t require fuel, so they don’t increase gas or electricity costs for existing customers. And they are affordable — onshore wind and solar are the cheapest forms of generation in America, and they remain cost-competitive with natural gas even when including the cost of batteries. Some tech firms already recognize this opportunity. Google’s upcoming Minnesota data center will be powered by 1.6 GW of wind and solar with 300 MW of battery storage. And Amazon recently outbid a local utility to purchase 1.2 GW of solar capacity and an equal amount of battery storage to supply its Oregon data centers. While clean energy is already an affordable and reliable solution, policy can help make it standard for data centers. State policymakers can use siting and zoning requirements, air quality regulations, or new legislation to require that data centers build enough pollution-free capacity to supply their electricity needs, protecting communities and electric ratepayers. This must be accompanied by permitting, siting and interconnection support that allows clean energy to quickly meet new demand. For instance, states can adopt “permit-by-rule” to automatically permit renewable energy projects that comply with standardized regulations. States should also pre-authorize zones where renewables and transmission can connect without extensive permits or impact assessments such as Texas’ Competitive Renewable Energy Zones , Nevada’s Solar Energy Zones , and Arizona’s Renewable Energy Incentive Districts . Simultaneously, they should set standards that harmonize local permitting requirements and prevent localities from enforcing onerous rules intended to block renewables. Smart examples include Michigan’s HB 5120 and Illinois’s HB 4412 , both enacted in 2023. Public support for data center development is at an all-time low. Most U.S. voters now oppose data centers out of concern for their impacts on home energy costs, the environment and the quality of life of nearby residents, which can be harmed by constant noise and soot from gas turbines. A “bring your own clean energy” mandate can help address all three concerns, ensuring the data centers powering the AI revolution don’t come at the expense of Americans’ wallets, health and well-being. passages: Your Oct 21 piece on data-center developers announcing more than 100 GW of their own power plants, and having to rethink how you track them, is close to home for us: we see the same plans show up in filings.
At the time, developers had announced about 90 GW of behind-the-meter generation, roughly nine New York Cities’ worth of power.

The data center campus it powers, and the plant’s developer
Firm output, the power a plant can actually deliver to its data center, where a developer or permit discloses it
The thing I'd spell out for a newcomer: 100 GW is the width of the hose, not the water that comes out.
A plant rated at 100 MW and running half the time delivers half the energy of one running flat out.

Data center developers are building their own gas power plants rather than wait years for a grid connection. In June, we published our second report on this trend. At the time, developers had announced about 90 GW of behind-the-meter generation, roughly nine New York Cities’ worth of power. Our original plan was to publish a quarterly report on this topic. But we soon realized this was too infrequent given the speed at which this trend was evolving. To illustrate what we mean, consider a few data points: The amount of operating behind-the-meter capacity has nearly doubled since we published our last report. Capacity under construction has roughly quadrupled. Anthropic has gone from an insignificant buyer of behind-the-meter gas power to one of the largest. So we decided to scrap our original plan and build something much better. Today we’re excited to announce Cleanview’s live behind-the-meter gas plant tracker. It covers more than 100 gas plants built to power data centers, and we update it every day. For each behind-the-meter gas plant, we now show: The data center campus it powers, and the plant’s developer Every generating unit: its technology (simple-cycle turbine, reciprocating engine, combined cycle or fuel cell), manufacturer, model, unit count and nameplate capacity The status of each unit (Announced, Permitted, Under construction, Operating or Canceled) and the year it’s expected to come online Firm output, the power a plant can actually deliver to its data center, where a developer or permit discloses it The plant’s location, air permit and primary sources All of this data is available in our data platform, CSV exports, and API. On our data platform, we also provide satellite images of all the projects we track. Below is an example of a project that recently began operating despite receiving almost no media attention. It’s one of the largest behind-the-meter projects operating in the country. In our research on this topic, we’ve come across some power strategies that have surprised us. Some developers are using mobile gas generators strapped to semitrucks. Others are using aeroderivative turbines originally designed for aircraft and warships. To better understand these power strategies we built an equipment library with illustrated 3D models of every piece of power generation equipment at the behind-the-meter data centers we track. extraction.body: Jensen Huang made a dramatic return as Nvidia CEO on Monday, less than a week after board Chairman Harvey Jones said directors did not intend to reinstate him. The board later voted unanimously to bring Huang back. Nvidia shares surged as much as 36% during the session and closed 31% higher. The reversal followed a steep decline in Nvidia shares, which closed at $125.53 on Friday even after the company reported strong third-quarter results . A petition calling for Huang's return had drawn more than 200,000 signatures, according to its organizers. The rally spread across the broader market, with the Nasdaq Composite gaining 6.5% and the S&P 500 rising 4.7%, each posting its strongest session since April 2025. Nvidia's board said it had received input from senior U.S. government officials and that its investigation into Huang's conduct would continue. Still, the board's reversal, President Donald Trump's administration's role and continued scrutiny of Nvidia's China business leave major questions for both investors and lawmakers. Sen. Jack Reed, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, urged Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Monday to appear before the committee to discuss the case. Reed did not lay out a specific list of questions for the two officials, but his statement cited reporting that Trump had been briefed by intelligence officials led by then-National Security Adviser Marco Rubio before intervening in support of Huang's return. Reed's call adds to mounting pressure on both Nvidia and the Trump administration to explain what they knew and when. Rep. Gabe Amo, D-R.I., vice ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said Huang’s reinstatement could broaden congressional scrutiny rather than bring it to a close. “I think it frankly broadens the scope of the query,” Amo told CNBC, adding that lawmakers should also examine administration officials involved in decisions affecting Nvidia and chip sales to China. Amo said he expects the planned closed-door interview with Huang on Dec. 1 to proceed and that Congress would continue seeking answers both privately and publicly in the coming months. “He should start purchasing his plane tickets to Washington,” he said. “It is abundantly clear that this is ripe for questioning by Congress.” On Nvidia's third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 17, Jones said the board had accepted Huang's resignation and did not intend to reinstate him. Less than a week later, the board reversed course, saying Monday that it had unanimously voted to bring Huang back after discussions with him and input from senior U.S. government officials. "The board decided to do what we wanted to do," Trump told CNBC , adding that he believed his intervention had been important. "I've been speaking to the board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it," he said. Trump also called into an Nvidia board meeting to argue for Huang's return, Semafor reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Reed has called on Huang to disclose his communications with Trump and on Nvidia to release a transcript of the board's call with the president. Lawmakers are still seeking answers about the alleged smuggling of Nvidia products to China, their possible diversion for military use and possible advancement of Chinese AI capabilities. The Senate Banking Committee has scheduled Huang to testify on U.S. export controls on Dec. 3. House lawmakers have also confirmed closed-door interviews with Huang on Dec. 1 and Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter on Dec. 2. "The Nvidia board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," Reps. John Moolenaar, Rick Crawford and Brian Mast said in a joint statement. Their inquiry may also examine what Nvidia knew about the customers and resellers involved, as well as what controls the company had in place. Other lawmakers have also sought to preserve the paper trail. Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons had asked senior administration officials on Nov. 11 to retain records related to Nvidia exports of advanced AI chips to China and associated national security concerns. Nvidia has promised to hire a chief compliance officer and establish a committee overseeing national security and export controls. The board's investigation into Huang's conduct also remains underway. Josh Gilbert, eToro's lead analyst for APAC and the Middle East, said investors will be watching whether those new safeguards carry meaningful authority. Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson, said Nvidia has a limited window to prepare for the possibility that a future president may be less supportive of Huang. With Trump's term ending in two years, Luria argued that Nvidia needs a clearer plan for who could take over if Huang were forced to leave again. Gilbert pointed to Nvidia's roughly 75% revenue-growth forecast for the next financial year as evidence of strong near-term demand. The longer-term question, he said, is whether customer orders and artificial intelligence investment can sustain that pace. Luria told CNBC that concerns about the broader AI trade remain, including the cost of financing data centers, potential overbuilding by neocloud companies and obstacles to building new facilities. Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon said worries about whether AI spending is achievable and sustainable were not caused solely by Huang's departure. UBS, meanwhile, flagged Nvidia's roughly $390 billion in supply commitments and the need to keep demand flowing through its ecosystem. Gilbert said part of Monday's rally reflected investors recovering earlier losses rather than pricing in new growth. Bernstein restored its "Outperform" rating and kept its $200 price target, while UBS maintained its $220 target. "For the share price, it comes down to whether Nvidia can keep delivering as it has done over recent years," said Gilbert, adding that Huang's return could ease some concerns about Nvidia's longer-term outlook. "The real worry has been what happens beyond next year. Having Huang back at the helm goes a long way to easing those concerns, because he's the one who sits down with the biggest customers and gets those multi-year orders over the line," he said. — CNBC's David Sucherman, Justin Papp and Eko Prasetyo contributed to the story

sources.title: The questions Jensen Huang and Nvidia will still have to answer about Megaspeed
passages: Members of Congress from both parties say they want answers from Nvidia, with many citing alarm about China and some questioning the White House’s role in Huang’s return.
Three committees in the House of Representatives will privately interview Huang and Nvidia’s top lawyer, Tim Teter, next week.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, were part of a network of businesses that funneled chips to a company in Shanghai.
Kang also reportedly introduced his wife to Jensen Huang, whom he had known for a decade.

In a news conference Tuesday, Blanche said that Nvidia was “a good corporate citizen” and suggested it is not the target of an investigation, but Blanche declined to answer questions about the government’s investigation into Megaspeed, which the Justice Department said was ongoing as recently as last week.

The chipmaker still needs to address multiple inquiries into allegations that its advanced GPUs were smuggled into China by a customer, the Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed, in violation of U.S. export rules designed to slow China’s development of frontier AI models.
Singapore also began investigating similar allegations in 2025.
On Monday, the U.S. government added Megaspeed and its affiliates to a list of companies restricted from U.S. trade due to national security concerns.
Nvidia, meanwhile, said it would stop selling licensed chips to China and laid out plans to hire its first compliance officer and create a new board committee focused on export controls.
President Donald Trump later said he called into the meeting to give them that assurance.

“We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of Nvidia products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary’s AI capabilities,” the Republican chairs of House committees focused on foreign affairs, intelligence, and China said in a joint statement.
Diversion of this kind would be a fairly routine issue for a company like Nvidia, whose in-demand chips are the targets of smugglers and resellers.
When it comes to compliance and liability for export-control violations, Nvidia and other chip sellers need assurances that the end users of their chips are obeying the rules.
However, they also cannot ignore other information that might call the reliability of those assurances into question, export-control attorneys told TechCrunch.
Nvidia faces investigations by California Attorney General Rob Bonta and, reportedly , the SEC, both tied to its corporate disclosures.

While many details of the investigation still aren’t known, short sellers complained about the company’s decision to stop breaking out its exports to Singapore in financial filings after journalists raised concerns about chip diversion.
The Senate Banking Committee will also question Huang in a public hearing on December 3.

extraction.body: Jensen Huang’s return as CEO to Nvidia hasn’t eased the scrutiny the company faces. The chipmaker still needs to address multiple inquiries into allegations that its advanced GPUs were smuggled into China by a customer, the Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed, in violation of U.S. export rules designed to slow China’s development of frontier AI models. The central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where those chips ended up and whether Huang’s affair with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed’s assurances. Huang’s return doesn’t settle that. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche has suggested Nvidia isn’t a target of an investigation, but California’s attorney general and Congress are pressing ahead, and the Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating, too. The U.S. government opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 and requested information from Nvidia about its billions of dollars in sales to the company, concerned that some of the chips Megaspeed bought for data center projects in Malaysia were in fact being diverted to China. Singapore also began investigating similar allegations in 2025. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing. Diversion of this kind would be a fairly routine issue for a company like Nvidia, whose in-demand chips are the targets of smugglers and resellers. When it comes to compliance and liability for export-control violations, Nvidia and other chip sellers need assurances that the end users of their chips are obeying the rules. However, they also cannot ignore other information that might call the reliability of those assurances into question, export-control attorneys told TechCrunch. And that’s why Jensen Huang’s affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang was such a problem for Nvidia, likely even more so than her alleged role as a source for Chinese intelligence agencies. If Nvidia personnel, from lower-level employees up to the CEO, had reason to believe that statements from Megaspeed weren’t reliable, the attorneys said, that would increase the company’s legal risk. “Government investigators likely would want to know, notwithstanding whatever formal assurances were exchanged between the parties, what anyone at Nvidia actually knew about the end use and end users of the chips,” Dan Fisher-Owens, an attorney at the firm Berliner Corcoran & Rowe, told TechCrunch last week. The concern Nvidia’s board faced when it decided to oust Huang is that he knew more about what Megaspeed was doing with Nvidia’s products than was reflected in any of the compliance statements. The Wall Street Journal reported that Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, were part of a network of businesses that funneled chips to a company in Shanghai. Kang also reportedly introduced his wife to Jensen Huang, whom he had known for a decade. On Monday, the U.S. government added Megaspeed and its affiliates to a list of companies restricted from U.S. trade due to national security concerns. The U.S. also issued new rules last week barring large data centers that purchase U.S. chips from serving customers in China and other nations seen as problematic by the U.S. government. Nvidia, meanwhile, said it would stop selling licensed chips to China and laid out plans to hire its first compliance officer and create a new board committee focused on export controls. Nvidia’s board said it reinstated Huang on Monday after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that left it confident his return posed no national security risk. President Donald Trump later said he called into the meeting to give them that assurance. In a news conference Tuesday, Blanche said that Nvidia was “a good corporate citizen” and suggested it is not the target of an investigation, but Blanche declined to answer questions about the government’s investigation into Megaspeed, which the Justice Department said was ongoing as recently as last week. “When you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don’t know what you’re talking about,” Blanche said. Other authorities may be more demanding. Nvidia faces investigations by California Attorney General Rob Bonta and, reportedly , the SEC, both tied to its corporate disclosures. While many details of the investigation still aren’t known, short sellers complained about the company’s decision to stop breaking out its exports to Singapore in financial filings after journalists raised concerns about chip diversion. Members of Congress from both parties say they want answers from Nvidia, with many citing alarm about China and some questioning the White House’s role in Huang’s return. Three committees in the House of Representatives will privately interview Huang and Nvidia’s top lawyer, Tim Teter, next week. Teter reportedly intervened in the Department of Commerce’s investigation of Megaspeed last year. “We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of Nvidia products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary’s AI capabilities,” the Republican chairs of House committees focused on foreign affairs, intelligence, and China said in a joint statement. Rep. Brian Mast, the chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has also demanded that the Department of Commerce share extensive data regarding its investigation into chip smuggling, including by Megaspeed and its affiliates. The Senate Banking Committee will also question Huang in a public hearing on December 3. “Mr. Huang, Nvidia executives, and the company’s board still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with U.S. export controls,” Senator Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democratic member on the committee, said in a statement. “The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what ‘input’ was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement.” Get an Early Peek at the Next TechCrunch Disrupt Disrupt, Startup Battlefield, and more will return next year, and you can be at the front of the line. extraction.body: Three senior House Republicans want Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in a closed room on November 18. Their question is narrow but awkward: how well does he know Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed, whom US officials determined was passing information to Chinese intelligence?The request came on November 5 from Brian Mast, chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, John Moolenaar, who heads the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and Rick Crawford, who leads the House Intelligence Committee. In a joint letter, they asked Huang to brief them on his interactions with Alice Huang and on how Nvidia guards against espionage by foreign adversaries. He has until November 11 to accept the date or suggest another.The chairmen wrote that Congress needs to establish "the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk." Nvidia has not said whether its CEO will attend. Spokesperson John Rizzo told The New York Times that Huang has "an outstanding security team that accompanies him where needed."Who Alice Huang is and how she came on the US radarAlice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen who was listed as Megaspeed's managing director for the company's first eight months before her name was removed from that role in corporate filings. Megaspeed was formed in 2023 when Chinese gaming company 7Road spun off its overseas operation in Singapore. The two Huangs are not related.According to NYT, American spy agencies learned about her relationship with the Nvidia chief while she was under surveillance. An earlier NYT investigation described a late-night gathering of Nvidia's Asian customers at a Taipei bar, where she told the group, "I bet you guys I can get Jensen here." He turned up shortly after. The two were photographed together again in May 2025, leaving a Taipei restaurant after a business dinner.Megaspeed bought billions of dollars of Nvidia AI hardwareMegaspeed's Malaysian sister company bought at least $4.8 billion of advanced AI equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026, NYT reported, citing trade records from the platform ImportGenius. A large share of the early shipments came from Aivres, the California-based arm of Inspur, a Chinese firm the US has sanctioned for supporting the Chinese military.US officials have been examining Megaspeed since late 2024, when a Commerce Department official visited its Malaysian data centre and found Nvidia equipment still packed in boxes. Singapore police are also investigating the company.Nvidia says it complies with the law and has seen no evidence that its chips were smuggled into China. Rizzo has said that meeting customers comes with a CEO's job, and that Huang speaks with thousands of customer executives every year. Megaspeed has said it follows all applicable laws, including US export controls.Why Republicans are now asking tech hard questionsThe letter is a break from form. Republican leaders have mostly followed President Trump's hands-off line on the tech industry, and Huang has grown close to Trump over the past two years. Voters made it clear they are worried about AI eating into jobs and giant data centres coming up near their homes, and that sentiment largely helped Democrats. NYT sees the letter as an early signal that Republicans do not want to leave that issue to the other side.Democrats have been pressing too. He declined, and she renewed the request last week.So far, Nvidia has answered the Alice Huang question through a spokesperson. extraction.body: [DigitalToday reporter Jinju Hong] Nvidia will report quarterly results for the first time since Jensen Huang resigned. Market attention is focused not only on revenue and profitability but also on controversy over chip sales to China, how the company is responding to a management vacuum and the next leadership. It is also drawing attention because acting CEO Colette Kress, who has served as chief financial officer for a long time, will explain results and the business outlook in person for the first time.According to IT outlet TechCrunch on Nov. 16 (local time), Kress is expected to face questions during the earnings release on key issues including Nvidia's financial performance, the direction of its China business and executive succession.The biggest focus is what leadership structure the company will build after Huang's resignation. Huang is known as a figure who has been deeply involved across the company's management, with as many as 60 people reporting directly to him. The market is therefore watching whether Huang has fully stepped away from day-to-day management and whether there remains a possibility of a return.Another point of interest is whether the board is pushing for Huang's return. Online, a petition calling for his return has emerged with more than 180,000 signatures. The company has not officially announced any plan for Huang to return or a succession process. How Kress sets out her position on Huang's role and the future management structure during the earnings release will be closely watched.Chip sales to China and export controls are also key issues. Huang has argued for easing U.S. restrictions on semiconductor exports to China and has spoken to the effect that he has never seen evidence that Nvidia chips entered China through diversions via normal purchasing channels. In October 2025, however, it became known that Megaspeed, allegedly involving Alice Huang, a person linked to Huang, was investigated by U.S. authorities over suspicions it diverted Nvidia chips to China.Nvidia's response related to Megaspeed is also expected to come under scrutiny. The company explained at the time that Megaspeed was legally using Nvidia chips on its cloud, but later said it voluntarily halted additional chip supplies to the firm starting in June 2025. The market is expected to demand a detailed explanation of how much Nvidia tracks final end-users of its semiconductors and how it manages distribution channels for chips subject to export controls.Questions also remain over revenue in Singapore. Nvidia introduced Singapore last year as one of its fast-growing markets, and at the time Singapore accounted for 22 percent of total revenue in the second quarter. After suspicions linked to Megaspeed surfaced, the company changed its revenue tallying standard from the shipping destination to the location of customers' headquarters.That has made it difficult to compare the scale of business reflected in Singapore revenue in the same way as in the past. The market is expected to examine the actual scale of Singapore-based cloud business, the impact of the disclosure change on financial information and the outlook for sales to China.Whether its China strategy will change is also in focus. Huang previously argued that it would be difficult for the United States to block China from developing high-performance artificial intelligence models, and that it would be better to supply even relatively lower-performance Nvidia chips to China to maintain market dependence. In contrast, China hawks in the United States have countered that exporting advanced semiconductors could end up helping China's technological development.After Huang stepped down, the key question is whether Kress will keep China business targets unchanged or adjust strategy in consideration of export regulations and geopolitical risks. How Nvidia approaches the China market is tied not only to its medium- and long-term revenue outlook but also to U.S. government export control policy.Its stance on AI infrastructure investment is also under review. Kress has been cited as someone who took a cautious view, during her tenure as CFO, of Huang's aggressive AI-related deals and investment expansion. The market is watching whether large-scale investment and deals will continue, along with the impact of existing big contracts on the company's finances. The company's risk management and financial judgment on controversial contracts are also expected to be key questions.Whether there will be governance restructuring also cannot be left out. How decision-making authority will be allocated after Huang's resignation and whether the board will strengthen oversight of management are emerging as standards for restoring corporate trust. It is also of interest whether a succession plan, including the appointment of a successor and decentralisation of authority, will be fleshed out.This earnings release is expected to be the first test of whether Nvidia can maintain its existing growth strategy in Huang's absence. Beyond revenue and earnings guidance, explanations on transparency in the China business, risk management for AI investments and the next management structure are cited as key variables that will shape the market's assessment.

extraction.body: Jensen Huang made a dramatic return as Nvidia CEO on Monday, less than a week after board Chairman Harvey Jones said directors did not intend to reinstate him. The board later voted unanimously to bring Huang back. Nvidia shares surged as much as 36% during the session and closed 31% higher. The reversal followed a steep decline in Nvidia shares, which closed at $125.53 on Friday even after the company reported strong third-quarter results . A petition calling for Huang's return had drawn more than 200,000 signatures, according to its organizers. The rally spread across the broader market, with the Nasdaq Composite gaining 6.5% and the S&P 500 rising 4.7%, each posting its strongest session since April 2025. Nvidia's board said it had received input from senior U.S. government officials and that its investigation into Huang's conduct would continue. Still, the board's reversal, President Donald Trump's administration's role and continued scrutiny of Nvidia's China business leave major questions for both investors and lawmakers. Sen. Jack Reed, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, urged Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Monday to appear before the committee to discuss the case. The chipmaker still needs to address multiple inquiries into allegations that its advanced GPUs were smuggled into China by a customer, the Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed, in violation of U.S. export rules designed to slow China’s development of frontier AI models.

President Donald Trump later said he called into the meeting to give them that assurance.

Diversion of this kind would be a fairly routine issue for a company like Nvidia, whose in-demand chips are the targets of smugglers and resellers.
When it comes to compliance and liability for export-control violations, Nvidia and other chip sellers need assurances that the end users of their chips are obeying the rules.
However, they also cannot ignore other information that might call the reliability of those assurances into question, export-control attorneys told TechCrunch.

The chipmaker still needs to address multiple inquiries into allegations that its advanced GPUs were smuggled into China by a customer, the Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed, in violation of U.S. export rules designed to slow China’s development of frontier AI models. The central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where those chips ended up and whether Huang’s affair with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed’s assurances. Huang’s return doesn’t settle that. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche has suggested Nvidia isn’t a target of an investigation, but California’s attorney general and Congress are pressing ahead, and the Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating, too. The U.S. government opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 and requested information from Nvidia about its billions of dollars in sales to the company, concerned that some of the chips Megaspeed bought for data center projects in Malaysia were in fact being diverted to China. Singapore also began investigating similar allegations in 2025. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing. Diversion of this kind would be a fairly routine issue for a company like Nvidia, whose in-demand chips are the targets of smugglers and resellers. When it comes to compliance and liability for export-control violations, Nvidia and other chip sellers need assurances that the end users of their chips are obeying the rules. However, they also cannot ignore other information that might call the reliability of those assurances into question, export-control attorneys told TechCrunch. And that’s why Jensen Huang’s affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang was such a problem for Nvidia, likely even more so than her alleged role as a source for Chinese intelligence agencies. If Nvidia personnel, from lower-level employees up to the CEO, had reason to believe that statements from Megaspeed weren’t reliable, the attorneys said, that would increase the company’s legal risk. “Government investigators likely would want to know, notwithstanding whatever formal assurances were exchanged between the parties, what anyone at Nvidia actually knew about the end use and end users of the chips,” Dan Fisher-Owens, an attorney at the firm Berliner Corcoran & Rowe, told TechCrunch last week. The concern Nvidia’s board faced when it decided to oust Huang is that he knew more about what Megaspeed was doing with Nvidia’s products than was reflected in any of the compliance statements. Kang also reportedly introduced his wife to Jensen Huang, whom he had known for a decade. On Monday, the U.S. government added Megaspeed and its affiliates to a list of companies restricted from U.S. trade due to national security concerns. The U.S. also issued new rules last week barring large data centers that purchase U.S. chips from serving customers in China and other nations seen as problematic by the U.S. government. Nvidia, meanwhile, said it would stop selling licensed chips to China and laid out plans to hire its first compliance officer and create a new board committee focused on export controls. President Donald Trump later said he called into the meeting to give them that assurance.
