extraction.body: [DigitalToday reporter Jinju Hong] Nvidia will report quarterly results for the first time since Jensen Huang resigned. Market attention is focused not only on revenue and profitability but also on controversy over chip sales to China, how the company is responding to a management vacuum and the next leadership. It is also drawing attention because acting CEO Colette Kress, who has served as chief financial officer for a long time, will explain results and the business outlook in person for the first time.According to IT outlet TechCrunch on Nov. 16 (local time), Kress is expected to face questions during the earnings release on key issues including Nvidia's financial performance, the direction of its China business and executive succession.The biggest focus is what leadership structure the company will build after Huang's resignation. Huang is known as a figure who has been deeply involved across the company's management, with as many as 60 people reporting directly to him. The market is therefore watching whether Huang has fully stepped away from day-to-day management and whether there remains a possibility of a return.Another point of interest is whether the board is pushing for Huang's return. Online, a petition calling for his return has emerged with more than 180,000 signatures. The company has not officially announced any plan for Huang to return or a succession process. How Kress sets out her position on Huang's role and the future management structure during the earnings release will be closely watched.Chip sales to China and export controls are also key issues. Huang has argued for easing U.S. restrictions on semiconductor exports to China and has spoken to the effect that he has never seen evidence that Nvidia chips entered China through diversions via normal purchasing channels. In October 2025, however, it became known that Megaspeed, allegedly involving Alice Huang, a person linked to Huang, was investigated by U.S. authorities over suspicions it diverted Nvidia chips to China.Nvidia's response related to Megaspeed is also expected to come under scrutiny. The company explained at the time that Megaspeed was legally using Nvidia chips on its cloud, but later said it voluntarily halted additional chip supplies to the firm starting in June 2025. The market is expected to demand a detailed explanation of how much Nvidia tracks final end-users of its semiconductors and how it manages distribution channels for chips subject to export controls.Questions also remain over revenue in Singapore. Nvidia introduced Singapore last year as one of its fast-growing markets, and at the time Singapore accounted for 22 percent of total revenue in the second quarter. After suspicions linked to Megaspeed surfaced, the company changed its revenue tallying standard from the shipping destination to the location of customers' headquarters.That has made it difficult to compare the scale of business reflected in Singapore revenue in the same way as in the past. The market is expected to examine the actual scale of Singapore-based cloud business, the impact of the disclosure change on financial information and the outlook for sales to China.Whether its China strategy will change is also in focus. Huang previously argued that it would be difficult for the United States to block China from developing high-performance artificial intelligence models, and that it would be better to supply even relatively lower-performance Nvidia chips to China to maintain market dependence. In contrast, China hawks in the United States have countered that exporting advanced semiconductors could end up helping China's technological development.After Huang stepped down, the key question is whether Kress will keep China business targets unchanged or adjust strategy in consideration of export regulations and geopolitical risks. How Nvidia approaches the China market is tied not only to its medium- and long-term revenue outlook but also to U.S. government export control policy.Its stance on AI infrastructure investment is also under review. Kress has been cited as someone who took a cautious view, during her tenure as CFO, of Huang's aggressive AI-related deals and investment expansion. The market is watching whether large-scale investment and deals will continue, along with the impact of existing big contracts on the company's finances. The company's risk management and financial judgment on controversial contracts are also expected to be key questions.Whether there will be governance restructuring also cannot be left out. How decision-making authority will be allocated after Huang's resignation and whether the board will strengthen oversight of management are emerging as standards for restoring corporate trust. It is also of interest whether a succession plan, including the appointment of a successor and decentralisation of authority, will be fleshed out.This earnings release is expected to be the first test of whether Nvidia can maintain its existing growth strategy in Huang's absence. Beyond revenue and earnings guidance, explanations on transparency in the China business, risk management for AI investments and the next management structure are cited as key variables that will shape the market's assessment.

Elon Musk's out-of-this world plan for data centers in space has gotten a key green light from the feds. The Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday authorized Musk's SpaceX to launch 1 million satellites for a "constellation" of data centers in the Earth's orbit. In approving a request that SpaceX made earlier this year, the FCC said SpaceX's "Starmind" system will help meet the nation's growing demand for AI computing power. The orbital compute modules launched into space will be used to process massive amounts of data to be used back on Earth, the FCC said. "Compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America's leadership in SI [Super Intelligence]," FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement. "By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment," he added. Musk previously argued that putting data centers in space could save on costs and avoid pushback from voters — who widely rejected construction of new data sites on terra firma in this month's midterms. "It's a no-brainer, building solar-power data centers in space … the lowest-cost place to put AI will be space, and that will be true within two years, three at the latest," Musk said at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in January. He repeated the sentiment in the immediate aftermath of the midterms, when anti-data center pols won office nationwide. "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk wrote. In its request to the FCC, SpaceX said its satellites will "achieve transformative cost and energy efficiency" from near-constant solar power while reducing the environmental impact on Earth. The FCC said its license requires SpaceX to begin deployment no later than November 2033, deploy 10% of the 1 million satellites no later than November 2035 and deploy 50% by November 2038. Data centers require vast amounts of power, and residents living near the massive structures have claimed they've faced higher utility bills. Noise and light pollution figure in local objections, too. It was not immediately clear whether SpaceX is planning to launch the full 1 million satellites — companies sometimes request approvals for larger launches than what they actually have planned. SpaceX previously requested approval for 42,000 Starlink satellites for a program that currently has just over 11,000 satellites in space, for example. The company did not immediately respond to The Post's request for comment. SpaceX's futuristic data center plans rely heavily on the success of its Starship rocket, a massive launch model designed to be fully reusable – which could drastically lower costs. Amazon – which owns Leo, a rival satellite business – has been one of the most outspoken critics of SpaceX's proposal, arguing it would take centuries to deploy all 1 million satellites. Carr lashed out at Amazon's criticism during an interview with Reuters in March. "I think Amazon should focus on getting Amazon's house in order with their own launches and their own satellite constellation, rather than worrying about other people that are actually out there launching satellites at the pace and cadence that SpaceX is," he said. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also called Musk's plans for data centers in space "ridiculous." The FCC said it is also approving SpaceX's requests to back up its optical network and that it is continuing to review additional orbital data center proposals. "This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said of the data centers on Wednesday.

extraction.body: See more of our coverage in your search results. Elon Musk’s out-of-this world plan for data centers in space has gotten a key green light from the feds. The Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday authorized Musk’s SpaceX to launch 1 million satellites for a “constellation” of data centers in the Earth’s orbit. In approving a request that SpaceX made earlier this year, the FCC said SpaceX’s “Starmind” system will help meet the nation’s growing demand for AI computing power. The orbital compute modules launched into space will be used to process massive amounts of data to be used back on Earth, the FCC said. “Compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America’s leadership in SI [Super Intelligence],” FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement. “By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” he added. Musk previously argued that putting data centers in space could save on costs and avoid pushback from voters — who widely rejected construction of new data sites on terra firma in this month’s midterms. “It’s a no-brainer, building solar-power data centers in space … the lowest-cost place to put AI will be space, and that will be true within two years, three at the latest,” Musk said at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in January. He repeated the sentiment in the immediate aftermath of the midterms, when anti-data center pols won office nationwide. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk wrote. In its request to the FCC, SpaceX said its satellites will “achieve transformative cost and energy efficiency” from near-constant solar power while reducing the environmental impact on Earth. The FCC said its license requires SpaceX to begin deployment no later than November 2033, deploy 10% of the 1 million satellites no later than November 2035 and deploy 50% by November 2038. Data centers require vast amounts of power, and residents living near the massive structures have claimed they’ve faced higher utility bills. Noise and light pollution figure in local objections, too. It was not immediately clear whether SpaceX is planning to launch the full 1 million satellites — companies sometimes request approvals for larger launches than what they actually have planned. SpaceX previously requested approval for 42,000 Starlink satellites for a program that currently has just over 11,000 satellites in space, for example. The company did not immediately respond to The Post’s request for comment. SpaceX’s futuristic data center plans rely heavily on the success of its Starship rocket, a massive launch model designed to be fully reusable – which could drastically lower costs. Amazon – which owns Leo, a rival satellite business – has been one of the most outspoken critics of SpaceX’s proposal, arguing it would take centuries to deploy all 1 million satellites. Carr lashed out at Amazon’s criticism during an interview with Reuters in March. “I think Amazon should focus on getting Amazon’s house in order with their own launches and their own satellite constellation, rather than worrying about other people that are actually out there launching satellites at the pace and cadence that SpaceX is,” he said. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also called Musk’s plans for data centers in space “ridiculous.” The FCC said it is also approving SpaceX’s requests to back up its optical network and that it is continuing to review additional orbital data center proposals. “This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home,” Carr said of the data centers on Wednesday.

extraction.body: Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has conditionally approved SpaceX’s plan to build a satellite constellation for its space data center business.On Nov. 25, major foreign media reported that the FCC authorised SpaceX to deploy and operate up to 1 million satellites. It is the first time in the United States that a satellite constellation dedicated to a space data center has been approved.The decision lends support to Elon Musk’s push for a space-based artificial intelligence (AI) data center. SpaceX plans to deploy satellites known as “Starmind” at altitudes of 500 to 1,002 km. The satellites will process data directly in orbit, and use lasers for key communications between satellites. They will also connect to the Starlink satellite network. The FCC also authorised backup and emergency radio-frequency communications to support satellite telemetry, tracking and control if laser communications fail. The frequencies must be used on the condition that they do not interfere with other communications.The approval does not sign off on all operational plans. The FCC put on hold SpaceX’s request for an exception on disposal methods after the end of a mission for satellites above 600 km. Under existing rules, satellites at altitudes of 2,000 km or lower must re-enter Earth’s atmosphere within 5 years after completing their missions. SpaceX asked to move some retired satellites to other Earth orbits or to orbits around the sun, but the FCC found there was not enough information. To deploy satellites at those altitudes, SpaceX must submit a final space-debris mitigation plan and obtain separate approval.Objections to the decision were also raised by Amazon, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society. They cited concerns about space debris, orbital congestion, radio interference, and impacts on environmental and astronomical research. Amazon in particular said SpaceX’s application lacked basic details, and criticised Starmind as “a grand vision rather than an actual plan.” It also said the plan “risks causing substantial harm.” The FCC excluded some concerns related to environmental and scientific research from its review, judging them to be outside its regulatory authority.FCC Chairman Brendan Carr (Brendan Carr) said the decision “opens a new area of computing infrastructure needed to support U.S. leadership and growth.” Elon Musk also wrote on X, formerly Twitter, “Thank you very much. It will be a great asset to the United States and the world.”Still, technical and economic challenges remain before a space data center can be realised. Manufacturing and launch costs must be lowered significantly, and cooling technology is needed to dissipate heat generated by AI semiconductors in space. Securing funding to procure the chips to be put into orbit is also a challenge. SpaceX must deploy its first operational satellite within 7 years and the full constellation within 14 years. Under the FCC schedule, it must operate the first satellite by November 2033, and deploy 10 percent by 2035, 50 percent by 2038 and the full constellation by 2040.SpaceX is not the only company pursuing a space data center business. Google is developing space AI computing infrastructure through “Project Suncatcher” and sent its first chip into space in October. Blue Origin, led by Jeff Bezos, also applied to the FCC in March to build “Project Sunrise,” a constellation of up to 51,600 satellites. Competition among companies over space-based computing is also gaining momentum.

Elon Musk's out-of-this world plan for data centers in space has gotten a key green light from the feds. The Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday authorized Musk's SpaceX to launch 1 million satellites for a "constellation" of data centers in the Earth's orbit. In approving a request that SpaceX made earlier this year, the FCC said SpaceX's "Starmind" system will help meet the nation's growing demand for AI computing power. The orbital compute modules launched into space will be used to process massive amounts of data to be used back on Earth, the FCC said. "Compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America's leadership in SI [Super Intelligence]," FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement. "By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment," he added. Musk previously argued that putting data centers in space could save on costs and avoid pushback from voters — who widely rejected construction of new data sites on terra firma in this month's midterms. "It's a no-brainer, building solar-power data centers in space … the lowest-cost place to put AI will be space, and that will be true within two years, three at the latest," Musk said at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in January. He repeated the sentiment in the immediate aftermath of the midterms, when anti-data center pols won office nationwide. "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk wrote. In its request to the FCC, SpaceX said its satellites will "achieve transformative cost and energy efficiency" from near-constant solar power while reducing the environmental impact on Earth. The FCC said its license requires SpaceX to begin deployment no later than November 2033, deploy 10% of the 1 million satellites no later than November 2035 and deploy 50% by November 2038. Data centers require vast amounts of power, and residents living near the massive structures have claimed they've faced higher utility bills. Noise and light pollution figure in local objections, too. It was not immediately clear whether SpaceX is planning to launch the full 1 million satellites — companies sometimes request approvals for larger launches than what they actually have planned. SpaceX previously requested approval for 42,000 Starlink satellites for a program that currently has just over 11,000 satellites in space, for example. The company did not immediately respond to The Post's request for comment. SpaceX's futuristic data center plans rely heavily on the success of its Starship rocket, a massive launch model designed to be fully reusable – which could drastically lower costs. Amazon – which owns Leo, a rival satellite business – has been one of the most outspoken critics of SpaceX's proposal, arguing it would take centuries to deploy all 1 million satellites. Carr lashed out at Amazon's criticism during an interview with Reuters in March. "I think Amazon should focus on getting Amazon's house in order with their own launches and their own satellite constellation, rather than worrying about other people that are actually out there launching satellites at the pace and cadence that SpaceX is," he said. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also called Musk's plans for data centers in space "ridiculous." The FCC said it is also approving SpaceX's requests to back up its optical network and that it is continuing to review additional orbital data center proposals. "This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said of the data centers on Wednesday.

extraction.body: Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has conditionally approved SpaceX’s plan to build a satellite constellation for its space data center business.On Nov. 25, major foreign media reported that the FCC authorised SpaceX to deploy and operate up to 1 million satellites. It is the first time in the United States that a satellite constellation dedicated to a space data center has been approved.The decision lends support to Elon Musk’s push for a space-based artificial intelligence (AI) data center. SpaceX plans to deploy satellites known as “Starmind” at altitudes of 500 to 1,002 km. The satellites will process data directly in orbit, and use lasers for key communications between satellites. They will also connect to the Starlink satellite network. The FCC also authorised backup and emergency radio-frequency communications to support satellite telemetry, tracking and control if laser communications fail. The frequencies must be used on the condition that they do not interfere with other communications.The approval does not sign off on all operational plans. The FCC put on hold SpaceX’s request for an exception on disposal methods after the end of a mission for satellites above 600 km. Under existing rules, satellites at altitudes of 2,000 km or lower must re-enter Earth’s atmosphere within 5 years after completing their missions. SpaceX asked to move some retired satellites to other Earth orbits or to orbits around the sun, but the FCC found there was not enough information. To deploy satellites at those altitudes, SpaceX must submit a final space-debris mitigation plan and obtain separate approval.Objections to the decision were also raised by Amazon, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society. They cited concerns about space debris, orbital congestion, radio interference, and impacts on environmental and astronomical research. Amazon in particular said SpaceX’s application lacked basic details, and criticised Starmind as “a grand vision rather than an actual plan.” It also said the plan “risks causing substantial harm.” The FCC excluded some concerns related to environmental and scientific research from its review, judging them to be outside its regulatory authority.FCC Chairman Brendan Carr (Brendan Carr) said the decision “opens a new area of computing infrastructure needed to support U.S. leadership and growth.” Elon Musk also wrote on X, formerly Twitter, “Thank you very much. It will be a great asset to the United States and the world.”Still, technical and economic challenges remain before a space data center can be realised. Manufacturing and launch costs must be lowered significantly, and cooling technology is needed to dissipate heat generated by AI semiconductors in space. Securing funding to procure the chips to be put into orbit is also a challenge. SpaceX must deploy its first operational satellite within 7 years and the full constellation within 14 years. Under the FCC schedule, it must operate the first satellite by November 2033, and deploy 10 percent by 2035, 50 percent by 2038 and the full constellation by 2040.SpaceX is not the only company pursuing a space data center business. Google is developing space AI computing infrastructure through “Project Suncatcher” and sent its first chip into space in October. Blue Origin, led by Jeff Bezos, also applied to the FCC in March to build “Project Sunrise,” a constellation of up to 51,600 satellites. Competition among companies over space-based computing is also gaining momentum.

sources.title: Amazon and Meta reportedly in talks to lift blockade on AI agent Muse
passages: Amazon may be having a change of heart about Meta’s AI agent, Muse.
According to a Wednesday report by Fortune , citing people familiar with the discussions, Amazon and Meta have held multiple rounds of talks about the matter.
Two key issues remain under negotiation: how search results would be presented and how advertising would be handled under a potential agreement.

The talks would mark a significant reversal from just two months ago, when Muse users discovered they were unable to purchase products on Amazon and instead received an error message when attempting to check out.
One of Amazon’s biggest concerns is how third-party shopping agents like Muse could affect its advertising business.
In October, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy argued that few customers were making purchases through outside shopping agents.
Meta and Amazon have not yet responded to TechCrunch’s requests for comment.
Amazon may also have been waiting for Muse to mature before agreeing to integrate it with its marketplace.
If Muse places the wrong order or creates a problem with a purchase, Amazon could ultimately be left dealing with frustrated customers and unhappy sellers.

passages: Amazon and Meta have reportedly held several rounds of talks about letting Meta’s Muse AI agent place orders directly on Amazon.
The discussions come two months after Muse users found they could browse for products but hit an error when they tried to check out.
Reportedly , two questions remain open, according to people familiar with the talks.
How would Muse present Amazon’s search results to shoppers?
And how would advertising work when a customer shops through Meta’s agent?
An agreement would give Muse a direct connection to Amazon’s store, a reversal of the checkout restriction users encountered two months ago.
In October, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said few customers were making purchases through outside shopping agents.
Reliability may also help explain Amazon’s caution.
If Muse orders the wrong item or makes another mistake during checkout, Amazon could be the company that has to resolve the problem with the buyer and the seller.
Additionally, Meta employees testing Muse recently flagged the AI agent for reading encrypted Signal messages, sending fake bank balances, and mixing up conversations between users.
Apple is reportedly working on an AI agent that can complete tasks on behalf of users.

sources.title: Exclusive: Meta and Amazon discuss ending Muse shopping bot blockade, as ads, search emerge as key issues - Fortune
passages: Amazon and Meta Platforms are in ongoing discussions over a potential deal to connect Meta’s popular Muse AI agent to the e-commerce giant’s online store and end a blockade of the shopping bot imposed by Amazon two months ago.

The negotiations are being closely followed because they have major implications for the future of online shopping and represent an important test case for how large corporations respond to the advent of AI agents.

As agents like Muse become more widely used, companies like Amazon are scrambling to understand how the bots alter typical shopping patterns as well as the valued connections that brands and retailers have with consumers.

The two tech giants have held talks on multiple occasions, and two major factors being negotiated are how the companies will handle search results and advertising in any deal, according to people familiar with the matter.
Discussions are fluid, and it’s unclear if or how soon an agreement will be struck.
There are numerous issues, ranging from Amazon’s own AI shopping ambitions to how, exactly, Muse would connect to Amazon.
Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse app from accessing its store in September, saying at the time that Muse’s access would violate its user agreements.

Muse, which Meta released in the U.S. that month, is a personalized AI agent that users can name and direct to autonomously carry out tasks on their behalf, such as checking email, managing calendars, and booking reservations.
Chief executive Mark Zuckerberg has said shopping is Muse’s top use case.
One of Amazon’s main concerns is how shopping agents such as Muse will affect its advertising business.

In October, Amazon chief executive Andy Jassy, while not naming Muse, tried to quell investor concern by saying few customers are buying with outside shopping agents because the experience is “still not great, nor more convenient than coming to a retailer directly.”
Meta and Amazon have partnered on e-commerce before.
In 2023, the companies struck a deal that allowed Facebook and Instagram users to purchase Amazon products without leaving the apps.
Meta makes money from ads it serves users on its apps, including for Amazon products, and Amazon earns revenue through the actual purchases.
The partnership was made as TikTok expanded into U.S. e-commerce.
Aside from Meta, OpenAI launched its Dots personal AI agents in September, and startup Instinct’s personal assistant has also become a mainstream AI agent.
Amazon has its own shopping agent for its website, dubbed “Alexa for shopping,” which Jassy said has been used by more than 400 million customers in the past year.
Meta signed on other partners early in its Muse efforts, including Amazon rivals such as Shopify, Walmart , and Best Buy .

Thus, retailers have gained another channel for selling products as Meta tries to grow Muse, and according to Zuckerberg, the company eventually plans to profit by taking a “small fee from transactions.”
AI agents promise to bring major changes to many industries.
Analysts at JPMorgan have praised Muse as a powerful agent, recently writing that tens of millions of businesses could eventually use the tool.
The talks are ongoing as Amazon prepares for another Black Friday and Cyber Monday, one of its most critical shopping periods of the year.
This year, roughly half of holiday shoppers plan to use AI in some way to help make purchases, a National Retail Federation survey this month showed.
“We think that billions of Muses in a network at scale will be able to get more done for people and businesses by working together,” Zuckerberg said last month on a call with analysts.
“We’d like to create a large-scale Muse network as quickly as possible.”

According to a Wednesday report by Fortune , citing people familiar with the discussions, Amazon and Meta have held multiple rounds of talks about the matter.
Two key issues remain under negotiation: how search results would be presented and how advertising would be handled under a potential agreement.

The talks would mark a significant reversal from just two months ago, when Muse users discovered they were unable to purchase products on Amazon and instead received an error message when attempting to check out.
One of Amazon’s biggest concerns is how third-party shopping agents like Muse could affect its advertising business.
In October, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy argued that few customers were making purchases through outside shopping agents.
Meta and Amazon have not yet responded to TechCrunch’s requests for comment.
Amazon may also have been waiting for Muse to mature before agreeing to integrate it with its marketplace.
If Muse places the wrong order or creates a problem with a purchase, Amazon could ultimately be left dealing with frustrated customers and unhappy sellers.

Reliability may also help explain Amazon’s caution.
If Muse orders the wrong item or makes another mistake during checkout, Amazon could be the company that has to resolve the problem with the buyer and the seller.

sources.title: Exclusive: Meta and Amazon discuss ending Muse shopping bot blockade, as ads, search emerge as key issues - Fortune
passages: Amazon and Meta Platforms are in ongoing discussions over a potential deal to connect Meta’s popular Muse AI agent to the e-commerce giant’s online store and end a blockade of the shopping bot imposed by Amazon two months ago.

The negotiations are being closely followed because they have major implications for the future of online shopping and represent an important test case for how large corporations respond to the advent of AI agents.

As agents like Muse become more widely used, companies like Amazon are scrambling to understand how the bots alter typical shopping patterns as well as the valued connections that brands and retailers have with consumers.

The two tech giants have held talks on multiple occasions, and two major factors being negotiated are how the companies will handle search results and advertising in any deal, according to people familiar with the matter.
Discussions are fluid, and it’s unclear if or how soon an agreement will be struck.
There are numerous issues, ranging from Amazon’s own AI shopping ambitions to how, exactly, Muse would connect to Amazon.
Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse app from accessing its store in September, saying at the time that Muse’s access would violate its user agreements.

Muse, which Meta released in the U.S. that month, is a personalized AI agent that users can name and direct to autonomously carry out tasks on their behalf, such as checking email, managing calendars, and booking reservations.
Chief executive Mark Zuckerberg has said shopping is Muse’s top use case.
One of Amazon’s main concerns is how shopping agents such as Muse will affect its advertising business.

In October, Amazon chief executive Andy Jassy, while not naming Muse, tried to quell investor concern by saying few customers are buying with outside shopping agents because the experience is “still not great, nor more convenient than coming to a retailer directly.”
Meta and Amazon have partnered on e-commerce before.
In 2023, the companies struck a deal that allowed Facebook and Instagram users to purchase Amazon products without leaving the apps.
Meta makes money from ads it serves users on its apps, including for Amazon products, and Amazon earns revenue through the actual purchases.
The partnership was made as TikTok expanded into U.S. e-commerce.
Aside from Meta, OpenAI launched its Dots personal AI agents in September, and startup Instinct’s personal assistant has also become a mainstream AI agent.
Amazon has its own shopping agent for its website, dubbed “Alexa for shopping,” which Jassy said has been used by more than 400 million customers in the past year.
Meta signed on other partners early in its Muse efforts, including Amazon rivals such as Shopify, Walmart , and Best Buy .

Thus, retailers have gained another channel for selling products as Meta tries to grow Muse, and according to Zuckerberg, the company eventually plans to profit by taking a “small fee from transactions.”
AI agents promise to bring major changes to many industries.
Analysts at JPMorgan have praised Muse as a powerful agent, recently writing that tens of millions of businesses could eventually use the tool.
The talks are ongoing as Amazon prepares for another Black Friday and Cyber Monday, one of its most critical shopping periods of the year.
This year, roughly half of holiday shoppers plan to use AI in some way to help make purchases, a National Retail Federation survey this month showed.
“We think that billions of Muses in a network at scale will be able to get more done for people and businesses by working together,” Zuckerberg said last month on a call with analysts.
“We’d like to create a large-scale Muse network as quickly as possible.”

passages: SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space.
The Starmind satellites would primarily communicate using lasers to connect with other satellites, including SpaceX’s Starlink.
The company must also clear other regulatory hurdles.
SpaceX requested a waiver of existing FCC rules, which requires satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometers reenter Earth’s atmosphere within five years of completing those missions.
The company is interested in moving some of these retired satellites into other orbits around Earth or even around the sun, according to the FCC authorization document .

SpaceX faces a number of technical and economic challenges, including how to dramatically reduce the cost of manufacturing and launching satellites, cool processors in space, and even how to secure financing for chips that are destined for orbit.
The FCC has given SpaceX time to sort out these issues.
Under the approval, SpaceX has seven years to get its first operational satellite into orbit and 14 years to deploy the entire constellation.

extraction.body: SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space. The FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences. Amazon, which is building a competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink service, argued in its petition that the application lacked basic details and described it as a “lofty ambition rather than a real plan.” Despite that lack of detail, Amazon also said the proposal “risks real harm.” The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority. FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement that the action “opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.” Musk thanked Carr in a post on X , writing “Much appreciate. This will be a great asset to America and the world.” This initial regulatory approval doesn’t mean orbital data centers are imminent. SpaceX faces a number of technical and economic challenges, including how to dramatically reduce the cost of manufacturing and launching satellites, cool processors in space, and even how to secure financing for chips that are destined for orbit. The company must also clear other regulatory hurdles. The FCC has not yet approved SpaceX’s plans to handle orbital debris for satellites that would operate above 600 kilometers, for instance. SpaceX requested a waiver of existing FCC rules, which requires satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometers reenter Earth’s atmosphere within five years of completing those missions. The company is interested in moving some of these retired satellites into other orbits around Earth or even around the sun, according to the FCC authorization document . SpaceX has said it plans to deploy the satellites, known as Starmind, at altitudes ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers. The FCC’s approval gives SpaceX the authority to use radiofrequency communications to maintain contact with and control its orbital data centers from Earth if their primary communications systems fail. The Starmind satellites would primarily communicate using lasers to connect with other satellites, including SpaceX’s Starlink. The FCC has given SpaceX time to sort out these issues. Under the approval, SpaceX has seven years to get its first operational satellite into orbit and 14 years to deploy the entire constellation. extraction.body: The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approved Elon Musk’s plan for his company SpaceX to launch up to 1 million orbital data centers into space, citing a need to meet growing AI computing demand. FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement that “by moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment.” “This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home,” Carr continued. He added that “compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America’s leadership in” artificial intelligence. The approval gives SpaceX a 15-year permit to accomplish its goals of launching 1 million data centers. The firm must launch its first station into orbit by Nov. The FCC chair expressed on social media Wednesday that this was the first time the agency had authorized a permit for 1 million orbital data centers, which are set to be arranged in a constellation called “Starmind.” Musk responded to Carr’s post, writing, “Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world.” Data centers have quickly lost favor among Americans, with many cities across the country voting against approving projects or permits for the computing infrastructure in November’s midterm elections. Amid the growing dissatisfaction, Musk’s SpaceX and other tech firms began experimenting with launching orbital data centers that relied on solar power to fuel its computing. Musk stated earlier this year that putting data centers in space could also work as a potential solution to the rising energy demands of AI. Jared Isaacman, administrator of NASA, signaled his support for the idea in August, saying the move would “have immense benefits,” as companies could leverage solar energy to power data centers. “Let’s take our data centers, put them in Earth orbit, take advantage of that free fusion reactor that’s out there for us and use that to ensure we do win the … space race for sure, but the AI race, too,” Isaacman said in an interview with Vinay Simlot, Nexstar Media Group’s Washington, D.C., correspondent. SpaceX did not respond immediately to The Hill's request for comment.

sources.title: FCC Approves SpaceX Plan for 1 Million Satellites to Power Space-Based Data Centers
passages: The Federal Communications Commission has authorized SpaceX to deploy a constellation of up to 1 million satellites designed to operate as data centers in space, approving a proposal the company says could help meet rapidly growing demand for artificial intelligence computing.
SpaceX applied earlier this year to launch as many as 1 million orbital computing modules.
SpaceX has argued that orbital data centers could use near-constant solar power, potentially reducing operating and maintenance costs compared with facilities on Earth.
SpaceX followed a similar approach with Starlink: it sought approval for 42,000 satellites, while the network now has just over 11,000 in space.
SpaceX must begin deploying the satellites by November 2033, place at least 100,000 in orbit by November 2035, and deploy at least half of the authorized total by November 2038.
SpaceX’s proposal would move some computing capacity into orbit, where satellites could be powered by solar energy.
Satellite operators sometimes seek approval for more satellites than they ultimately plan to launch, giving them flexibility as designs and business plans change.
FCC Chair Brendan Carr dismissed that criticism in March, saying Amazon should focus on advancing its own launches and satellite network rather than questioning SpaceX’s deployment pace.
Amazon’s satellite unit, Leo, and other critics have questioned whether SpaceX could deploy all the satellites, arguing that completing the constellation could take centuries.

extraction.body: The Federal Communications Commission has authorized SpaceX to deploy a constellation of up to 1 million satellites designed to operate as data centers in space, approving a proposal the company says could help meet rapidly growing demand for artificial intelligence computing. SpaceX applied earlier this year to launch as many as 1 million orbital computing modules. The FCC said its approval of the proposed “Starmind” constellation would allow the company to develop technology intended to support AI workloads and strengthen U.S. leadership in space and artificial intelligence. SpaceX must begin deploying the satellites by November 2033, place at least 100,000 in orbit by November 2035, and deploy at least half of the authorized total by November 2038. SpaceX has argued that orbital data centers could use near-constant solar power, potentially reducing operating and maintenance costs compared with facilities on Earth. The company told the FCC that the system could improve energy and cost efficiency while reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial data centers. Data centers are a central part of the infrastructure behind artificial intelligence, but they require large amounts of electricity. SpaceX’s proposal would move some computing capacity into orbit, where satellites could be powered by solar energy. The scale of the plan, however, is uncertain. About 17,000 satellites are currently in orbit, and it is unclear whether SpaceX intends to deploy the full 1 million authorized for Starmind. Satellite operators sometimes seek approval for more satellites than they ultimately plan to launch, giving them flexibility as designs and business plans change. SpaceX followed a similar approach with Starlink: it sought approval for 42,000 satellites, while the network now has just over 11,000 in space. The Starmind proposal also depends in part on lower launch costs from Starship, SpaceX’s next-generation reusable rocket, which is still under development. The company’s ability to deploy a constellation on the proposed scale would therefore depend on the rocket’s progress and the pace of future launches. Amazon’s satellite unit, Leo, and other critics have questioned whether SpaceX could deploy all the satellites, arguing that completing the constellation could take centuries. FCC Chair Brendan Carr dismissed that criticism in March, saying Amazon should focus on advancing its own launches and satellite network rather than questioning SpaceX’s deployment pace. The FCC also approved SpaceX’s requests to add communications capabilities intended to back up the constellation’s optical network.

extraction.body: U.S. FCC Approves SpaceX Deployment of 1 Million Satellites for Space Data Centers SpaceX, the space company led by Elon Musk, has received approval from U.S. regulators to place up to 1 million satellites in Earth orbit to build artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. On November 25 (local time), the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said it had approved the launch and operation of satellites for SpaceX's space data center project, "Starmind." This is the first time U.S. regulators have approved the operation of a satellite constellation to build space data centers. The approval came about 10 months after SpaceX submitted its application in January. SpaceX plans to place satellites equipped with AI semiconductors in low Earth orbit and use electricity generated by solar power to process large volumes of data. Data processed in space will be transmitted to Earth via high-speed laser communications and the satellite network of Starlink, SpaceX's satellite internet service. CEO Musk unveiled plans to build space data centers while pursuing a merger between SpaceX and AI company xAI. The plan is based on the view that it could overcome challenges involved in securing the enormous amounts of electricity and water, as well as the land, needed to build data centers on the ground. Musk has previously predicted that space will become the least expensive place to operate AI data centers within the next two to three years. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said, "Data centers are essential for the United States to maintain its leadership in the field of superintelligence (SI)." He emphasized that the decision would combine the strengths of the U.S. space industry and advanced technology and help strengthen the country's economic leadership. Under the approval, SpaceX must deploy its first satellite by November 2033. It must then deploy 100,000 satellites by November 2035 and 500,000 by November 2038. The deadline for deploying the full constellation is November 2040. However, environmental concerns and technical challenges related to deploying satellites on such a large scale remain. Amazon, competitors, and the American Astronomical Society have raised concerns about the possibility of collisions between satellites, an increase in space debris, and interference with astronomical observations. Despite these objections, the FCC approved SpaceX's satellite constellation without conducting a separate additional environmental impact assessment. However, it deferred approval of SpaceX's request to move some satellites at the end of their operational lives to a separate orbit for disposal, rather than having them reenter the atmosphere, saying that it lacked sufficient information. © The Asia Business Daily. SpaceX, the space company led by Elon Musk, has received approval from U.S. regulators to place up to 1 million satellites in Earth orbit to build artificial intelligence (AI) data centers.

On November 25 (local time), the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said it had approved the launch and operation of satellites for SpaceX's space data center project, "Starmind." This is the first time U.S. regulators have approved the operation of a satellite constellation to build space data centers. The approval came about 10 months after SpaceX submitted its application in January.

SpaceX plans to place satellites equipped with AI semiconductors in low Earth orbit and use electricity generated by solar power to process large volumes of data. Data processed in space will be transmitted to Earth via high-speed laser communications and the satellite network of Starlink, SpaceX's satellite internet service.

CEO Musk unveiled plans to build space data centers while pursuing a merger between SpaceX and AI company xAI. The plan is based on the view that it could overcome challenges involved in securing the enormous amounts of electricity and water, as well as the land, needed to build data centers on the ground. Musk has previously predicted that space will become the least expensive place to operate AI data centers within the next two to three years.

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said, "Data centers are essential for the United States to maintain its leadership in the field of superintelligence (SI)." He emphasized that the decision would combine the strengths of the U.S. space industry and advanced technology and help strengthen the country's economic leadership.

Under the approval, SpaceX must deploy its first satellite by November 2033. It must then deploy 100,000 satellites by November 2035 and 500,000 by November 2038. The deadline for deploying the full constellation is November 2040.

However, environmental concerns and technical challenges related to deploying satellites on such a large scale remain. Amazon, competitors, and the American Astronomical Society have raised concerns about the possibility of collisions between satellites, an increase in space debris, and interference with astronomical observations.

Despite these objections, the FCC approved SpaceX's satellite constellation without conducting a separate additional environmental impact assessment. However, it deferred approval of SpaceX's request to move some satellites at the end of their operational lives to a separate orbit for disposal, rather than having them reenter the atmosphere, saying that it lacked sufficient information.

The FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences. Amazon, which is building a competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink service, argued in its petition that the application lacked basic details and described it as a “lofty ambition rather than a real plan.” Despite that lack of detail, Amazon also said the proposal “risks real harm.” The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority. FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement that the action “opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.” Musk thanked Carr in a post on X , writing “Much appreciate. This will be a great asset to America and the world.” This initial regulatory approval doesn’t mean orbital data centers are imminent. SpaceX faces a number of technical and economic challenges, including how to dramatically reduce the cost of manufacturing and launching satellites, cool processors in space, and even how to secure financing for chips that are destined for orbit. The company must also clear other regulatory hurdles. The FCC has not yet approved SpaceX’s plans to handle orbital debris for satellites that would operate above 600 kilometers, for instance. SpaceX requested a waiver of existing FCC rules, which requires satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometers reenter Earth’s atmosphere within five years of completing those missions. The company is interested in moving some of these retired satellites into other orbits around Earth or even around the sun, according to the FCC authorization document . SpaceX has said it plans to deploy the satellites, known as Starmind, at altitudes ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers. The FCC’s approval gives SpaceX the authority to use radiofrequency communications to maintain contact with and control its orbital data centers from Earth if their primary communications systems fail. The Starmind satellites would primarily communicate using lasers to connect with other satellites, including SpaceX’s Starlink. The FCC has given SpaceX time to sort out these issues. Under the approval, SpaceX has seven years to get its first operational satellite into orbit and 14 years to deploy the entire constellation. FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement that “by moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment.” “This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home,” Carr continued. He added that “compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America’s leadership in” artificial intelligence. The approval gives SpaceX a 15-year permit to accomplish its goals of launching 1 million data centers. The firm must launch its first station into orbit by Nov. SpaceX applied earlier this year to launch as many as 1 million orbital computing modules. The FCC said its approval of the proposed “Starmind” constellation would allow the company to develop technology intended to support AI workloads and strengthen U.S. leadership in space and artificial intelligence. SpaceX must begin deploying the satellites by November 2033, place at least 100,000 in orbit by November 2035, and deploy at least half of the authorized total by November 2038. SpaceX has argued that orbital data centers could use near-constant solar power, potentially reducing operating and maintenance costs compared with facilities on Earth. The company told the FCC that the system could improve energy and cost efficiency while reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial data centers. Data centers are a central part of the infrastructure behind artificial intelligence, but they require large amounts of electricity. SpaceX’s proposal would move some computing capacity into orbit, where satellites could be powered by solar energy. The scale of the plan, however, is uncertain. About 17,000 satellites are currently in orbit, and it is unclear whether SpaceX intends to deploy the full 1 million authorized for Starmind. SpaceX followed a similar approach with Starlink: it sought approval for 42,000 satellites, while the network now has just over 11,000 in space. The Starmind proposal also depends in part on lower launch costs from Starship, SpaceX’s next-generation reusable rocket, which is still under development. The company’s ability to deploy a constellation on the proposed scale would therefore depend on the rocket’s progress and the pace of future launches. Amazon’s satellite unit, Leo, and other critics have questioned whether SpaceX could deploy all the satellites, arguing that completing the constellation could take centuries. FCC Chair Brendan Carr dismissed that criticism in March, saying Amazon should focus on advancing its own launches and satellite network rather than questioning SpaceX’s deployment pace. The FCC also approved SpaceX’s requests to add communications capabilities intended to back up the constellation’s optical network.

On November 25 (local time), the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said it had approved the launch and operation of satellites for SpaceX's space data center project, "Starmind." This is the first time U.S. regulators have approved the operation of a satellite constellation to build space data centers. The approval came about 10 months after SpaceX submitted its application in January. SpaceX plans to place satellites equipped with AI semiconductors in low Earth orbit and use electricity generated by solar power to process large volumes of data. Data processed in space will be transmitted to Earth via high-speed laser communications and the satellite network of Starlink, SpaceX's satellite internet service. CEO Musk unveiled plans to build space data centers while pursuing a merger between SpaceX and AI company xAI. The plan is based on the view that it could overcome challenges involved in securing the enormous amounts of electricity and water, as well as the land, needed to build data centers on the ground. Musk has previously predicted that space will become the least expensive place to operate AI data centers within the next two to three years. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said, "Data centers are essential for the United States to maintain its leadership in the field of superintelligence (SI)." He emphasized that the decision would combine the strengths of the U.S. space industry and advanced technology and help strengthen the country's economic leadership. Under the approval, SpaceX must deploy its first satellite by November 2033. It must then deploy 100,000 satellites by November 2035 and 500,000 by November 2038. The deadline for deploying the full constellation is November 2040. However, environmental concerns and technical challenges related to deploying satellites on such a large scale remain. Amazon, competitors, and the American Astronomical Society have raised concerns about the possibility of collisions between satellites, an increase in space debris, and interference with astronomical observations. Despite these objections, the FCC approved SpaceX's satellite constellation without conducting a separate additional environmental impact assessment. To reduce the amount of lead dust released into surrounding areas and the environment, the Army said it took several additional precautions as part of today’s detonation.

The Iowa ammunition plant housed 68 barrels containing about 9,700 pounds of lead azide, representing the country’s remaining stockpile. However, the decision was made to detonate the stockpile after an inspection by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms (ATF) discovered “significant crystallization on the exterior of the barrels” last March. Ahead of today’s detonation, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) supported a recommended, but voluntary, temporary relocation of all the residents of Middletown and immediate surrounding areas that began yesterday. To reduce the amount of lead dust released into surrounding areas and the environment, the Army said it took several additional precautions as part of today’s detonation. Walls made of four 16,000-gallon water tanks were installed to capture lead particulate, while the aging earth-covered magazines holding the barrels were covered with tarps and lead containment screens and flooded with foam.

extraction.body: Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle announced what he described as a major success following the controlled detonation of nearly five tons of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, saying the operation eliminated the threat of an uncontrolled spontaneous explosion. His November 25 statement praised the soldiers involved, credited President Donald Trump and his administration with coordinating a large federal response, and highlighted initial environmental monitoring results showing no detected readings above zero. The Army’s controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success. The threat of an uncontrolled spontaneous detonation has been eliminated. Thank you to President Trump and his administration for mobilizing an unprecedented whole of government approach to fix this problem once and for all tor the great people of Iowa. To the people of Iowa, we are with you all the way. The operation addressed a serious explosives hazard at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The Army had identified approximately 68 deteriorating drums containing more than 9,700 pounds of lead azide. The material had developed crystallized deposits that made the containers increasingly dangerous to handle, with the potential for an accidental explosion from friction, vibration, heat or shock. The Army said the material had been deteriorating over approximately eight months. The decision was made to conduct an in-place controlled detonation using military explosive ordnance disposal personnel. The Army said temperature fluctuations and the increasingly unstable condition of the material made it important to eliminate the explosive hazard before an uncontrolled detonation occurred. The Army’s mitigation plan involved several federal agencies, including the Environmental Protection Agency, Federal Emergency Management Agency, Department of Health and Human Services and Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. The response included environmental modeling, air monitoring, physical barriers, water-based containment measures, foam and gel materials designed to limit the movement of lead-containing particles. The recommended relocation zone covered Middletown and a five-mile area extending southwest of the installation. Telle’s praise of the soldiers involved reflects the Army’s reliance on specialized explosive ordnance disposal personnel. The work required personnel to execute a carefully coordinated detonation while federal partners monitored the surrounding environment and implemented measures intended to reduce potential contamination. His statement also specifically credits Trump and the administration for mobilizing what he called an unprecedented whole-of-government approach. The operation involved military personnel, environmental regulators, emergency-management officials, public-health agencies and state and local authorities. The environmental monitoring results became an important part of the Army’s public assessment following the explosion. On November 25, the EPA reported that its real-time air monitors showed zero detection of airborne lead approximately one hour after the controlled detonation. The agency said its monitoring equipment continued collecting data throughout the operation. The EPA also reported that it had collected approximately 1,200 samples of air, land, dust and water before the detonation. The agency said further monitoring would continue after the operation, meaning the initial zero readings should not be interpreted as a final determination that every surrounding surface or environmental medium is free of lead contamination. The distinction matters because lead exposure can occur through more than airborne inhalation. Lead-containing particles can settle on soil, surfaces and other materials, creating potential exposure pathways after an event. State public-health guidance specifically warned residents about airborne particles and dust that could be carried indoors on clothing and shoes. Telle’s statement that the spontaneous explosion threat has been eliminated addresses the immediate explosive hazard the Army set out to resolve. It does not, by itself, establish that all environmental and public-health questions have been resolved. Those issues remain subject to post-detonation monitoring, testing and public reporting by the responsible agencies. The operation also raises longer-term questions about the Army’s handling and monitoring of hazardous materials stored at military installations. The Army’s own account described the material as having deteriorated over several months, while federal officials had to coordinate an emergency disposal effort involving a substantial quantity of explosive material. The incident has brought renewed attention to ammunition storage, explosives safety and the environmental responsibilities associated with military facilities. Telle said the Army would continue watching the EPA sensor network and provide additional public updates throughout the day. His statement marks the administration’s initial assessment of the operation as a success, while continued environmental sampling will determine whether further protective measures or cleanup work are necessary.

extraction.body: Published Nov. 25, 2026, 12:51 p.m. ET | Updated Nov. 25, 2026 MIDDLETOWN, Iowa — The U.S. Army carried out a controlled, mitigated detonation of 68 barrels of deteriorated lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Wednesday morning, with federal and state officials reporting a complete detonation and no initial detection of airborne lead across the region. The detonation was executed at 9 a.m. CT by U.S. Army Sustainment Command following days of interagency preparation, court clearances and voluntary evacuations for residents within a five-mile area southwest of the plant along the projected plume path. President Donald Trump praised the operation in a post on Truth Social shortly after the blast. “Early reports from Iowa are that the Army’s mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations,” Trump wrote. During a live interagency briefing following the detonation, Army Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, commanding general of U.S. Army Sustainment Command, said explosive ordnance disposal teams eliminated the threat without any secondary explosions, debris being thrown beyond the containment area or infrastructure damage. “Well, I would characterize the controlled detonation as exceeding expectations,” Shirley said. “Every indication is that all of the munitions that were employed absolutely reduced the lead azide threat. passages: Published Nov. 25, 2026, 12:51 p.m. ET | Updated Nov. 25, 2026

MIDDLETOWN, Iowa — The U.S. Army carried out a controlled, mitigated detonation of 68 barrels of deteriorated lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Wednesday morning, with federal and state officials reporting a complete detonation and no initial detection of airborne lead across the region.

The detonation was executed at 9 a.m. CT by U.S. Army Sustainment Command following days of interagency preparation, court clearances and voluntary evacuations for residents within a five-mile area southwest of the plant along the projected plume path.
President Donald Trump praised the operation in a post on Truth Social shortly after the blast.
“Early reports from Iowa are that the Army’s mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations,” Trump wrote.

During a live interagency briefing following the detonation, Army Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, commanding general of U.S. Army Sustainment Command, said explosive ordnance disposal teams eliminated the threat without any secondary explosions, debris being thrown beyond the containment area or infrastructure damage.

“Well, I would characterize the controlled detonation as exceeding expectations,” Shirley said. “Every indication is that all of the munitions that were employed absolutely reduced the lead azide threat. As we saw in the immediate aftermath through overhead coverage, all of the lead azide barrels were definitively removed.”

Shirley said crews applied more than 3,600 gallons of aqueous foam via fire trucks alongside continuous mister systems, two-story sand barriers and gel blocks to suppress dust and contain lead particles.

“I believe absolutely that we reduced as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” Shirley said.

Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives Director Robert Cekada said the roughly 10,000-pound stockpile had been consolidated and moved to earth-covered magazines at the Iowa plant in 2009. By March 2026, inspectors discovered dangerous crystallization on the barrels, lids and bolts, prompting the Trump administration to assemble a multi-agency mitigation plan.

“I absolutely can confirm that those mitigation efforts and the design plan laid out by the EOD personnel ensured that the blast drove the explosion into the ground and followed a blast channel that was designed to go down the right path to minimize any sort of dispersion of lead into the atmosphere—100% as planned,” Cekada said.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency announced on X that its continuous, real-time air monitors across the region showed “ZERO detection of airborne lead throughout the region” immediately following the blast, noting that monitoring equipment never stopped collecting data during the event.
FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton also confirmed the blast went as planned.

“We believe that is a successful detonation,” Hamilton said . “The elements which were ultimately connected to explosives and set for a time charge, we believe they fully ignited — so that’s a fully and complete successful detonation.”
Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds said state officials remain in close contact with federal teams as the State Emergency Operations Center tracks incoming data.

“Initial feedback from our state experts and federal partners is that the detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant was successful,” Reynolds wrote on X . “We remain in close contact with authorities on the ground, while state agencies continue to monitor incoming data from the State Emergency Operations Center. We will keep Iowans informed as details become available.”

In neighboring Missouri, which liess within the Army’s projected southwest plume path, Gov. Mike Kehoe said state agencies are continuing to track air and environmental data after activating Missouri’s emergency operations center ahead of the blast.

“Initial analysis shared with us by federal partners and Iowa Homeland Security and Emergency Management indicates that the mitigation measures appear to have been successful and the explosion was well-contained,” Kehoe wrote on X . “Our state agencies will continue monitoring efforts.”

Assistant Secretary of the Army for Installations, Energy and Environment Jordan Gillis said officials were forced to weigh a scheduled, contained operation against the risk of an accidental blast as the stockpiled material degraded.

“The choice that we faced here was between a spontaneous, uncontrolled detonation of dangerous material, or a controlled detonation where we could choose the time and place to optimize the conditions and deliver the best result, not just for our operations but for the safety of the public and the surrounding communities,” Gillis said.

Ahead of the detonation, the Army deployed physical containment measures—including two-story sand barriers, aqueous foam, gel blocks and water misters—to suppress dust and limit the spread of lead particles beyond the installation. Gillis said those safeguards were designed to protect both public health and the surrounding environment while simplifying post-blast remediation.

“An example is the aqueous foam and the gel blocks that we are deploying to minimize lead particulate release from the controlled detonation are the same things that are going to ease our environmental cleanup,” Gillis said. “By capturing the lead particles, we’re not only ensuring public health and safety, but we are maintaining our environmental responsibilities and leaving behind a clean site for continued plant operations and a cleaner off-site for the health and benefit of the public.”
EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said federal teams are immediately shifting to post-blast environmental testing and any needed cleanup.

“We’re going to immediately be deploying on the ground manpower, soil and water sampling — any remediation efforts that are necessary in the immediate hours that follow the controlled detonation that just finished,” Zeldin said .

The EPA said roughly 300 agency employees and contractors are deployed across Iowa and surrounding states after collecting 1,216 baseline samples—including 650 soil, 297 dust, 210 water and 59 air samples—at schools, churches, playgrounds and homes prior to Wednesday’s operation. The agency is coordinating its testing with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to protect vulnerable groups, including infants, young children and pregnant women.

“It is the top priority of this agency to ensure impacted residents can swiftly be and feel safe and comfortable in their homes, at their schools, in recreational spaces, and in their community,” Tom Croci, EPA associate administrator for national security and operations coordination said .

Officials had previously advised residents near the evacuation zone to shelter in place, close all windows and doors, set heating systems to recirculation mode, keep children and pets indoors and cover livestock feed, water sources and crops. The EPA also encouraged residents to wipe down outdoor surfaces children touch—such as play sets, railings and windowsills—with a wet cloth.
Real-time air monitoring and post-detonation sampling results are being posted publicly by the EPA as data is verified.

MIDDLETOWN, IA — The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) reported Wednesday that initial air monitoring showed no detections of airborne lead following the controlled detonation of crystallized lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. According to the EPA, all of the agency’s real-time air monitors throughout the region reported zero detections of airborne lead one hour after the detonation. The agency said its monitors continued collecting data throughout the event. Approximately 300 EPA employees and contractors are positioned in the area to conduct environmental monitoring, collect air, land and water samples, and carry out remediation efforts if necessary. Before the detonation, the EPA collected approximately 1,200 samples of air, land, dust and water to establish baseline environmental conditions, including samples from surrounding agricultural operations. “We stand ready to provide any and all necessary support.” Iowa Army Ammunition Plant | Middletown, Iowa Monitoring data provided by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins also announced Wednesday that initial assessments indicated the controlled mitigation efforts were successful. USDA has more than 1,900 employees based in Iowa and more than 140 offices within a 100-mile radius of the facility. Department personnel will continue assisting farmers and ranchers in the potentially affected area. USDA Under Secretary for Farm Production and Conservation Richard Fordyce has been deployed to Iowa to coordinate efforts with federal, state and local government partners. Under Secretary for Rural Development Glen Smith has also been assisting with coordination. USDA stated that the food supply remains safe and that federal agencies have protocols in place to prevent lead and other heavy metals from entering the food supply chain. The initial air monitoring results are preliminary and do not represent a completed assessment of potential environmental impacts. The Army has used lead azide in munitions for nearly a century but began transitioning away from the material around 15 years ago because it can be difficult to transport and store. The Iowa ammunition plant housed 68 barrels containing about 9,700 pounds of lead azide, representing the country’s remaining stockpile. However, the decision was made to detonate the stockpile after an inspection by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms (ATF) discovered “significant crystallization on the exterior of the barrels” last March. Ahead of today’s detonation, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) supported a recommended, but voluntary, temporary relocation of all the residents of Middletown and immediate surrounding areas that began yesterday. To reduce the amount of lead dust released into surrounding areas and the environment, the Army said it took several additional precautions as part of today’s detonation. Walls made of four 16,000-gallon water tanks were installed to capture lead particulate, while the aging earth-covered magazines holding the barrels were covered with tarps and lead containment screens and flooded with foam.
