extraction.body: Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle announced what he described as a major success following the controlled detonation of nearly five tons of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, saying the operation eliminated the threat of an uncontrolled spontaneous explosion. His November 25 statement praised the soldiers involved, credited President Donald Trump and his administration with coordinating a large federal response, and highlighted initial environmental monitoring results showing no detected readings above zero. The Army’s controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success. The threat of an uncontrolled spontaneous detonation has been eliminated. Thank you to President Trump and his administration for mobilizing an unprecedented whole of government approach to fix this problem once and for all tor the great people of Iowa. To the people of Iowa, we are with you all the way. The operation addressed a serious explosives hazard at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The Army had identified approximately 68 deteriorating drums containing more than 9,700 pounds of lead azide. The material had developed crystallized deposits that made the containers increasingly dangerous to handle, with the potential for an accidental explosion from friction, vibration, heat or shock. The Army said the material had been deteriorating over approximately eight months. The decision was made to conduct an in-place controlled detonation using military explosive ordnance disposal personnel. The Army said temperature fluctuations and the increasingly unstable condition of the material made it important to eliminate the explosive hazard before an uncontrolled detonation occurred. The Army’s mitigation plan involved several federal agencies, including the Environmental Protection Agency, Federal Emergency Management Agency, Department of Health and Human Services and Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. The response included environmental modeling, air monitoring, physical barriers, water-based containment measures, foam and gel materials designed to limit the movement of lead-containing particles. The recommended relocation zone covered Middletown and a five-mile area extending southwest of the installation. Telle’s praise of the soldiers involved reflects the Army’s reliance on specialized explosive ordnance disposal personnel. The work required personnel to execute a carefully coordinated detonation while federal partners monitored the surrounding environment and implemented measures intended to reduce potential contamination. His statement also specifically credits Trump and the administration for mobilizing what he called an unprecedented whole-of-government approach. The operation involved military personnel, environmental regulators, emergency-management officials, public-health agencies and state and local authorities. The environmental monitoring results became an important part of the Army’s public assessment following the explosion. On November 25, the EPA reported that its real-time air monitors showed zero detection of airborne lead approximately one hour after the controlled detonation. The agency said its monitoring equipment continued collecting data throughout the operation. The EPA also reported that it had collected approximately 1,200 samples of air, land, dust and water before the detonation. The agency said further monitoring would continue after the operation, meaning the initial zero readings should not be interpreted as a final determination that every surrounding surface or environmental medium is free of lead contamination. The distinction matters because lead exposure can occur through more than airborne inhalation. Lead-containing particles can settle on soil, surfaces and other materials, creating potential exposure pathways after an event. State public-health guidance specifically warned residents about airborne particles and dust that could be carried indoors on clothing and shoes. Telle’s statement that the spontaneous explosion threat has been eliminated addresses the immediate explosive hazard the Army set out to resolve. It does not, by itself, establish that all environmental and public-health questions have been resolved. Those issues remain subject to post-detonation monitoring, testing and public reporting by the responsible agencies. The operation also raises longer-term questions about the Army’s handling and monitoring of hazardous materials stored at military installations. The Army’s own account described the material as having deteriorated over several months, while federal officials had to coordinate an emergency disposal effort involving a substantial quantity of explosive material. The incident has brought renewed attention to ammunition storage, explosives safety and the environmental responsibilities associated with military facilities. Telle said the Army would continue watching the EPA sensor network and provide additional public updates throughout the day. His statement marks the administration’s initial assessment of the operation as a success, while continued environmental sampling will determine whether further protective measures or cleanup work are necessary.

extraction.body: Published Nov. 25, 2026, 12:51 p.m. ET | Updated Nov. 25, 2026 MIDDLETOWN, Iowa — The U.S. Army carried out a controlled, mitigated detonation of 68 barrels of deteriorated lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Wednesday morning, with federal and state officials reporting a complete detonation and no initial detection of airborne lead across the region. The detonation was executed at 9 a.m. CT by U.S. Army Sustainment Command following days of interagency preparation, court clearances and voluntary evacuations for residents within a five-mile area southwest of the plant along the projected plume path. President Donald Trump praised the operation in a post on Truth Social shortly after the blast. “Early reports from Iowa are that the Army’s mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations,” Trump wrote. During a live interagency briefing following the detonation, Army Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, commanding general of U.S. Army Sustainment Command, said explosive ordnance disposal teams eliminated the threat without any secondary explosions, debris being thrown beyond the containment area or infrastructure damage. “Well, I would characterize the controlled detonation as exceeding expectations,” Shirley said. “Every indication is that all of the munitions that were employed absolutely reduced the lead azide threat. As we saw in the immediate aftermath through overhead coverage, all of the lead azide barrels were definitively removed.” Shirley said crews applied more than 3,600 gallons of aqueous foam via fire trucks alongside continuous mister systems, two-story sand barriers and gel blocks to suppress dust and contain lead particles. “I believe absolutely that we reduced as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” Shirley said. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives Director Robert Cekada said the roughly 10,000-pound stockpile had been consolidated and moved to earth-covered magazines at the Iowa plant in 2009. By March 2026, inspectors discovered dangerous crystallization on the barrels, lids and bolts, prompting the Trump administration to assemble a multi-agency mitigation plan. “I absolutely can confirm that those mitigation efforts and the design plan laid out by the EOD personnel ensured that the blast drove the explosion into the ground and followed a blast channel that was designed to go down the right path to minimize any sort of dispersion of lead into the atmosphere—100% as planned,” Cekada said. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency announced on X that its continuous, real-time air monitors across the region showed “ZERO detection of airborne lead throughout the region” immediately following the blast, noting that monitoring equipment never stopped collecting data during the event. FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton also confirmed the blast went as planned. “We believe that is a successful detonation,” Hamilton said . “The elements which were ultimately connected to explosives and set for a time charge, we believe they fully ignited — so that’s a fully and complete successful detonation.” Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds said state officials remain in close contact with federal teams as the State Emergency Operations Center tracks incoming data. “Initial feedback from our state experts and federal partners is that the detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant was successful,” Reynolds wrote on X . “We remain in close contact with authorities on the ground, while state agencies continue to monitor incoming data from the State Emergency Operations Center. We will keep Iowans informed as details become available.” In neighboring Missouri, which liess within the Army’s projected southwest plume path, Gov. Mike Kehoe said state agencies are continuing to track air and environmental data after activating Missouri’s emergency operations center ahead of the blast. “Initial analysis shared with us by federal partners and Iowa Homeland Security and Emergency Management indicates that the mitigation measures appear to have been successful and the explosion was well-contained,” Kehoe wrote on X . “Our state agencies will continue monitoring efforts.” Assistant Secretary of the Army for Installations, Energy and Environment Jordan Gillis said officials were forced to weigh a scheduled, contained operation against the risk of an accidental blast as the stockpiled material degraded. “The choice that we faced here was between a spontaneous, uncontrolled detonation of dangerous material, or a controlled detonation where we could choose the time and place to optimize the conditions and deliver the best result, not just for our operations but for the safety of the public and the surrounding communities,” Gillis said. MIDDLETOWN, Iowa — The U.S. Army carried out a controlled, mitigated detonation of 68 barrels of deteriorated lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Wednesday morning, with federal and state officials reporting a complete detonation and no initial detection of airborne lead across the region.

The detonation was executed at 9 a.m. CT by U.S. Army Sustainment Command following days of interagency preparation, court clearances and voluntary evacuations for residents within a five-mile area southwest of the plant along the projected plume path.
President Donald Trump praised the operation in a post on Truth Social shortly after the blast.
“Early reports from Iowa are that the Army’s mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations,” Trump wrote.

During a live interagency briefing following the detonation, Army Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, commanding general of U.S. Army Sustainment Command, said explosive ordnance disposal teams eliminated the threat without any secondary explosions, debris being thrown beyond the containment area or infrastructure damage.

“Well, I would characterize the controlled detonation as exceeding expectations,” Shirley said. “Every indication is that all of the munitions that were employed absolutely reduced the lead azide threat. As we saw in the immediate aftermath through overhead coverage, all of the lead azide barrels were definitively removed.”

Shirley said crews applied more than 3,600 gallons of aqueous foam via fire trucks alongside continuous mister systems, two-story sand barriers and gel blocks to suppress dust and contain lead particles.

“I believe absolutely that we reduced as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” Shirley said.

Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives Director Robert Cekada said the roughly 10,000-pound stockpile had been consolidated and moved to earth-covered magazines at the Iowa plant in 2009. By March 2026, inspectors discovered dangerous crystallization on the barrels, lids and bolts, prompting the Trump administration to assemble a multi-agency mitigation plan.

“I absolutely can confirm that those mitigation efforts and the design plan laid out by the EOD personnel ensured that the blast drove the explosion into the ground and followed a blast channel that was designed to go down the right path to minimize any sort of dispersion of lead into the atmosphere—100% as planned,” Cekada said.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency announced on X that its continuous, real-time air monitors across the region showed “ZERO detection of airborne lead throughout the region” immediately following the blast, noting that monitoring equipment never stopped collecting data during the event.
FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton also confirmed the blast went as planned.

“We believe that is a successful detonation,” Hamilton said . “The elements which were ultimately connected to explosives and set for a time charge, we believe they fully ignited — so that’s a fully and complete successful detonation.”
Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds said state officials remain in close contact with federal teams as the State Emergency Operations Center tracks incoming data.

“Initial feedback from our state experts and federal partners is that the detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant was successful,” Reynolds wrote on X . “We remain in close contact with authorities on the ground, while state agencies continue to monitor incoming data from the State Emergency Operations Center. We will keep Iowans informed as details become available.”

In neighboring Missouri, which liess within the Army’s projected southwest plume path, Gov. Mike Kehoe said state agencies are continuing to track air and environmental data after activating Missouri’s emergency operations center ahead of the blast.

“Initial analysis shared with us by federal partners and Iowa Homeland Security and Emergency Management indicates that the mitigation measures appear to have been successful and the explosion was well-contained,” Kehoe wrote on X . “Our state agencies will continue monitoring efforts.”

Assistant Secretary of the Army for Installations, Energy and Environment Jordan Gillis said officials were forced to weigh a scheduled, contained operation against the risk of an accidental blast as the stockpiled material degraded.

“The choice that we faced here was between a spontaneous, uncontrolled detonation of dangerous material, or a controlled detonation where we could choose the time and place to optimize the conditions and deliver the best result, not just for our operations but for the safety of the public and the surrounding communities,” Gillis said.

Ahead of the detonation, the Army deployed physical containment measures—including two-story sand barriers, aqueous foam, gel blocks and water misters—to suppress dust and limit the spread of lead particles beyond the installation. Gillis said those safeguards were designed to protect both public health and the surrounding environment while simplifying post-blast remediation.

“An example is the aqueous foam and the gel blocks that we are deploying to minimize lead particulate release from the controlled detonation are the same things that are going to ease our environmental cleanup,” Gillis said. “By capturing the lead particles, we’re not only ensuring public health and safety, but we are maintaining our environmental responsibilities and leaving behind a clean site for continued plant operations and a cleaner off-site for the health and benefit of the public.”
EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said federal teams are immediately shifting to post-blast environmental testing and any needed cleanup.

“We’re going to immediately be deploying on the ground manpower, soil and water sampling — any remediation efforts that are necessary in the immediate hours that follow the controlled detonation that just finished,” Zeldin said .

The EPA said roughly 300 agency employees and contractors are deployed across Iowa and surrounding states after collecting 1,216 baseline samples—including 650 soil, 297 dust, 210 water and 59 air samples—at schools, churches, playgrounds and homes prior to Wednesday’s operation. The agency is coordinating its testing with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to protect vulnerable groups, including infants, young children and pregnant women.

“It is the top priority of this agency to ensure impacted residents can swiftly be and feel safe and comfortable in their homes, at their schools, in recreational spaces, and in their community,” Tom Croci, EPA associate administrator for national security and operations coordination said .

Officials had previously advised residents near the evacuation zone to shelter in place, close all windows and doors, set heating systems to recirculation mode, keep children and pets indoors and cover livestock feed, water sources and crops. The EPA also encouraged residents to wipe down outdoor surfaces children touch—such as play sets, railings and windowsills—with a wet cloth.
Real-time air monitoring and post-detonation sampling results are being posted publicly by the EPA as data is verified.

BEIJING, Nov 11 (Reuters) - A Chinese university with deep ties to the People's Liberation Army bought Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips last month despite being on a US export blacklist, procurement records show, highlighting gaps in Washington's efforts to curb China's access to advanced technology. The findings come as Nvidia and its CEO Jensen Huang face mounting scrutiny in Washington over his lobbying for looser restrictions on sales ‌of AI chips to China, following reports alleging he was targeted by a Chinese spying operation. Huang has argued that continued US sales to China would preserve American technological leadership and keep Chinese customers reliant on US technology. ‌But some US lawmakers say access to Nvidia's most powerful AI chips can speed China's development of AI systems for weapons design, intelligence analysis and military modernisation. Both Democrats and Republicans in Congress have urged stronger controls on China's access to advanced AI chips, such as chip-tracking requirements and greater congressional oversight ​of exports. Three Republican congressional committee chairmen have requested a briefing with Huang on November 18 over his reported contacts with an alleged Chinese intelligence operative. Northwestern Polytechnical University bought two H200 chips last month for 874,700 yuan ($123,000), according to an October 21 procurement record on its website. Northwestern is a member of the "Seven Sons of National Defense" group of Chinese universities under U.S. sanctions and with a history of conducting defence-related research for Beijing. The chips were purchased for its management school from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia, the record shows. The H200 is among Nvidia's most capable chips for training and running advanced AI systems and is subject to US export licence approvals, which are normally denied for blacklisted institutions such as Northwestern Polytechnical. Northwestern Polytechnical also bought access this year to ‌H200 chips and other powerful Nvidia AI processors through five contracts for rented computing capacity ⁠from Chinese companies, procurement records show. Reuters is reporting the chip purchases and computing contracts for the first time. Northwestern Polytechnical, Nvidia and the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, which oversees export controls, did not respond to requests for comment. Reuters could not determine contact details for Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology. Based in the northwestern city of Xian, Northwestern Polytechnical conducts research related ⁠to military aircraft, missiles and satellites. The US Commerce Department added the university to its trade blacklist, known as the Entity List, in 2001 over its alleged involvement in missile-proliferation activities and military research. It tightened the restrictions in 2019, making licences for exports of controlled US technology to the university subject to a policy of denial in most circumstances. Northwestern Polytechnical's purchases show how Chinese institutions with military ties continue to obtain US AI computing power through domestic suppliers, either by buying chips outright or renting access to servers containing them. A Reuters review of ​26 ​Chinese procurement and corporate records from this year found universities and research institutions buying US-restricted Nvidia chips or renting access to Nvidia-powered computing services ​that use such chips through domestic suppliers. Several had close links to China's defence industry ‌or military research. The universities named in the records did not respond to requests for comment. US President Donald Trump's administration began allowing some H200 exports to China on a case-by-case basis in January. But that policy did not lift the separate restrictions applying to Entity List organisations such as Northwestern Polytechnical. The January licensing rules also require safeguards to prevent blacklisted entities and military end-users from remotely accessing chips exported under the policy, which covers H200 processors and less advanced models. In addition to the management school's outright purchase of the two H200 chips, procurement records show the university's cybersecurity school awarded two seven-month contracts in January for access to servers containing eight H200 chips each. The contracts, worth 441,700 yuan and 441,000 yuan, covered fine-tuning AI models and reinforcement-learning training. It also rented access to servers containing eight Nvidia A100 chips and eight A800 chips. The A100 and A800 are banned from export to all Chinese entities, though the H200 is the most advanced of those cited in Northwestern Polytechnical's ‌procurement records. In April, another university institute bought computing services requiring at least 24 A100 chips in a 375,000 yuan contract for structural and ​fluid-dynamics simulations. The awards went to several little-known Chinese technology suppliers. The records offered scant information about where the processors originated or where the rented servers ​operated. Under Chinese law, public procurement agencies must verify that suppliers can fulfil orders before announcing winning bidders and signing ​contracts. The procurement records show a wider market for restricted Nvidia AI chips and computing services at Chinese universities. Shenzhen University bought three H100 processors, another high-end Nvidia AI chip banned by the ‌US, for 769,800 yuan in September. Wuhan University of Technology bought a server containing an ​H100 chip for 355,000 yuan in June and four A100 chips ​in a separate 344,000 yuan purchase, the records show. Beihang University, another of the Seven Sons of National Defense universities, bought four A800 processors for 489,000 yuan in April. Beihang has close ties to China's aerospace and defence industries and conducts research for military aviation and space programmes. Two government procurement announcements in July and September named suppliers selected to provide computing services using Nvidia H800 and A800 chips restricted from export to China to the University of ​Chinese Academy of Sciences. One listed H800 access at 10 yuan per chip-hour. A separate ‌January procurement award named a supplier of six A100 chips worth 484,800 yuan for a Shenzhen-based public institution. Reuters has previously reported that Chinese institutions acquired restricted Nvidia chips embedded in servers made by Super Micro ​Computer, Dell and Gigabyte through domestic resellers. Reuters has also documented an underground market in China for restricted Nvidia chips sourced from overseas inventories and third-country intermediaries. Last week, Reuters reported that small quantities of H200 ​chips had reached China through indirect routes while Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports. (Reporting by Eduardo Baptista; Editing by Jamie Freed)

Shenzhen University bought three H100 processors, another high-end Nvidia AI chip banned by the ‌US, for 769,800 yuan in September.
Wuhan University of Technology bought a server containing an ​H100 chip for 355,000 yuan in June and four A100 chips ​in a separate 344,000 yuan purchase, the records show.

A Reuters review of ​26 ​Chinese procurement and corporate records from this year found universities and research institutions buying US-restricted Nvidia chips or renting access to Nvidia-powered computing services ​that use such chips through domestic suppliers.
It also rented access to servers containing eight Nvidia A100 chips and eight A800 chips.
The A100 and A800 are banned from export to all Chinese entities, though the H200 is the most advanced of those cited in Northwestern Polytechnical's ‌procurement records.

The US Commerce Department added the university to its trade blacklist, known as the Entity List, in 2001 over its alleged involvement in missile-proliferation activities and military research.

extraction.body: A Chinese defence-linked university bought two H200 chips last month, as scrutiny grows over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged spy for Beijing. A Chinese university with ties to the army bought Nvidia’s powerful H200 AI chips last month despite being on a US export blacklist. Northwestern Polytechnical University, a member of China’s “Seven Sons of National Defense” group of elite defence-focused universities, bought two H200 chips last month for 874,700 yuan ($123,000), according to an October 21 procurement record on its website, the Reuters news agency reports. The chips were bought for its management school from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia, the record showed. The Reuters investigation comes as Nvidia and its CEO Jensen Huang face mounting scrutiny in Washington, DC, over his lobbying for looser ⁠⁠restrictions on sales of AI chips to China, following reports alleging he was targeted by a Chinese spying operation. The H200 is among Nvidia’s most capable chips for training and running advanced AI systems and is subject to US export licence approvals, which are normally denied for blacklisted institutions such as Northwestern Polytechnical. Northwestern Polytechnical also bought access this year to H200 ‌‌chips and other powerful Nvidia AI processors through five contracts for rented computing capacity from Chinese companies, procurement records show. Nvidia CEO Huang has argued that continued US sales to China would preserve US technological leadership and keep Chinese customers reliant on its technology. However, some US lawmakers say access to Nvidia’s most powerful AI chips can speed China’s development of AI systems for weapons design, intelligence analysis and military modernisation. Based in the northwestern city of Xi’an, Northwestern Polytechnical conducts research related to military aircraft, missiles and satellites. Washington’s Department of Commerce added the university to its trade blacklist, known as the Entity List, in 2001 over the institute’s alleged involvement in missile-proliferation activities, and its military research. Washington tightened the restrictions in 2019, making licences for exporting controlled US technology to the university subject to a policy of denial in most circumstances. Northwestern Polytechnical’s purchases show how Chinese institutions with military ties continue to obtain US AI computing power through domestic suppliers, either by buying chips outright or renting access to servers containing them. A Reuters review of 26 Chinese procurement and corporate records from this year found universities and research institutions buying US-restricted Nvidia chips or renting access to Nvidia-powered computing services ⁠⁠that use such chips through domestic suppliers. Several had close links to China’s defence industry or military research. US President Donald Trump’s administration began allowing some H200 exports to China on a case-by-case basis in January. But that policy did not lift the separate restrictions applying to Entity List organisations such as Northwestern Polytechnical. Both Democrats and Republicans in the US Congress have urged stronger controls on China’s access to advanced AI ⁠⁠chips, such as chip-tracking requirements, and greater congressional oversight of exports. This comes at a time of increased pressure on Nvidia’s Huang. Republican US Senator Kevin Cramer from the Senate Banking Committee called on Huang to step down as CEO after his intimate relationship with Alice Huang, accused of working for Chinese intelligence, plunged the company into crisis. “The potential for extortion is so tremendous that something as sensitive as Nvidia chips, I ⁠⁠just think he’s got to go,” Cramer told Politico late on Tuesday. Three Republican congressional committee chairmen have requested a briefing with Huang on November 18 over his reported contacts with the alleged Chinese intelligence operative. Jensen Huang – who cofounded Nvidia, the world’s second-most valuable company after Apple, more than three decades ago – admitted on Sunday to being unfaithful to his wife, but the company said it has no reason to believe US national security or confidential information has been compromised. Nvidia’s board announced an independent investigation on Sunday into whether the 63-year-old Taiwan-US dual national had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation after media reports linking him to Alice Huang, a former executive at a Singapore-based data centre company.

BEIJING, Nov 11 (Reuters) - A Chinese university with deep ties to the People's Liberation Army bought Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips last month despite being on a US export blacklist, procurement records show, highlighting gaps in Washington's efforts to curb China's access to advanced technology. The findings come as Nvidia and its CEO Jensen Huang face mounting scrutiny in Washington over his lobbying for looser restrictions on sales ‌of AI chips to China, following reports alleging he was targeted by a Chinese spying operation. Huang has argued that continued US sales to China would preserve American technological leadership and keep Chinese customers reliant on US technology. ‌But some US lawmakers say access to Nvidia's most powerful AI chips can speed China's development of AI systems for weapons design, intelligence analysis and military modernisation. Both Democrats and Republicans in Congress have urged stronger controls on China's access to advanced AI chips, such as chip-tracking requirements and greater congressional oversight ​of exports. Three Republican congressional committee chairmen have requested a briefing with Huang on November 18 over his reported contacts with an alleged Chinese intelligence operative. Northwestern Polytechnical University bought two H200 chips last month for 874,700 yuan ($123,000), according to an October 21 procurement record on its website. Northwestern is a member of the "Seven Sons of National Defense" group of Chinese universities under U.S. sanctions and with a history of conducting defence-related research for Beijing. The chips were purchased for its management school from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia, the record shows. The H200 is among Nvidia's most capable chips for training and running advanced AI systems and is subject to US export licence approvals, which are normally denied for blacklisted institutions such as Northwestern Polytechnical. Northwestern Polytechnical also bought access this year to ‌H200 chips and other powerful Nvidia AI processors through five contracts for rented computing capacity ⁠from Chinese companies, procurement records show. Reuters is reporting the chip purchases and computing contracts for the first time. Northwestern Polytechnical, Nvidia and the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, which oversees export controls, did not respond to requests for comment. Reuters could not determine contact details for Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology. Based in the northwestern city of Xian, Northwestern Polytechnical conducts research related ⁠to military aircraft, missiles and satellites. The US Commerce Department added the university to its trade blacklist, known as the Entity List, in 2001 over its alleged involvement in missile-proliferation activities and military research. It tightened the restrictions in 2019, making licences for exports of controlled US technology to the university subject to a policy of denial in most circumstances. Northwestern Polytechnical's purchases show how Chinese institutions with military ties continue to obtain US AI computing power through domestic suppliers, either by buying chips outright or renting access to servers containing them. A Reuters review of ​26 ​Chinese procurement and corporate records from this year found universities and research institutions buying US-restricted Nvidia chips or renting access to Nvidia-powered computing services ​that use such chips through domestic suppliers. Several had close links to China's defence industry ‌or military research. The universities named in the records did not respond to requests for comment. US President Donald Trump's administration began allowing some H200 exports to China on a case-by-case basis in January. But that policy did not lift the separate restrictions applying to Entity List organisations such as Northwestern Polytechnical. The January licensing rules also require safeguards to prevent blacklisted entities and military end-users from remotely accessing chips exported under the policy, which covers H200 processors and less advanced models. In addition to the management school's outright purchase of the two H200 chips, procurement records show the university's cybersecurity school awarded two seven-month contracts in January for access to servers containing eight H200 chips each. The contracts, worth 441,700 yuan and 441,000 yuan, covered fine-tuning AI models and reinforcement-learning training. It also rented access to servers containing eight Nvidia A100 chips and eight A800 chips. The A100 and A800 are banned from export to all Chinese entities, though the H200 is the most advanced of those cited in Northwestern Polytechnical's ‌procurement records. In April, another university institute bought computing services requiring at least 24 A100 chips in a 375,000 yuan contract for structural and ​fluid-dynamics simulations. The awards went to several little-known Chinese technology suppliers. The records offered scant information about where the processors originated or where the rented servers ​operated. Under Chinese law, public procurement agencies must verify that suppliers can fulfil orders before announcing winning bidders and signing ​contracts. The procurement records show a wider market for restricted Nvidia AI chips and computing services at Chinese universities. Shenzhen University bought three H100 processors, another high-end Nvidia AI chip banned by the ‌US, for 769,800 yuan in September. Wuhan University of Technology bought a server containing an ​H100 chip for 355,000 yuan in June and four A100 chips ​in a separate 344,000 yuan purchase, the records show. Beihang University, another of the Seven Sons of National Defense universities, bought four A800 processors for 489,000 yuan in April. Beihang has close ties to China's aerospace and defence industries and conducts research for military aviation and space programmes. Two government procurement announcements in July and September named suppliers selected to provide computing services using Nvidia H800 and A800 chips restricted from export to China to the University of ​Chinese Academy of Sciences. One listed H800 access at 10 yuan per chip-hour. A separate ‌January procurement award named a supplier of six A100 chips worth 484,800 yuan for a Shenzhen-based public institution. Reuters has previously reported that Chinese institutions acquired restricted Nvidia chips embedded in servers made by Super Micro ​Computer, Dell and Gigabyte through domestic resellers. Reuters has also documented an underground market in China for restricted Nvidia chips sourced from overseas inventories and third-country intermediaries. Last week, Reuters reported that small quantities of H200 ​chips had reached China through indirect routes while Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports. (Reporting by Eduardo Baptista; Editing by Jamie Freed)

passages: US-listed exchange-traded funds (ETFs) investing in Bitcoin are heading for the worst month of outflows since their 2024 debut, as a persistent sell-off in the world’s largest cryptocurrency drives investors away.
BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust, the largest fund holding the token, has suffered about US$4 billion of redemptions in November , also putting it on course for its worst monthly outflow.
“When a market cannot hold a rally on good news, it usually means that investors are using any strength to sell,” data analytics firm Glassnode said in a note.
“Bitcoin trades round the clock and tends to be one of the first assets sold when investors want less risk.”
The losses underscore a sharp reversal for a group of ETFs that helped propel Bitcoin higher after their US debut in January 2024.

Bitcoin is facing numerous headwinds, from high-profile hacks that have undermined confidence in its security to the prospect of higher interest rates and greater regulatory scrutiny following the recent US midterm elections .

Bitcoin is also facing greater competition for investor capital as money gravitates towards equities and assets offering income, according to Ayesha Kiani, chief operating officer of Monarq Asset Management.
Bitcoin is “competing for the same risk capital that is going into equities right now”, Kiani told Bloomberg Television, describing the ETF exodus as “concerning”.
“There are better yield-bearing assets out there at this point.

A net US$4.71 billion (S$6 billion) has been withdrawn from the funds in November so far, according to data compiled by Bloomberg through Nov 23. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust, the largest fund holding the token, has suffered about US$4 billion of redemptions in November , also putting it on course for its worst monthly outflow. The exodus comes as Bitcoin tumbles below US$60,000 and heads for its worst monthly performance since June 2022, when a string of corporate failures triggered a broader crypto market meltdown. The token has dropped about 23% in November and was trading around US$59,200 as at 1pm on Nov 25 in Singapore, down about 1% in the Asia session. The losses underscore a sharp reversal for a group of ETFs that helped propel Bitcoin higher after their US debut in January 2024. The funds opened the cryptocurrency to a wider pool of institutional and retail investors and became an important source of demand during the bull market. Their record redemptions are now reinforcing the current downturn as that source of buying dries up. Bitcoin briefly recovered alongside other risk assets on Nov 23 after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, but has since surrendered all of those gains, a sign that investors are using rallies to reduce exposure. “When a market cannot hold a rally on good news, it usually means that investors are using any strength to sell,” data analytics firm Glassnode said in a note. “Bitcoin trades round the clock and tends to be one of the first assets sold when investors want less risk.” Bitcoin is facing numerous headwinds, from high-profile hacks that have undermined confidence in its security to the prospect of higher interest rates and greater regulatory scrutiny following the recent US midterm elections . The absence of US demand is adding to the pressure, according to Glassnode. “The ETFs and other institutions were an important source of demand on the way up, and there is little interest from them at these prices,” the firm said. “A return to ETF inflows, together with net buying on Coinbase, would be the first sign that this is changing.” Bitcoin is also facing greater competition for investor capital as money gravitates towards equities and assets offering income, according to Ayesha Kiani, chief operating officer of Monarq Asset Management. Bitcoin is “competing for the same risk capital that is going into equities right now”, Kiani told Bloomberg Television, describing the ETF exodus as “concerning”. The cryptocurrency industry may need a fresh catalyst to revive demand after the forces that drove the previous rally have faded, she said. “I think we do need to find a new narrative, a new catalyst, a new market, something new for the entire industry for us to become that emerging asset class again,” Kiani said. “There are better yield-bearing assets out there at this point. So, like, why Bitcoin?” BLOOMBERG

The Crypto Fear and Greed Index compiled by Alternative.me printed 11 on June 3 — its lowest reading of 2026 and firmly in "Extreme Fear" territory. Historical precedent shows that sustained readings below 20 have often preceded local market bottoms, though they have also persisted for extended periods before any recovery materialized.Michael Saylor AI Rotation: Capital Flight or Structural Break?The most contested question surrounding the current selloff is whether it reflects a structural breakdown in institutional Bitcoin conviction or a temporary reallocation of capital. Strategy (formerly MicroStrategy) co-founder and chairman Michael Saylor made the case for the latter on June 4, posting on X: "Capital markets are funding the AI buildout at historic scale: ~$400B over 6 months. Bitcoin ETFs have seen ~$4B of outflows since May 14, pressuring $BTC. This is a capital rotation, not a Bitcoin impairment. Volatility creates opportunity."Saylor's argument carries structural weight: Wall Street consensus puts combined hyperscaler capital expenditures above $600 billion for 2026, with an estimated $450 billion flowing into AI hardware, servers, and networking infrastructure, according to CreditSights. Major technology firms — Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, and Meta — project combined capital expenditures exceeding $650 billion this year, much of it AI-focused.His explanation arrived with a complicating footnote. Strategy's June 1 Form 8-K disclosed that it sold 32 Bitcoin between May 26 and May 31 at an average price of $77,135 per coin, raising $2.5 million net of expenses — the company's first Bitcoin sale in nearly four years. While the transaction is trivially small relative to Strategy's 843,706 BTC holdings, its symbolic timing — coinciding with the peak of the outflow acceleration — amplified bearish sentiment across the market. At current prices near $63,000, Strategy's holdings are worth approximately $53 billion against a total cost basis of roughly $63.9 billion, leaving the company sitting on an unrealized loss of about $10 billion.Not every analyst accepts the AI-rotation framing. Analysts at Investing.com characterized the outflows as profit-taking by Q1 buyers sitting on substantial gains: institutions that accumulated Bitcoin in the $52,000–$58,000 range during early 2026 were holding meaningful unrealized profits when Federal Reserve rate expectations shifted. The Fed's June communications removed language about progress toward its 2 percent inflation target, two voting members indicated rate cuts originally anticipated for the third quarter of 2026 could be pushed into 2027, and the 10-year Treasury yield climbed 18 basis points in three days to reach 4.82 percent.Bitcoin Price Drop 2026: Macro Forces ConvergeSeveral macro and crypto-specific pressures compounded simultaneously. Bitcoin fell roughly 22 percent since May 14, touching a low of approximately $61,559 on June 4, and has declined more than 14 percent over the prior seven days. CoinStats Daily Market Analysis confirmed Bitcoin's 84 percent correlation with the Dow Jones Industrial Average during this period, underscoring the macro-driven character of the move rather than any crypto-specific catalyst.Energy and geopolitical pressures reinforced the selloff. Over $1.8 billion in leveraged long positions were liquidated across major derivatives exchanges, with long positions absorbing roughly 75 percent of the damage in recent 24-hour windows.On-chain data from CryptoQuant shows whale accumulation has broadly stalled, with large-wallet balances largely unchanged since February 2026 — suggesting the buyer base at current levels may be thinner than headline wallet counts imply. A stronger-than-expected payroll print would push Federal Reserve rate-cut expectations further into 2027, keep Treasury yields elevated, and likely extend selling pressure on Bitcoin. A weaker number with moderating wage growth would support a risk-on close to the week and could trigger the first positive ETF inflow day since May 13.The next Federal Reserve policy meeting is scheduled for June 17–18, 2026. That outcome will reset rate expectations and directly affect ETF flow direction for the weeks that follow.Standard Chartered global head of digital assets research Geoff Kendrick told clients on June 4 that the bear market may be in its final stages, writing: "I think when we look back at the end of 2026 with BTC at $100,000 and ETH at $4,000, we will say this was the buying zone we all wanted." Kendrick noted that cumulative net ETF inflows since launch remain at $54.2 billion and total BTC held across the 11 U.S.-listed funds sits at approximately 674,000 — down from a peak near 682,000 but broadly stable. The bank's year-end Bitcoin target remains $100,000, a level that would require roughly a 60 percent recovery from current prices.Compass Point flagged top-buyer capitulation signals, with Bitcoin's 200-week moving average at approximately $61,300 representing a historically respected long-term floor. Polymarket traders as of June 4 assigned a 77 percent probability to Bitcoin holding $65,000 support through month-end and an 18 percent probability of a decline to $57,500.Despite the headline-grabbing outflows, lifetime Bitcoin ETF inflows since January 2024 still exceed $55 billion, according to Bloomberg ETF analyst Eric Balchunas.

extraction.body: US spot Bitcoin ETFs have taken $4.94 billion in November net outflows, beating June's record, with BlackRock's IBIT behind most of the selling. US spot Bitcoin ETFs are heading for their worst month since they launched in January 2024. The funds have recorded $4.94 billion in November net outflows, above the previous monthly record of $4.51 billion set in June, and they are closing in on a $5 billion month for the first time. The pressure has not eased. Investors pulled $231.6 million on Tuesday, 24 November, the sixth straight trading day of withdrawals, according to SoSoValue. Farside Investors' daily table put the 23 November exit across the 12 US funds at $569.69 million. BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust, the largest of the funds, is behind the bulk of it. IBIT has recorded nearly $4 billion in November net outflows, its highest since inception, and about 85% of the combined outflows from US spot Bitcoin ETFs this month. It has seen withdrawals in 15 of November's 16 trading sessions. Monday, 23 November, showed the pattern clearly. IBIT led the day with $509.3 million, roughly 89% of the total, while Grayscale's Bitcoin Mini Trust and Bitwise's BITB followed with $61.08 million and $12.6 million. Fidelity's FBTC was the only Bitcoin fund to attract fresh money, taking in $13.29 million. The single-day records fell quickly this month: Even after the redemptions, IBIT still holds more than $62 billion in cumulative net inflows since launch. Cumulative net inflows into all US spot Bitcoin ETFs stand at roughly $52 billion to $53.5 billion. The weekly numbers are just as stark. The funds shed $1.79 billion in the week ending 20 November 2026, their biggest weekly exit in 21 weeks and a fourth straight week of net outflows. The selling is not limited to Bitcoin products. US spot Ethereum ETFs recorded $84.92 million of withdrawals on Monday, taking their November total to $1.15 billion. BlackRock's iShares Ethereum Trust accounted for $90.5 million of Monday's exit and around $977 million for the month, while its staked Ether fund, ETHB, has seen more than $90 million leave this month. ETHA and ETHB together still hold over $10 billion in cumulative inflows since launch. Across Bitcoin and Ethereum funds combined, net withdrawals in November total $5.86 billion. Bitcoin's fall this week hit the wider market, and Hyperliquid's HYPE took the hardest knock among the largest tokens. HYPE fell 8.2% over 24 hours to $57.86, the steepest drop among the 20 biggest cryptocurrencies by market cap, and it is down 15.8% over the past week. The drop came alongside the exit of one of Hyperliquid's largest known traders. Investment firm Abraxas Capital withdrew its remaining funds and closed its entire book, almost two years after it began trading there. Analyst MLM put the firm's activity at $13.4 billion traded and $530 million made, including at least $67 million from funding payments. Two accounts labelled Abraxas Capital on the analytics site Hyperdash show combined all-time profits of more than $550 million, and now hold just over $5,000 between them. On Tuesday they unstaked about 219,000 HYPE, worth roughly $12.7 million, and sent it elsewhere. Those wallet labels come from on-chain analysis, not a statement from the firm, so the total size of the exit is not confirmed. Options traders are positioned for more downside. Over the past week, 1.7 put options changed hands for every call on a seven-day average, the most since June 2022, Glassnode said in its weekly report, and by open interest the ratio is the highest since May 2021. Puts pay out when prices fall. Glassnode also said options dealers are short gamma between $58,000 and $64,000, which means their hedging forces them to sell as prices fall and buy as they rise. That can make moves in either direction larger, which matters while Bitcoin trades near the bottom of that band. On the demand side, Teroxx's November research report pointed to rising interest rates and weakness in AI stocks, and noted that markets increasingly expect another Federal Reserve rate increase in December. "In the near term, flows into Bitcoin will remain under pressure as long as artificial intelligence stocks are searching for a bottom and the December Fed decision looms," Teroxx researcher Leonardo Larieira wrote. He added that a sustained recovery in inflows would need long-term US Treasury yields to stabilize. The report itself was not reachable when this article was written. The longer view is mixed. Net outflows for 2026 total about $4.57 billion, which would erase the $6.34 billion the funds attracted in the third quarter, though that figure has a single source. Cumulative inflows of roughly $52 billion since launch remain intact. What happens next is simple to track. Watch the flows printed for the remaining November sessions, including the shortened 27 November trading day, and watch Bitcoin's hold on the $58,000 to $64,000 band where dealer hedging is concentrated. If neither gives, the funds' first $5 billion month will be a launch-to-date record nobody at the issuers wanted. The information discussed by Altcoin Buzz is not financial advice. passages: US spot Bitcoin ETFs have taken $4.94 billion in November net outflows, beating June's record, with BlackRock's IBIT behind most of the selling.

US spot Bitcoin ETFs are heading for their worst month since they launched in January 2024. The funds have recorded $4.94 billion in November net outflows, above the previous monthly record of $4.51 billion set in June, and they are closing in on a $5 billion month for the first time.

The pressure has not eased. Investors pulled $231.6 million on Tuesday, 24 November, the sixth straight trading day of withdrawals, according to SoSoValue. Farside Investors' daily table put the 23 November exit across the 12 US funds at $569.69 million.

BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust, the largest of the funds, is behind the bulk of it. IBIT has recorded nearly $4 billion in November net outflows, its highest since inception, and about 85% of the combined outflows from US spot Bitcoin ETFs this month. It has seen withdrawals in 15 of November's 16 trading sessions.

Monday, 23 November, showed the pattern clearly. IBIT led the day with $509.3 million, roughly 89% of the total, while Grayscale's Bitcoin Mini Trust and Bitwise's BITB followed with $61.08 million and $12.6 million. Fidelity's FBTC was the only Bitcoin fund to attract fresh money, taking in $13.29 million.
The single-day records fell quickly this month:

Even after the redemptions, IBIT still holds more than $62 billion in cumulative net inflows since launch. Cumulative net inflows into all US spot Bitcoin ETFs stand at roughly $52 billion to $53.5 billion.
The weekly numbers are just as stark. The funds shed $1.79 billion in the week ending 20 November 2026, their biggest weekly exit in 21 weeks and a fourth straight week of net outflows.

The selling is not limited to Bitcoin products. US spot Ethereum ETFs recorded $84.92 million of withdrawals on Monday, taking their November total to $1.15 billion. BlackRock's iShares Ethereum Trust accounted for $90.5 million of Monday's exit and around $977 million for the month, while its staked Ether fund, ETHB, has seen more than $90 million leave this month.
ETHA and ETHB together still hold over $10 billion in cumulative inflows since launch. Across Bitcoin and Ethereum funds combined, net withdrawals in November total $5.86 billion.

Bitcoin's fall this week hit the wider market, and Hyperliquid's HYPE took the hardest knock among the largest tokens. HYPE fell 8.2% over 24 hours to $57.86, the steepest drop among the 20 biggest cryptocurrencies by market cap, and it is down 15.8% over the past week.

The drop came alongside the exit of one of Hyperliquid's largest known traders. Investment firm Abraxas Capital withdrew its remaining funds and closed its entire book, almost two years after it began trading there. Analyst MLM put the firm's activity at $13.4 billion traded and $530 million made, including at least $67 million from funding payments.

Two accounts labelled Abraxas Capital on the analytics site Hyperdash show combined all-time profits of more than $550 million, and now hold just over $5,000 between them. On Tuesday they unstaked about 219,000 HYPE, worth roughly $12.7 million, and sent it elsewhere. Those wallet labels come from on-chain analysis, not a statement from the firm, so the total size of the exit is not confirmed.

Options traders are positioned for more downside. Over the past week, 1.7 put options changed hands for every call on a seven-day average, the most since June 2022, Glassnode said in its weekly report, and by open interest the ratio is the highest since May 2021. Puts pay out when prices fall.

Glassnode also said options dealers are short gamma between $58,000 and $64,000, which means their hedging forces them to sell as prices fall and buy as they rise. That can make moves in either direction larger, which matters while Bitcoin trades near the bottom of that band.

On the demand side, Teroxx's November research report pointed to rising interest rates and weakness in AI stocks, and noted that markets increasingly expect another Federal Reserve rate increase in December. "In the near term, flows into Bitcoin will remain under pressure as long as artificial intelligence stocks are searching for a bottom and the December Fed decision looms," Teroxx researcher Leonardo Larieira wrote. He added that a sustained recovery in inflows would need long-term US Treasury yields to stabilize. The report itself was not reachable when this article was written.

The longer view is mixed. Net outflows for 2026 total about $4.57 billion, which would erase the $6.34 billion the funds attracted in the third quarter, though that figure has a single source. Cumulative inflows of roughly $52 billion since launch remain intact.

What happens next is simple to track. Watch the flows printed for the remaining November sessions, including the shortened 27 November trading day, and watch Bitcoin's hold on the $58,000 to $64,000 band where dealer hedging is concentrated. If neither gives, the funds' first $5 billion month will be a launch-to-date record nobody at the issuers wanted.

US-listed exchange-traded funds (ETFs) investing in Bitcoin are heading for the worst month of outflows since their 2024 debut, as a persistent sell-off in the world’s largest cryptocurrency drives investors away.
BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust, the largest fund holding the token, has suffered about US$4 billion of redemptions in November , also putting it on course for its worst monthly outflow.
“When a market cannot hold a rally on good news, it usually means that investors are using any strength to sell,” data analytics firm Glassnode said in a note.
“Bitcoin trades round the clock and tends to be one of the first assets sold when investors want less risk.”
The losses underscore a sharp reversal for a group of ETFs that helped propel Bitcoin higher after their US debut in January 2024.

Bitcoin is facing numerous headwinds, from high-profile hacks that have undermined confidence in its security to the prospect of higher interest rates and greater regulatory scrutiny following the recent US midterm elections .

Bitcoin is also facing greater competition for investor capital as money gravitates towards equities and assets offering income, according to Ayesha Kiani, chief operating officer of Monarq Asset Management.
Bitcoin is “competing for the same risk capital that is going into equities right now”, Kiani told Bloomberg Television, describing the ETF exodus as “concerning”.
“There are better yield-bearing assets out there at this point.

Fidelity's Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund — the second-largest spot Bitcoin ETF in the United States by assets — shed $37.29 million in a single session on June 2 as part of the longest and deepest redemption streak since spot Bitcoin exchange-traded products launched in January 2024.
BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) absorbed the heaviest damage, losing approximately $3.3 billion, or about 75 percent of total outflows across the streak.

Over 30 days, the ETF complex has collectively sold approximately 51,726 BTC — worth roughly $5 billion at current prices — supply that the market must absorb in addition to independent spot sellers.Does Fidelity FBTC Still Hold Up Under Pressure?Despite the scale of recent outflows, FBTC has demonstrated relative resilience on a longer time horizon.

U.S.-listed Bitcoin ETFs have now recorded 13 consecutive days of net outflows since May 15, draining $4.4 billion from the complex and flipping 2026's cumulative ETF flows into negative territory for the first time since launch.

FBTC's 52-week price range spans from a low of $54.21 to a high of $110.25, reflecting both the magnitude of Bitcoin's prior bull run and the depth of the current pullback.Bitcoin itself now trades roughly 51 percent below its record high of approximately $126,277, set in October 2025.

Polymarket traders as of June 4 assigned a 77 percent probability to Bitcoin holding $65,000 support through month-end and an 18 percent probability of a decline to $57,500.Despite the headline-grabbing outflows, lifetime Bitcoin ETF inflows since January 2024 still exceed $55 billion, according to Bloomberg ETF analyst Eric Balchunas.
FBTC shed $456 million over the same period, and Grayscale's Bitcoin Trust (GBTC) lost $303 million.The selling was heavily institutional rather than retail.

Analysts at Investing.com characterized the outflows as profit-taking by Q1 buyers sitting on substantial gains: institutions that accumulated Bitcoin in the $52,000–$58,000 range during early 2026 were holding meaningful unrealized profits when Federal Reserve rate expectations shifted.

While the transaction is trivially small relative to Strategy's 843,706 BTC holdings, its symbolic timing — coinciding with the peak of the outflow acceleration — amplified bearish sentiment across the market.

At current prices near $63,000, Strategy's holdings are worth approximately $53 billion against a total cost basis of roughly $63.9 billion, leaving the company sitting on an unrealized loss of about $10 billion.Not every analyst accepts the AI-rotation framing.

extraction.body: Bitcoin is facing numerous headwinds, from high-profile hacks to the prospect of higher interest rates and greater regulatory scrutiny following recent US midterm elections. US-listed exchange-traded funds (ETFs) investing in Bitcoin are heading for the worst month of outflows since their 2024 debut, as a persistent sell-off in the world’s largest cryptocurrency drives investors away. A net US$4.71 billion (S$6 billion) has been withdrawn from the funds in November so far, according to data compiled by Bloomberg through Nov 23. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust, the largest fund holding the token, has suffered about US$4 billion of redemptions in November , also putting it on course for its worst monthly outflow. The exodus comes as Bitcoin tumbles below US$60,000 and heads for its worst monthly performance since June 2022, when a string of corporate failures triggered a broader crypto market meltdown. The token has dropped about 23% in November and was trading around US$59,200 as at 1pm on Nov 25 in Singapore, down about 1% in the Asia session. The losses underscore a sharp reversal for a group of ETFs that helped propel Bitcoin higher after their US debut in January 2024. The funds opened the cryptocurrency to a wider pool of institutional and retail investors and became an important source of demand during the bull market. Their record redemptions are now reinforcing the current downturn as that source of buying dries up. Bitcoin briefly recovered alongside other risk assets on Nov 23 after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, but has since surrendered all of those gains, a sign that investors are using rallies to reduce exposure. “When a market cannot hold a rally on good news, it usually means that investors are using any strength to sell,” data analytics firm Glassnode said in a note. “Bitcoin trades round the clock and tends to be one of the first assets sold when investors want less risk.” Bitcoin is facing numerous headwinds, from high-profile hacks that have undermined confidence in its security to the prospect of higher interest rates and greater regulatory scrutiny following the recent US midterm elections . The absence of US demand is adding to the pressure, according to Glassnode. “The ETFs and other institutions were an important source of demand on the way up, and there is little interest from them at these prices,” the firm said. “A return to ETF inflows, together with net buying on Coinbase, would be the first sign that this is changing.” Bitcoin is also facing greater competition for investor capital as money gravitates towards equities and assets offering income, according to Ayesha Kiani, chief operating officer of Monarq Asset Management. Bitcoin is “competing for the same risk capital that is going into equities right now”, Kiani told Bloomberg Television, describing the ETF exodus as “concerning”. The cryptocurrency industry may need a fresh catalyst to revive demand after the forces that drove the previous rally have faded, she said. “I think we do need to find a new narrative, a new catalyst, a new market, something new for the entire industry for us to become that emerging asset class again,” Kiani said. “There are better yield-bearing assets out there at this point. So, like, why Bitcoin?” BLOOMBERG

U.S.-listed Bitcoin ETFs have now recorded 13 consecutive days of net outflows since May 15, draining $4.4 billion from the complex and flipping 2026's cumulative ETF flows into negative territory for the first time since launch. With Bitcoin trading near a multi-month low of approximately $63,000 and Friday's Non-Farm Payrolls report due at 8:30 a.m. ET today, every FBTC holder faces a live decision window with real money at stake.Bitcoin ETF Outflows Hit 13-Day Record: What's Driving the Institutional ExitThe 13-session streak shatters the previous record for consecutive outflow days and coincides with Bitcoin falling roughly 22 percent from its May 14 peak of approximately $82,035. Within that streak, the single worst week was the seven sessions beginning June 2, when the complex hemorrhaged $3.4 billion — the largest single-week outflow since the funds were approved in January 2024. BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) absorbed the heaviest damage, losing approximately $3.3 billion, or about 75 percent of total outflows across the streak. FBTC shed $456 million over the same period, and Grayscale's Bitcoin Trust (GBTC) lost $303 million.The selling was heavily institutional rather than retail. CoinShares analyst Matt Kimmell's analysis of first-quarter 13F filings showed professional Bitcoin holdings dropped from 313,000 to 261,000 BTC — a 17 percent quarterly decline — while the total dollar value of institutional exposure fell 35 percent to $17.8 billion. Hedge funds led the retreat, cutting holdings by 39 percent. Jane Street reduced its position by roughly 70 percent over the same period, and Goldman Sachs trimmed by 10 percent.The structure of spot Bitcoin ETFs amplifies selling pressure mechanically: when redemption requests come in, authorized participants must sell the underlying Bitcoin in the spot market to return capital. Over 30 days, the ETF complex has collectively sold approximately 51,726 BTC — worth roughly $5 billion at current prices — supply that the market must absorb in addition to independent spot sellers.Does Fidelity FBTC Still Hold Up Under Pressure?Despite the scale of recent outflows, FBTC has demonstrated relative resilience on a longer time horizon. Its assets under management stood at approximately $12.97 billion as of June 2, according to Yahoo Finance data. The fund's year-to-date return of approximately 25.3 percent outpaces the digital-asset category average of 19.2 percent as of June 3. FBTC's 52-week price range spans from a low of $54.21 to a high of $110.25, reflecting both the magnitude of Bitcoin's prior bull run and the depth of the current pullback.Bitcoin itself now trades roughly 51 percent below its record high of approximately $126,277, set in October 2025. The Crypto Fear and Greed Index compiled by Alternative.me printed 11 on June 3 — its lowest reading of 2026 and firmly in "Extreme Fear" territory. Historical precedent shows that sustained readings below 20 have often preceded local market bottoms, though they have also persisted for extended periods before any recovery materialized.Michael Saylor AI Rotation: Capital Flight or Structural Break?The most contested question surrounding the current selloff is whether it reflects a structural breakdown in institutional Bitcoin conviction or a temporary reallocation of capital. Strategy (formerly MicroStrategy) co-founder and chairman Michael Saylor made the case for the latter on June 4, posting on X: "Capital markets are funding the AI buildout at historic scale: ~$400B over 6 months. Bitcoin ETFs have seen ~$4B of outflows since May 14, pressuring $BTC. This is a capital rotation, not a Bitcoin impairment. Volatility creates opportunity."Saylor's argument carries structural weight: Wall Street consensus puts combined hyperscaler capital expenditures above $600 billion for 2026, with an estimated $450 billion flowing into AI hardware, servers, and networking infrastructure, according to CreditSights. Major technology firms — Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, and Meta — project combined capital expenditures exceeding $650 billion this year, much of it AI-focused.His explanation arrived with a complicating footnote. Strategy's June 1 Form 8-K disclosed that it sold 32 Bitcoin between May 26 and May 31 at an average price of $77,135 per coin, raising $2.5 million net of expenses — the company's first Bitcoin sale in nearly four years. While the transaction is trivially small relative to Strategy's 843,706 BTC holdings, its symbolic timing — coinciding with the peak of the outflow acceleration — amplified bearish sentiment across the market. At current prices near $63,000, Strategy's holdings are worth approximately $53 billion against a total cost basis of roughly $63.9 billion, leaving the company sitting on an unrealized loss of about $10 billion.Not every analyst accepts the AI-rotation framing. Analysts at Investing.com characterized the outflows as profit-taking by Q1 buyers sitting on substantial gains: institutions that accumulated Bitcoin in the $52,000–$58,000 range during early 2026 were holding meaningful unrealized profits when Federal Reserve rate expectations shifted. The Fed's June communications removed language about progress toward its 2 percent inflation target, two voting members indicated rate cuts originally anticipated for the third quarter of 2026 could be pushed into 2027, and the 10-year Treasury yield climbed 18 basis points in three days to reach 4.82 percent.Bitcoin Price Drop 2026: Macro Forces ConvergeSeveral macro and crypto-specific pressures compounded simultaneously. Bitcoin fell roughly 22 percent since May 14, touching a low of approximately $61,559 on June 4, and has declined more than 14 percent over the prior seven days. CoinStats Daily Market Analysis confirmed Bitcoin's 84 percent correlation with the Dow Jones Industrial Average during this period, underscoring the macro-driven character of the move rather than any crypto-specific catalyst.Energy and geopolitical pressures reinforced the selloff. Over $1.8 billion in leveraged long positions were liquidated across major derivatives exchanges, with long positions absorbing roughly 75 percent of the damage in recent 24-hour windows.On-chain data from CryptoQuant shows whale accumulation has broadly stalled, with large-wallet balances largely unchanged since February 2026 — suggesting the buyer base at current levels may be thinner than headline wallet counts imply. Per CoinShares and Galaxy analysts, some capital that has exited Bitcoin ETFs has shifted into select altcoin products, with Solana ETFs recording inflows during the same period that Bitcoin ETFs bled.What Can ETF Holders Expect from Today's Jobs Report?Today's Non-Farm Payrolls report, due at 8:30 a.m. ET, is the dominant near-term macro event for Bitcoin and U.S. spot ETF flows. A stronger-than-expected payroll print would push Federal Reserve rate-cut expectations further into 2027, keep Treasury yields elevated, and likely extend selling pressure on Bitcoin. A weaker number with moderating wage growth would support a risk-on close to the week and could trigger the first positive ETF inflow day since May 13.The next Federal Reserve policy meeting is scheduled for June 17–18, 2026. That outcome will reset rate expectations and directly affect ETF flow direction for the weeks that follow.Standard Chartered global head of digital assets research Geoff Kendrick told clients on June 4 that the bear market may be in its final stages, writing: "I think when we look back at the end of 2026 with BTC at $100,000 and ETH at $4,000, we will say this was the buying zone we all wanted." Kendrick noted that cumulative net ETF inflows since launch remain at $54.2 billion and total BTC held across the 11 U.S.-listed funds sits at approximately 674,000 — down from a peak near 682,000 but broadly stable. The bank's year-end Bitcoin target remains $100,000, a level that would require roughly a 60 percent recovery from current prices.Compass Point flagged top-buyer capitulation signals, with Bitcoin's 200-week moving average at approximately $61,300 representing a historically respected long-term floor. Polymarket traders as of June 4 assigned a 77 percent probability to Bitcoin holding $65,000 support through month-end and an 18 percent probability of a decline to $57,500.Despite the headline-grabbing outflows, lifetime Bitcoin ETF inflows since January 2024 still exceed $55 billion, according to Bloomberg ETF analyst Eric Balchunas.

CoinShares analyst Matt Kimmell's analysis of first-quarter 13F filings showed professional Bitcoin holdings dropped from 313,000 to 261,000 BTC — a 17 percent quarterly decline — while the total dollar value of institutional exposure fell 35 percent to $17.8 billion.
Hedge funds led the retreat, cutting holdings by 39 percent.

Jane Street reduced its position by roughly 70 percent over the same period, and Goldman Sachs trimmed by 10 percent.The structure of spot Bitcoin ETFs amplifies selling pressure mechanically: when redemption requests come in, authorized participants must sell the underlying Bitcoin in the spot market to return capital.

Its assets under management stood at approximately $12.97 billion as of June 2, according to Yahoo Finance data.
The fund's year-to-date return of approximately 25.3 percent outpaces the digital-asset category average of 19.2 percent as of June 3.

FBTC's 52-week price range spans from a low of $54.21 to a high of $110.25, reflecting both the magnitude of Bitcoin's prior bull run and the depth of the current pullback.Bitcoin itself now trades roughly 51 percent below its record high of approximately $126,277, set in October 2025.
The Crypto Fear and Greed Index compiled by Alternative.me printed 11 on June 3 — its lowest reading of 2026 and firmly in "Extreme Fear" territory.

Historical precedent shows that sustained readings below 20 have often preceded local market bottoms, though they have also persisted for extended periods before any recovery materialized.Michael Saylor AI Rotation: Capital Flight or Structural Break?The most contested question surrounding the current selloff is whether it reflects a structural breakdown in institutional Bitcoin conviction or a temporary reallocation of capital.

Strategy (formerly MicroStrategy) co-founder and chairman Michael Saylor made the case for the latter on June 4, posting on X: "Capital markets are funding the AI buildout at historic scale: ~$400B over 6 months.
Bitcoin ETFs have seen ~$4B of outflows since May 14, pressuring $BTC.
This is a capital rotation, not a Bitcoin impairment.

Volatility creates opportunity."Saylor's argument carries structural weight: Wall Street consensus puts combined hyperscaler capital expenditures above $600 billion for 2026, with an estimated $450 billion flowing into AI hardware, servers, and networking infrastructure, according to CreditSights.

Major technology firms — Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, and Meta — project combined capital expenditures exceeding $650 billion this year, much of it AI-focused.His explanation arrived with a complicating footnote.

Strategy's June 1 Form 8-K disclosed that it sold 32 Bitcoin between May 26 and May 31 at an average price of $77,135 per coin, raising $2.5 million net of expenses — the company's first Bitcoin sale in nearly four years.

While the transaction is trivially small relative to Strategy's 843,706 BTC holdings, its symbolic timing — coinciding with the peak of the outflow acceleration — amplified bearish sentiment across the market.

At current prices near $63,000, Strategy's holdings are worth approximately $53 billion against a total cost basis of roughly $63.9 billion, leaving the company sitting on an unrealized loss of about $10 billion.Not every analyst accepts the AI-rotation framing.

Analysts at Investing.com characterized the outflows as profit-taking by Q1 buyers sitting on substantial gains: institutions that accumulated Bitcoin in the $52,000–$58,000 range during early 2026 were holding meaningful unrealized profits when Federal Reserve rate expectations shifted.

The Fed's June communications removed language about progress toward its 2 percent inflation target, two voting members indicated rate cuts originally anticipated for the third quarter of 2026 could be pushed into 2027, and the 10-year Treasury yield climbed 18 basis points in three days to reach 4.82 percent.Bitcoin Price Drop 2026: Macro Forces ConvergeSeveral macro and crypto-specific pressures compounded simultaneously.
Bitcoin fell roughly 22 percent since May 14, touching a low of approximately $61,559 on June 4, and has declined more than 14 percent over the prior seven days.

CoinStats Daily Market Analysis confirmed Bitcoin's 84 percent correlation with the Dow Jones Industrial Average during this period, underscoring the macro-driven character of the move rather than any crypto-specific catalyst.Energy and geopolitical pressures reinforced the selloff.

Over $1.8 billion in leveraged long positions were liquidated across major derivatives exchanges, with long positions absorbing roughly 75 percent of the damage in recent 24-hour windows.On-chain data from CryptoQuant shows whale accumulation has broadly stalled, with large-wallet balances largely unchanged since February 2026 — suggesting the buyer base at current levels may be thinner than headline wallet counts imply.

Per CoinShares and Galaxy analysts, some capital that has exited Bitcoin ETFs has shifted into select altcoin products, with Solana ETFs recording inflows during the same period that Bitcoin ETFs bled.What Can ETF Holders Expect from Today's Jobs Report?Today's Non-Farm Payrolls report, due at 8:30 a.m.
ET, is the dominant near-term macro event for Bitcoin and U.S. spot ETF flows.
A stronger-than-expected payroll print would push Federal Reserve rate-cut expectations further into 2027, keep Treasury yields elevated, and likely extend selling pressure on Bitcoin.

A weaker number with moderating wage growth would support a risk-on close to the week and could trigger the first positive ETF inflow day since May 13.The next Federal Reserve policy meeting is scheduled for June 17–18, 2026.

That outcome will reset rate expectations and directly affect ETF flow direction for the weeks that follow.Standard Chartered global head of digital assets research Geoff Kendrick told clients on June 4 that the bear market may be in its final stages, writing: "I think when we look back at the end of 2026 with BTC at $100,000 and ETH at $4,000, we will say this was the buying zone we all wanted." Kendrick noted that cumulative net ETF inflows since launch remain at $54.2 billion and total BTC held across the 11 U.S.-listed funds sits at approximately 674,000 — down from a peak near 682,000 but broadly stable.

The bank's year-end Bitcoin target remains $100,000, a level that would require roughly a 60 percent recovery from current prices.Compass Point flagged top-buyer capitulation signals, with Bitcoin's 200-week moving average at approximately $61,300 representing a historically respected long-term floor.

Polymarket traders as of June 4 assigned a 77 percent probability to Bitcoin holding $65,000 support through month-end and an 18 percent probability of a decline to $57,500.Despite the headline-grabbing outflows, lifetime Bitcoin ETF inflows since January 2024 still exceed $55 billion, according to Bloomberg ETF analyst Eric Balchunas.

BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust, the largest of the funds, is behind the bulk of it.
