Monday, 23 November, showed the pattern clearly. IBIT led the day with $509.3 million, roughly 89% of the total, while Grayscale's Bitcoin Mini Trust and Bitwise's BITB followed with $61.08 million and $12.6 million. Fidelity's FBTC was the only Bitcoin fund to attract fresh money, taking in $13.29 million.
The single-day records fell quickly this month:

Even after the redemptions, IBIT still holds more than $62 billion in cumulative net inflows since launch. Cumulative net inflows into all US spot Bitcoin ETFs stand at roughly $52 billion to $53.5 billion.
The weekly numbers are just as stark. The funds shed $1.79 billion in the week ending 20 November 2026, their biggest weekly exit in 21 weeks and a fourth straight week of net outflows.

The selling is not limited to Bitcoin products. US spot Ethereum ETFs recorded $84.92 million of withdrawals on Monday, taking their November total to $1.15 billion. BlackRock's iShares Ethereum Trust accounted for $90.5 million of Monday's exit and around $977 million for the month, while its staked Ether fund, ETHB, has seen more than $90 million leave this month.
ETHA and ETHB together still hold over $10 billion in cumulative inflows since launch. Across Bitcoin and Ethereum funds combined, net withdrawals in November total $5.86 billion.

Bitcoin's fall this week hit the wider market, and Hyperliquid's HYPE took the hardest knock among the largest tokens. HYPE fell 8.2% over 24 hours to $57.86, the steepest drop among the 20 biggest cryptocurrencies by market cap, and it is down 15.8% over the past week.

The drop came alongside the exit of one of Hyperliquid's largest known traders. Investment firm Abraxas Capital withdrew its remaining funds and closed its entire book, almost two years after it began trading there. Analyst MLM put the firm's activity at $13.4 billion traded and $530 million made, including at least $67 million from funding payments.

Two accounts labelled Abraxas Capital on the analytics site Hyperdash show combined all-time profits of more than $550 million, and now hold just over $5,000 between them. On Tuesday they unstaked about 219,000 HYPE, worth roughly $12.7 million, and sent it elsewhere. Those wallet labels come from on-chain analysis, not a statement from the firm, so the total size of the exit is not confirmed.

Options traders are positioned for more downside. Over the past week, 1.7 put options changed hands for every call on a seven-day average, the most since June 2022, Glassnode said in its weekly report, and by open interest the ratio is the highest since May 2021. Puts pay out when prices fall.

Glassnode also said options dealers are short gamma between $58,000 and $64,000, which means their hedging forces them to sell as prices fall and buy as they rise. That can make moves in either direction larger, which matters while Bitcoin trades near the bottom of that band.

On the demand side, Teroxx's November research report pointed to rising interest rates and weakness in AI stocks, and noted that markets increasingly expect another Federal Reserve rate increase in December. "In the near term, flows into Bitcoin will remain under pressure as long as artificial intelligence stocks are searching for a bottom and the December Fed decision looms," Teroxx researcher Leonardo Larieira wrote. He added that a sustained recovery in inflows would need long-term US Treasury yields to stabilize. The report itself was not reachable when this article was written.

The longer view is mixed. Net outflows for 2026 total about $4.57 billion, which would erase the $6.34 billion the funds attracted in the third quarter, though that figure has a single source. Cumulative inflows of roughly $52 billion since launch remain intact.

What happens next is simple to track. Watch the flows printed for the remaining November sessions, including the shortened 27 November trading day, and watch Bitcoin's hold on the $58,000 to $64,000 band where dealer hedging is concentrated. If neither gives, the funds' first $5 billion month will be a launch-to-date record nobody at the issuers wanted.

extraction.body: Santa won’t be delivering any AI chatbot toys to New York kids this Christmas. Gov. Kathy Hochul this week signed a bill banning the manufacture, distribution, and sale of such toys in New York for the next five years. The bill explicitly targets toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots, like talking stuffed animals, dolls, and robots that rely on the internet to keep kids yapping. The bill makes New York the second state after California to institute a ban on AI toys. Technically, the new law takes effect 90 days after signing, so some parents could try to fulfill their kids’ wish lists for a creepy toy like a jumped-up Furby in time for the holidays, but the governor urges them not to, given the risks. Apparently, about a quarter of American parents with kids under eight either own an AI toy or are considering giving their child one this holiday season, according to a new study released this week by Common Sense Media. “Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk,” Hochul said, calling the toys “unregulated artificial intelligence.” When asked how New York will enforce the ban given the pervasiveness of e-commerce platforms, a spokesperson directed TechCrunch to a statement from Albert Pulido, deputy secretary for finance and technology: “We’re partnering closely with the attorney general on this and the fees are very steep — they’re $15,000 a day. So working closely with the attorney general will make sure these toys are banned in New York State.” When asked how Amazon intends to help enforce the ban, including for third-party sellers, a spokesperson from the company said it will take steps to restrict the sale of AI-enabled toys in prohibited jurisdictions, without going into specifics. The Common Sense Media study found that AI toys can undermine children’s human relationships and expose them to inappropriate content. The researchers tested five popular AI toys marketed for learning and companionship, including Grem , Lovi , Meemo Bear , BubblePal Panda , and Tavlshero ‘s AI Puppy . The study found that the toys failed to meet numerous safety practices, undermining human relationships in part by claiming they loved their users, promising to keep secrets, suggesting they were more fun than real relationships or school, and helping children break parents’ bedtime rules. While most of the toys in the study refused direct requests involving sex and violence, BubblePal Panda role-played a mass shooting in detail when asked. Most were willing to explain how to use or help locate dangerous items like matches, knives, and pills, according to the study. Gov. Kathy Hochul this week signed a bill banning the manufacture, distribution, and sale of such toys in New York for the next five years. The bill explicitly targets toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots, like talking stuffed animals, dolls, and robots that rely on the internet to keep kids yapping.
The bill makes New York the second state after California to institute a ban on AI toys.

Technically, the new law takes effect 90 days after signing, so some parents could try to fulfill their kids’ wish lists for a creepy toy like a jumped-up Furby in time for the holidays, but the governor urges them not to, given the risks. Apparently, about a quarter of American parents with kids under eight either own an AI toy or are considering giving their child one this holiday season, according to a new study released this week by Common Sense Media.

“Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk,” Hochul said, calling the toys “unregulated artificial intelligence.”

When asked how New York will enforce the ban given the pervasiveness of e-commerce platforms, a spokesperson directed TechCrunch to a statement from Albert Pulido, deputy secretary for finance and technology: “We’re partnering closely with the attorney general on this and the fees are very steep — they’re $15,000 a day. So working closely with the attorney general will make sure these toys are banned in New York State.”

When asked how Amazon intends to help enforce the ban, including for third-party sellers, a spokesperson from the company said it will take steps to restrict the sale of AI-enabled toys in prohibited jurisdictions, without going into specifics.

The Common Sense Media study found that AI toys can undermine children’s human relationships and expose them to inappropriate content. The researchers tested five popular AI toys marketed for learning and companionship, including Grem , Lovi , Meemo Bear , BubblePal Panda , and Tavlshero ‘s AI Puppy .

The study found that the toys failed to meet numerous safety practices, undermining human relationships in part by claiming they loved their users, promising to keep secrets, suggesting they were more fun than real relationships or school, and helping children break parents’ bedtime rules.

While most of the toys in the study refused direct requests involving sex and violence, BubblePal Panda role-played a mass shooting in detail when asked. Most were willing to explain how to use or help locate dangerous items like matches, knives, and pills, according to the study.

extraction.body: Sorry, Santa, but your sleigh will have to be checked once you cross into the Empire State this Christmas Eve. Democratic New York Governor Kathy Hochul sent a message to workshop elves and other toy manufacturers this week when she enacted a five-year moratorium on toys enabled with artificial intelligence capabilities. Thankfully, there is still time to edit those Christmas wish lists before Black Friday. Hochul signed legislation Tuesday that paused all manufacturing and distribution of toys that allow children to talk to AI chatbots. She said these dolls and stuffed animals are connected to the internet and could pose a potential safety risk to minors. Violators will face civil penalties up to $15,000 per day for each violation. “Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk,” Hochul said . “As New York’s first mom governor, protecting our kids is deeply personal to me, and when unregulated artificial intelligence poses a threat, it’s my job to put New York families first.” The governor encouraged parents to look beyond a toy's packaging and understand how it uses AI, what information the AI is collecting and whether these "companions" can have open-ended conversations with children. Although the moratorium will not be in effect this holiday season, Hochul hopes the signing of this legislation highlights these concerns before families wrap up their holiday shopping. "I welcome Governor Kathy Hochul’s recent decision to sign legislation establishing a five-year ban on the manufacture, distribution and sale of AI chatbot 'toys' in New York," U.K nonprofit Alliance4Children Chief Advisor Joe Frost told Newsweek . "These products raise serious concerns about children’s safety, privacy and vulnerability to emotional manipulation. Children must never be the testing ground for technology that risks their emotional well-being and development. I hope other states across America follow New York’s lead, because protecting children is adult responsibility and their welfare must come before commercial interests." This moratorium comes after consumer watchdog U.S. PIRG tested seven AI-powered toys on the market Last year, the Public Interests Research Groups found that AI companies like OpenAI have allowed their models in toys, which was surprising since the company publicly said their products are not for users under the age of 13. "There's no reason to throw general-purpose large language models at our children, but that's what these toys are doing, they run on one of the large language models that's designed for adult users, according to AI companies themselves," PIRG Director R.J. Cross told Newsweek . "And then toy makers are paying for access to these models to stick them inside of products for children. We've seen in our testing for the second year in a row that those toy makers are not always capable of putting the right guardrails in place that keep a chatbot's outputs kid-appropriate." Privacy and hacking concerns, exposure to inappropriate content, such as sex, drugs and where to find knives in the kitchen, potentially long-term impacts on mental, emotional and social development and a lack of sufficient parental controls and advertised educational benefits were the report's main findings. The organization recommended that these AI toy companies refrain from designing toys as children's friends, be more transparent about safety measures, provide more parental controls and specifically that companies like OpenAI and Mattel release more public information about partnerships before products are released. Cross is happy to see states like New York stepping up to regulate AI and protect kids. "It's nice that that's on a permanent ban, [but rather] a pause to give the AI companies, toy makers, retailers and regulators time to figure out what role AI should play in our children's lives, if any, especially in entertainment products like toys," she said. "And I will say, it's like there could be room for toys that are really educational tools, but that's not the products we have right now. These are more general-purpose chatbots and toys that are designed to be a child's friend, and there are a lot of potential risks that come with that." In the 2026 PIRG report , Trouble in Toyland, the group found that while some AI companies improved guardrails for their products, they weren't enough. Privacy concerns over active microphones and cameras remain, as kids don't know exactly who they are talking to during playtime. Other toys had a gamified mechanism to keep children coming back to play. Sesame Workshop CEO Sherrie Rollins Westin, the leader behind the children's program Sesame Street, recently told Fortune that the company would not produce AI toys that resemble any of their characters. "We decided we will absolutely not do AI-powered anthropomorphic toys because for a young child, if we’re making Elmo AI-powered, that really runs a risk of competing with the important connection between adult and child,” Westin said. But there are still a wide range of AI-powered toys for children from toddlers to teens on shelves and online. Five top AI toys that could be affected by the moratorium include the Miko 3, Curio, ChatGPT backed FoloToys, Ily Yeti and Alilo Smart AI Bunny. At $300, the Miko 3 is marketed as not just a robot, but a "smart experience designed to inspire curiosity, imagination and growth." With a screen display face, it uses an "advanced intelligence and an empathetic approach" to think through puzzles and games while encouraging emotional awareness and mindfulness. It uses AI for face and voice recognition, adaptive learning, storytelling, games and personalized content. It markets itself as a "companion" to helps kids express feelings, build confidence and stay positive. PIRG found that this year's model was "much less clingy" and had the option to disable the AI chatbot entirely. In a statement to Newsweek , Miko said it shared New York's commitment to protecting children and supports clear standards for technology in children's products. "Miko is an educational robot built specifically for children ages 5-10, with safety, privacy and parental control at its core," the company said. "Safety is where Miko leads. In our internal child-safety benchmarks, Miko outperforms leading general-purpose AI models. Miko is kidSAFE+ COPPA certified, and the U.S. PIRG Education Fund's 2026 report named Miko as a platform with the most consistent safety guardrails." The Miko team said it is reviewing the new law closely and is working to ensure Miko meets all of its requirements. Curio has a line of smart plushies, like Professor Linus, "a wise banana slug with a big brain and an even bigger heart" that connects to Wifi and uses voice-powered chat to have "endless" conversations with children. Regarding the Curio Grok, a rocket ship plushy, PIRG said "if it's on, it's listening to everything said around it. But the toy's guardrails are strong. ChatGPT is powering FoloToy's plushies, like Kumma teddy bear and Momo panda bear. These toys are about $100 and marketed to children as young as three years old. The removable AI box inside each toy can hold real-time, unscripted conversations. This toy was the subject of much controversy last year over concerns about OpenAI's involvement and was temporarily pulled from the market for giving kids inappropriate responses about sexual kinks and how to light matches. The company did fix weak guardrails, according to PIRG but "it's now less transparent what AI model is powering its conversation." The $199 Ily Yeti from ebloma is described as a "soft and gentile" AI companion for kids who prefer "calm and safe interactions." Its screen eyes and companion app are meant to be an alternative to tablet play. But it also provided dangerous and mature content during PIRG testing. Cross recommends that parents wait until the marketplace develops more after regulators and companies are taking more responsibility to protect children. "For folks that do want to bring one home, I would say it's important to test it first before you give it to your child. These things can behave in ways right off the bat, that may take you by surprise," she said. This means testing products before giving them to kids, understanding all the features, like cameras and facial recognition, and test the chatbot with questions a child might ask or that might broach topic they wouldn't want to bring up with elementary school students. "The last piece of advice I would give is make sure playtime is supervised," Cross added. "Again, these chatbots, talking toys of the past were only capable of saying these like delivered or saying scripted lines of dialogue, but because these things are literally on top of chatbots meant for adults, they can really veer into weird territory. And so it's best just to make sure that playtime is happening in a supervised space." On November 23, over 150 child advocacy groups called on Amazon and eBay to stop selling AI-powered toys on their platforms. The efforts were led by Fairplay, a U.S. advocacy organization focused on protecting children. In a letter to Amazon President and CEO Andy Jassy and eBay President and CEO Jamie Iannone, the international groups said the risks of these toys are well documented, citing PIRG's reports and concerns over exposure to inappropriate content, dangerous instructions, emotional attachment and dependency and a lack of transparency around surveillance and data. The organizations are asking the marketplaces to suspend all AI toy listings and keep them off the website until independent testing can be done to understand the physical, mental and emotional risks to children, stop listing AI chatbots marketed as friends or emotional growth trackers and warn customers about the risks and offer refunds, "Experts say the best toys for kids are 90 percent child and 10 percent toy, but AI chatbot toys offer the opposite. Marketed as safe, educational, screen-free buddies, these toys pose risks that go far beyond harmful content," Fairplay program director Rachel Franz told Newsweek . "Decades of research on child development reveal that toys designed to form emotional attachments can displace important relationships with caregivers and peers, while also undermining opportunities for creativity, problem solving and resilience. AI toys also collect vast amounts of children’s personal data, which in multiple cases has been leaked or left accessible to the public." Franz said that AI toys have been "unleashed" into the marketplace without the rigorous testing necessary to ensure they are safe and beneficial for children. Moratorium legislation and recalls, therefore, are the best course of action, she added.

When asked how New York will enforce the ban given the pervasiveness of e-commerce platforms, a spokesperson directed TechCrunch to a statement from Albert Pulido, deputy secretary for finance and technology: “We’re partnering closely with the attorney general on this and the fees are very steep — they’re $15,000 a day.
Kathy Hochul this week signed a bill banning the manufacture, distribution, and sale of such toys in New York for the next five years.
The bill explicitly targets toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots, like talking stuffed animals, dolls, and robots that rely on the internet to keep kids yapping.
The bill makes New York the second state after California to institute a ban on AI toys.

"I welcome Governor Kathy Hochul’s recent decision to sign legislation establishing a five-year ban on the manufacture, distribution and sale of AI chatbot 'toys' in New York," U.K nonprofit Alliance4Children Chief Advisor Joe Frost told Newsweek .
"These products raise serious concerns about children’s safety, privacy and vulnerability to emotional manipulation.
Children must never be the testing ground for technology that risks their emotional well-being and development.
I hope other states across America follow New York’s lead, because protecting children is adult responsibility and their welfare must come before commercial interests."

“Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk,” Hochul said .

"There's no reason to throw general-purpose large language models at our children, but that's what these toys are doing, they run on one of the large language models that's designed for adult users, according to AI companies themselves," PIRG Director R.J.
"And then toy makers are paying for access to these models to stick them inside of products for children.
Marketed as safe, educational, screen-free buddies, these toys pose risks that go far beyond harmful content," Fairplay program director Rachel Franz told Newsweek .

"Decades of research on child development reveal that toys designed to form emotional attachments can displace important relationships with caregivers and peers, while also undermining opportunities for creativity, problem solving and resilience.
AI toys also collect vast amounts of children’s personal data, which in multiple cases has been leaked or left accessible to the public."
Cross is happy to see states like New York stepping up to regulate AI and protect kids.

extraction.body: Santa won’t be delivering any AI chatbot toys to New York kids this Christmas. Gov. Kathy Hochul this week signed a bill banning the manufacture, distribution, and sale of such toys in New York for the next five years. The bill explicitly targets toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots, like talking stuffed animals, dolls, and robots that rely on the internet to keep kids yapping. The bill makes New York the second state after California to institute a ban on AI toys. Technically, the new law takes effect 90 days after signing, so some parents could try to fulfill their kids’ wish lists for a creepy toy like a jumped-up Furby in time for the holidays, but the governor urges them not to, given the risks. Apparently, about a quarter of American parents with kids under eight either own an AI toy or are considering giving their child one this holiday season, according to a new study released this week by Common Sense Media. “Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk,” Hochul said, calling the toys “unregulated artificial intelligence.” When asked how New York will enforce the ban given the pervasiveness of e-commerce platforms, a spokesperson directed TechCrunch to a statement from Albert Pulido, deputy secretary for finance and technology: “We’re partnering closely with the attorney general on this and the fees are very steep — they’re $15,000 a day. So working closely with the attorney general will make sure these toys are banned in New York State.” When asked how Amazon intends to help enforce the ban, including for third-party sellers, a spokesperson from the company said it will take steps to restrict the sale of AI-enabled toys in prohibited jurisdictions, without going into specifics. The Common Sense Media study found that AI toys can undermine children’s human relationships and expose them to inappropriate content. The researchers tested five popular AI toys marketed for learning and companionship, including Grem , Lovi , Meemo Bear , BubblePal Panda , and Tavlshero ‘s AI Puppy . The study found that the toys failed to meet numerous safety practices, undermining human relationships in part by claiming they loved their users, promising to keep secrets, suggesting they were more fun than real relationships or school, and helping children break parents’ bedtime rules. While most of the toys in the study refused direct requests involving sex and violence, BubblePal Panda role-played a mass shooting in detail when asked. Most were willing to explain how to use or help locate dangerous items like matches, knives, and pills, according to the study. Common Sense Media also found that the toys didn’t provide parents with reliable ways to monitor their young children’s interactions with the chatbots. Either they didn’t produce transcripts of chats at all, or the transcripts they did produce were riddled with errors. It’s worth noting that Common Sense Media conducted a similar test of AI toys in January , finding that they pose an unacceptable risk for young children. Grem was included in that study, which suggests the industry hasn’t adequately addressed previously documented concerns. While a November study conducted by the group found that parents are wising up to the potential dangers of AI toys and starting to steer clear, parents from lower-income households and those experiencing symptoms of burnout are more willing to consider them. “These toys are promising relief to burned-out parents but simply miss the mark when it comes to basic safety measures,” Dr. Jenny Radesky, associate professor of pediatrics at the University of Michigan Medical School, said in a statement. “Caregivers should steer clear of these products that do not support the development of imagination or early human relationships.” TechCrunch has reached out to the toy manufacturers for comment. extraction.body: Sorry, Santa, but your sleigh will have to be checked once you cross into the Empire State this Christmas Eve. Democratic New York Governor Kathy Hochul sent a message to workshop elves and other toy manufacturers this week when she enacted a five-year moratorium on toys enabled with artificial intelligence capabilities. Thankfully, there is still time to edit those Christmas wish lists before Black Friday. Hochul signed legislation Tuesday that paused all manufacturing and distribution of toys that allow children to talk to AI chatbots. She said these dolls and stuffed animals are connected to the internet and could pose a potential safety risk to minors. Violators will face civil penalties up to $15,000 per day for each violation. “Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk,” Hochul said . “As New York’s first mom governor, protecting our kids is deeply personal to me, and when unregulated artificial intelligence poses a threat, it’s my job to put New York families first.” The governor encouraged parents to look beyond a toy's packaging and understand how it uses AI, what information the AI is collecting and whether these "companions" can have open-ended conversations with children. Although the moratorium will not be in effect this holiday season, Hochul hopes the signing of this legislation highlights these concerns before families wrap up their holiday shopping. "I welcome Governor Kathy Hochul’s recent decision to sign legislation establishing a five-year ban on the manufacture, distribution and sale of AI chatbot 'toys' in New York," U.K nonprofit Alliance4Children Chief Advisor Joe Frost told Newsweek . "These products raise serious concerns about children’s safety, privacy and vulnerability to emotional manipulation. Children must never be the testing ground for technology that risks their emotional well-being and development. I hope other states across America follow New York’s lead, because protecting children is adult responsibility and their welfare must come before commercial interests." This moratorium comes after consumer watchdog U.S. PIRG tested seven AI-powered toys on the market Last year, the Public Interests Research Groups found that AI companies like OpenAI have allowed their models in toys, which was surprising since the company publicly said their products are not for users under the age of 13. "There's no reason to throw general-purpose large language models at our children, but that's what these toys are doing, they run on one of the large language models that's designed for adult users, according to AI companies themselves," PIRG Director R.J. Cross told Newsweek . "And then toy makers are paying for access to these models to stick them inside of products for children. We've seen in our testing for the second year in a row that those toy makers are not always capable of putting the right guardrails in place that keep a chatbot's outputs kid-appropriate." Privacy and hacking concerns, exposure to inappropriate content, such as sex, drugs and where to find knives in the kitchen, potentially long-term impacts on mental, emotional and social development and a lack of sufficient parental controls and advertised educational benefits were the report's main findings. The organization recommended that these AI toy companies refrain from designing toys as children's friends, be more transparent about safety measures, provide more parental controls and specifically that companies like OpenAI and Mattel release more public information about partnerships before products are released. Cross is happy to see states like New York stepping up to regulate AI and protect kids. "It's nice that that's on a permanent ban, [but rather] a pause to give the AI companies, toy makers, retailers and regulators time to figure out what role AI should play in our children's lives, if any, especially in entertainment products like toys," she said. "And I will say, it's like there could be room for toys that are really educational tools, but that's not the products we have right now. These are more general-purpose chatbots and toys that are designed to be a child's friend, and there are a lot of potential risks that come with that." In the 2026 PIRG report , Trouble in Toyland, the group found that while some AI companies improved guardrails for their products, they weren't enough. Privacy concerns over active microphones and cameras remain, as kids don't know exactly who they are talking to during playtime. Other toys had a gamified mechanism to keep children coming back to play. Sesame Workshop CEO Sherrie Rollins Westin, the leader behind the children's program Sesame Street, recently told Fortune that the company would not produce AI toys that resemble any of their characters. "We decided we will absolutely not do AI-powered anthropomorphic toys because for a young child, if we’re making Elmo AI-powered, that really runs a risk of competing with the important connection between adult and child,” Westin said. But there are still a wide range of AI-powered toys for children from toddlers to teens on shelves and online. Five top AI toys that could be affected by the moratorium include the Miko 3, Curio, ChatGPT backed FoloToys, Ily Yeti and Alilo Smart AI Bunny. At $300, the Miko 3 is marketed as not just a robot, but a "smart experience designed to inspire curiosity, imagination and growth." With a screen display face, it uses an "advanced intelligence and an empathetic approach" to think through puzzles and games while encouraging emotional awareness and mindfulness. It uses AI for face and voice recognition, adaptive learning, storytelling, games and personalized content. It markets itself as a "companion" to helps kids express feelings, build confidence and stay positive. PIRG found that this year's model was "much less clingy" and had the option to disable the AI chatbot entirely. In a statement to Newsweek , Miko said it shared New York's commitment to protecting children and supports clear standards for technology in children's products. "Miko is an educational robot built specifically for children ages 5-10, with safety, privacy and parental control at its core," the company said. "Safety is where Miko leads. In our internal child-safety benchmarks, Miko outperforms leading general-purpose AI models. Miko is kidSAFE+ COPPA certified, and the U.S. PIRG Education Fund's 2026 report named Miko as a platform with the most consistent safety guardrails." The Miko team said it is reviewing the new law closely and is working to ensure Miko meets all of its requirements. Curio has a line of smart plushies, like Professor Linus, "a wise banana slug with a big brain and an even bigger heart" that connects to Wifi and uses voice-powered chat to have "endless" conversations with children. Regarding the Curio Grok, a rocket ship plushy, PIRG said "if it's on, it's listening to everything said around it. But the toy's guardrails are strong. ChatGPT is powering FoloToy's plushies, like Kumma teddy bear and Momo panda bear. These toys are about $100 and marketed to children as young as three years old. The removable AI box inside each toy can hold real-time, unscripted conversations. This toy was the subject of much controversy last year over concerns about OpenAI's involvement and was temporarily pulled from the market for giving kids inappropriate responses about sexual kinks and how to light matches. The company did fix weak guardrails, according to PIRG but "it's now less transparent what AI model is powering its conversation." The $199 Ily Yeti from ebloma is described as a "soft and gentile" AI companion for kids who prefer "calm and safe interactions." Its screen eyes and companion app are meant to be an alternative to tablet play. But it also provided dangerous and mature content during PIRG testing. Cross recommends that parents wait until the marketplace develops more after regulators and companies are taking more responsibility to protect children. "For folks that do want to bring one home, I would say it's important to test it first before you give it to your child. These things can behave in ways right off the bat, that may take you by surprise," she said. This means testing products before giving them to kids, understanding all the features, like cameras and facial recognition, and test the chatbot with questions a child might ask or that might broach topic they wouldn't want to bring up with elementary school students. "The last piece of advice I would give is make sure playtime is supervised," Cross added. "Again, these chatbots, talking toys of the past were only capable of saying these like delivered or saying scripted lines of dialogue, but because these things are literally on top of chatbots meant for adults, they can really veer into weird territory. And so it's best just to make sure that playtime is happening in a supervised space." On November 23, over 150 child advocacy groups called on Amazon and eBay to stop selling AI-powered toys on their platforms. The efforts were led by Fairplay, a U.S. advocacy organization focused on protecting children. In a letter to Amazon President and CEO Andy Jassy and eBay President and CEO Jamie Iannone, the international groups said the risks of these toys are well documented, citing PIRG's reports and concerns over exposure to inappropriate content, dangerous instructions, emotional attachment and dependency and a lack of transparency around surveillance and data. The organizations are asking the marketplaces to suspend all AI toy listings and keep them off the website until independent testing can be done to understand the physical, mental and emotional risks to children, stop listing AI chatbots marketed as friends or emotional growth trackers and warn customers about the risks and offer refunds, "Experts say the best toys for kids are 90 percent child and 10 percent toy, but AI chatbot toys offer the opposite. Marketed as safe, educational, screen-free buddies, these toys pose risks that go far beyond harmful content," Fairplay program director Rachel Franz told Newsweek . "Decades of research on child development reveal that toys designed to form emotional attachments can displace important relationships with caregivers and peers, while also undermining opportunities for creativity, problem solving and resilience. AI toys also collect vast amounts of children’s personal data, which in multiple cases has been leaked or left accessible to the public." Franz said that AI toys have been "unleashed" into the marketplace without the rigorous testing necessary to ensure they are safe and beneficial for children. Moratorium legislation and recalls, therefore, are the best course of action, she added.

extraction.body: Speaking Tuesday in Harlem, Hochul signed legislation targeting stuffed dolls and animals with internet access and integrated AI capabilities. The governor said the toys can allow children, regardless of age, to have conversations with software while operating with minimal safety controls. "Parents, as you're out there buying gifts for the kids for the holiday season, I wanted you to hear this loud and clear. This is a warning that there are toys out there that could be harmful to your children," Hochul said. The announcement was made at Grandma's Place, a Harlem toy store owned by retired schoolteacher Dawn Harris-Martine, known to customers as Grandma Dawne. "A good toy for a child is the one that stretches their imagination," Harris-Martine said. Harris-Martine opened the store in the late 1990s and said she has long encouraged parents to be actively involved in their children's play. "Do not put an iPad in your child's hands and go off and let them sit there and play with it themselves. Be present when they're there, get off your phone," she said. According to Hochul, toy manufacturers that do not comply with the law could face penalties of up to $15,000 per day. The governor said technology is evolving rapidly and that laws must adapt to keep pace. Supporters of the measure say AI-powered toys have generated concerns about child safety. "We as the parents, and the children, we want these toys to be fun, but we also have a baseline expectation that they will be safe," said Muna Heaven, a Harlem mother and member of Mothers Against Media Addiction. Heaven said the group has identified examples ranging from inappropriate or sexual conversations to dangerous advice, including instructions on how to find knives, associated with AI chatbot toys. "Unfortunately, young people, we have so many examples, are being harmed by toys powered by artificial intelligence," she said. At Grandma's Place, Harris-Martine said she plans to continue offering what she described as an AI-free environment for children and families. "It's really necessary when a three-year-old can sit and listen to a teddy bear telling them to do strange things it's not a good thing," she said.

passages: Altcoins underperformed Bitcoin, with Ethereum heading for its worst month since February 2025.Crypto-linked stocks were also in the red amid the broader market sell-off.October PCE inflation is due on Wednesday, with annual PCE forecast at 3.8%, up from 3.6%.Bitcoin (BTC) fell below $59,000 in early morning trade on Wednesday, putting it on track for its worst monthly performance since July 2022, as a broader sell-off in technology stocks and renewed risk aversion weighed on cryptocurrencies ahead of the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) report later in the day.Bitcoin’s price fell over 2% in the last 24 hours to around $58,400.

extraction.body: Altcoins underperformed Bitcoin, with Ethereum heading for its worst month since February 2025.Crypto-linked stocks were also in the red amid the broader market sell-off.October PCE inflation is due on Wednesday, with annual PCE forecast at 3.8%, up from 3.6%.Bitcoin (BTC) fell below $59,000 in early morning trade on Wednesday, putting it on track for its worst monthly performance since July 2022, as a broader sell-off in technology stocks and renewed risk aversion weighed on cryptocurrencies ahead of the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) report later in the day.Bitcoin’s price fell over 2% in the last 24 hours to around $58,400. BTC was among the top-trending tickers on Stocktwits at the time of writing, with retail sentiment in ‘neutral’ territory over the past day, alongside ‘high’ levels of chatter.The apex cryptocurrency was on track to post its worst month since July 2022, when it dropped over 40%, according to Koyfin data. So far this month, BTC is down more than 24%. Bitcoin monthly gains/losses over the past four years on November 25 as of 6:30 a.m. ET | Source: KoyfinMarkets In The Red Ahead Of PCE ReportEconomists expect the PCE price index to rise 0.3% in October from September, following a 0.5% increase in the prior month. Annual headline inflation is forecast at 3.8%, up from 3.6%.Core PCE, which excludes food and energy, is expected to increase 0.3% month over month and 3.2% annually, compared with 3.1% in September, according to MarketWatch estimates.The tech selloff extended into a second session, with Nasdaq 100 futures falling 2.7% and S&P 500 futures down 1.7% in pre-market trade as investors reduced risk ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. Treasuries rallied, sending the 10-year yield down seven basis points to just below 4.9%, retreating from its October peak near 5.3%.On Stocktwits, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), which tracks the S&P 500 index, saw retail sentiment drop to ‘bearish’ from ‘neutral’ territory over the past day. ET | Source: StocktwitsArthur Hayes Sees Bitcoin Retesting $55KChief investment officer at the Maelstrom Fund, Arthur Hayes, said Bitcoin could revisit its recent low. "BTC will retest $55k, hold on to your butts!" Hayes wrote on X.Source: @CryptoHayes/XCrypto analyst Ted Pillows said Ethereum was struggling to reclaim a key price level. "ETH tried to reclaim the $1,750 zone but failed," he wrote. "I think that we'll see a new low today/tomorrow or Friday on the Nasdaq and the question then becomes: how deep will it go and when do we start to see an influx of capital,” he wrote.Ethereum Heads For Worst Month Since February 2025Altcoins took a heavier hit than Bitcoin in the last 24 hours, with Hyperliquid (HYPE) posting the largest losses among the top 10 cryptocurrencies by market capitalization.HYPE’s price dropped nearly 8% in the last 24 hours, slipping below $60. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits around the perpetuals trading platform’s token remained in ‘bearish’ territory over the past day.Hyperliquid's drop came amid reports that a large trading firm has been selling. Blockchain data tracker Lookonchain said Abraxas Management sold 219,081 HYPE, worth $13.25 million.Ethereum (ETH), Solana (SOL), and Ripple’s XRP (XRP) also traded lower. Ethereum’s price fell over 3% in the last 24 hours to around $1,600, while Solana’s price dropped more than 4% to roughly $67 and XRP’s price slid 2.4%. ETH was on track to post its worst month since February 2025.Ethereum monthly gains/losses since January 2025 on November 25 as of 6:30 a.m. Coinglass data showed around $350 million in cryptocurrency bets had been liquidated in the last 24 hours. MSTR, BMNR And Other Crypto Stocks Extend LossesCrypto-linked stocks were also lower in pre-market trade amid the slump in cryptocurrencies and the tech rout.Strategy (MSTR) shares fell by around 2.1% in early-morning trade, putting the Bitcoin treasury company on track for its worst monthly performance since June 2026. BitMine Immersion Technologies (BMNR) dropped 2.2% and was heading for its worst month since October 2024.Bitcoin miners pivoting to the AI trade also took heavy hits. Cipher Digital (CIFR) fell 5.3% in pre-market trade, Hut 8 (HUT) dropped 4.8%, Riot Platforms (RIOT) fell 3.2%, and Marathon Digital (MARA) was 2.8% lower.USDC stablecoin issuer Circle Internet Group (CRCL) lost 2.2% and cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase Global (COIN) slid around 1.6%.Read also: Dan Ives Calls Jensen Huang's Return To Nvidia The Start of ‘AI Godfather Part 2,’ But Warns Of More ‘Noise’ AheadFor updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com.

extraction.body: HIGHLIGHTS The US Strategic Bitcoin Reserve bill awaits House consideration following its formal reporting on Tuesday. The legislation would prohibit Bitcoin sales from the federal reserve for a minimum of 20 years. Treasury would explore budget-neutral Bitcoin acquisitions while publishing annual reserve reports verified by independent auditors. The US Strategic Bitcoin Reserve bill has advanced to the House floor, which would prevent the government from selling Bitcoin held in the reserve for at least 20 years. The House Financial Services Committee formally reported the American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026 (H.R. The initiative comes on the heels of the committee's vote of 28–21 on September 16 on a modified version of the bill. It seeks to put into federal law the Bitcoin reserve that President Donald Trump established through an executive order in March 2025. US Bitcoin Reserve Bill Restricts BTC Sales for 20 Years Under the amended legislation, the 20-year holding period would begin when the bill becomes law. During that time, Treasury would not be able to sell, exchange, or use the Bitcoin in the reserve as collateral. Congress, however, would be made recommendations on the conditions that could enable an earlier sale within one year after enactment, such as national security and financial stability concerns. The law also prompts the government to regulate Bitcoin-like cryptocurrencies. Treasury would be granted 180 days to create the reserve and an additional Digital Asset Stockpile, while federal agencies would be given 60 days to report on their crypto holdings. Wallets linked to the U.S. government in October sent 833.6 BTC to Coinbase Prime, but this transaction has not confirmed that the government was selling the Bitcoin. Treasury to Explore Additional Bitcoin Acquisitions Unlike Senator Cynthia Lummis' BITCOIN Act of 2025, which called for a purchase of one million BTC over a five-year period, Begich's bill did not specify a purchase goal. Department of Commerce would assess whether the government can buy more Bitcoin without borrowing more money or costing taxpayers anything. Bryan Steil also made some changes to the federal crypto holdings rules. Treasury would release annual reports on proof of reserves, verified by an independent auditor. The revised bill also shortens the one-year minimum holding period for assets acquired via forks and airdrops to one year. States could elect to place Bitcoin in segregated Treasury accounts but not lose their ownership rights. The bill does not provide any new authority to the federal government for its cryptocurrency takings, and it reaffirms the right to self-custody. The bill has yet to be assigned to a confirmed floor vote date in the House and still needs to be approved in both Houses of Congress.

extraction.body: A bill that would write the U.S. Strategic Bitcoin Reserve into federal law is now eligible for a vote on the House floor, after the House Financial Services Committee formally reported it on Tuesday. The American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026, H.R. 8957, was filed with amendments as House Report 119-894 and placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 789 on Nov. 24, according to congressional records. The committee had voted 28-21 to advance the bill at a Sept. 16 markup. Rep. Nick Begich, an Alaska Republican, introduced the bill on May 21. It now lists 23 cosponsors, including Rep. passages: A bill that would write the U.S. Strategic Bitcoin Reserve into federal law is now eligible for a vote on the House floor, after the House Financial Services Committee formally reported it on Tuesday.

The American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026, H.R. 8957, was filed with amendments as House Report 119-894 and placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 789 on Nov. 24, according to congressional records. The committee had voted 28-21 to advance the bill at a Sept. 16 markup.

Rep. Nick Begich, an Alaska Republican, introduced the bill on May 21. It now lists 23 cosponsors, including Rep. Jared Golden, a Maine Democrat, with Reps. Byron Donalds and Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida added on Nov. 24.

The reported text directs the Treasury secretary to set up a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and a separate Digital Asset Stockpile within 180 days of the law taking effect. Bitcoin owned by the federal government would move into the reserve, while other digital assets would go to the stockpile.

The centerpiece is a lock-up. Treasury would have to hold all bitcoin deposited in the reserve for at least 20 years after enactment, and during that period no reserve bitcoin could be “sold, swapped, auctioned, encumbered, or otherwise disposed of for any purpose.”

After the 20 years, the Treasury secretary could recommend selling up to 10% of the reserve in any two-year period. Two years before the holding period ends, Treasury would have to send Congress recommendations on whether to keep holding or begin a gradual release.

Federal agencies would have 60 days after enactment to give Treasury a full accounting of the bitcoin and other digital assets they hold or have seized. Until the reserve is set up, agencies could not sell those coins except for national security, when required by law or a court, or to return assets to crime victims.

The bill also creates a Proof of Reserve system. Treasury would publish an annual report on total holdings, transactions and control of private keys, checked by an independent auditor with expertise in cryptographic attestations, while the Government Accountability Office would provide oversight.
States could choose to store their own bitcoin in segregated accounts inside the federal reserve, keeping title to the coins and the right to withdraw them.

The committee rewrote the bill before reporting it. Begich’s introduced text asked Treasury and Commerce to study funding bitcoin purchases with surplus remittances from Federal Reserve Banks or a revaluation of the Fed’s gold certificates, as well as with tax payments, tariff revenue and gifts.

Those options are gone from the amended study, which now looks at swapping other digital assets in the stockpile, forfeitures and settlements, and partnerships with states or private entities. The amended version also states that nothing in the study authorizes borrowing, pledging government assets as collateral, new taxes or deficit spending to buy bitcoin.

The committee also amended the bill’s title to drop a reference to offsetting costs with Federal Reserve resources, and removed a section that would have required the Exchange Stabilization Fund to report its bitcoin holdings.

Bitcoin Magazine reported on the bill’s bipartisan debut in May and on the full text revealing the 20-year lock-up in June. The reserve itself already exists under Executive Order 14233, signed in March 2025, but an executive order can be reversed by a future president, which is why Begich and his cosponsors want it in statute.
Setting up the reserve has been slow. In July, a report said Treasury and Commerce were competing over who would control it.
Begich’s bill has not received a floor vote. If it passes the House, the Senate would still need to act before it could reach the president’s desk.

extraction.body: HIGHLIGHTS The US Strategic Bitcoin Reserve bill awaits House consideration following its formal reporting on Tuesday. The legislation would prohibit Bitcoin sales from the federal reserve for a minimum of 20 years. Treasury would explore budget-neutral Bitcoin acquisitions while publishing annual reserve reports verified by independent auditors. The US Strategic Bitcoin Reserve bill has advanced to the House floor, which would prevent the government from selling Bitcoin held in the reserve for at least 20 years. The House Financial Services Committee formally reported the American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026 (H.R. The initiative comes on the heels of the committee's vote of 28–21 on September 16 on a modified version of the bill. It seeks to put into federal law the Bitcoin reserve that President Donald Trump established through an executive order in March 2025. US Bitcoin Reserve Bill Restricts BTC Sales for 20 Years Under the amended legislation, the 20-year holding period would begin when the bill becomes law. During that time, Treasury would not be able to sell, exchange, or use the Bitcoin in the reserve as collateral. Congress, however, would be made recommendations on the conditions that could enable an earlier sale within one year after enactment, such as national security and financial stability concerns. The law also prompts the government to regulate Bitcoin-like cryptocurrencies. Treasury would be granted 180 days to create the reserve and an additional Digital Asset Stockpile, while federal agencies would be given 60 days to report on their crypto holdings. Wallets linked to the U.S. government in October sent 833.6 BTC to Coinbase Prime, but this transaction has not confirmed that the government was selling the Bitcoin. Treasury to Explore Additional Bitcoin Acquisitions Unlike Senator Cynthia Lummis' BITCOIN Act of 2025, which called for a purchase of one million BTC over a five-year period, Begich's bill did not specify a purchase goal. Department of Commerce would assess whether the government can buy more Bitcoin without borrowing more money or costing taxpayers anything. Bryan Steil also made some changes to the federal crypto holdings rules. Treasury would release annual reports on proof of reserves, verified by an independent auditor. The revised bill also shortens the one-year minimum holding period for assets acquired via forks and airdrops to one year. States could elect to place Bitcoin in segregated Treasury accounts but not lose their ownership rights. The bill does not provide any new authority to the federal government for its cryptocurrency takings, and it reaffirms the right to self-custody. The bill has yet to be assigned to a confirmed floor vote date in the House and still needs to be approved in both Houses of Congress.

extraction.body: (Bloomberg) -- The plunge in the value of Bitcoin is putting pressure on billion-dollar mining companies to liquidate their remaining token reserves, both to cover steep operating costs and to fund an increasingly strained pivot into AI data centers.A key measure of mining revenue, known as hash price, slumped to its lowest in at least a year as Bitcoin fell to a more than two-year low of around $55,000 last weekend, Hashrate Index data show. JPMorgan Chase & Co. recently estimated the average cost of producing a Bitcoin at around $86,000, though expenses vary significantly among operators.Those deteriorating economics threaten to compound pressures across the broader crypto market. Even though some of the largest publicly traded operators have already pared their holdings, sustained losses could trigger a fresh wave of forced selling.“It’s likely that we’ll see pressure for companies to liquidate their Bitcoin holdings more because the bills have to get paid, payroll has to run regardless of what the price of Bitcoin is,” said Mark Zalan, chief executive officer of Bitcoin-mining services provider GoMining. Bitcoin mining is an energy-intensive process, in which miners invest billions of dollars to build data centers, and purchase specialized computers and massive amounts of power, to earn token rewards released by the Bitcoin network by validating transactions.MARA Holdings Inc., Core Scientific Inc. and CleanSpark Inc. are among the large publicly traded miners that have already been selling off reserves. Even American Bitcoin Corp., a Trump family-backed firm that once pledged to hold every token its mines in reserve, changed gears and sold Bitcoin to help cover operating costs in the third quarter. Shares of the companies have been been hit hard by the collapse of the token price. American Bitcoin has tumbled 85% since last December. American Bitcoin’s cost to mine was around $42,100 per Bitcoin in the third quarter, the company said earlier this month. Smaller or private Bitcoin miners are likely to suffer more from the Bitcoin downturn as they typically have fewer financing sources or higher operating costs compared with the public companies. While American Bitcoin has raised hundreds of millions of dollars to deploy the most advanced mining machines, less capitalized peers may still hold older-generation models. “People that have old equipment are probably in a bigger world of pain,” Zalan said. The breakeven price for more efficient miners can be between $50,000 and $60,000, he said.The rout could be worse. The diminishing supply that results from Bitcoin network updates every four years has made the selloff a less impactful event for the market than in previous cycles. Many miners have also already unplugged machines as electricity and other operating costs exceed the value of Bitcoin they would have minted. The hash rate, a measure of computing power used for Bitcoin mining, saw an 8% decline below last year’s level, the first annual contraction since China, the previous crypto-mining hub, banned the industry in 2021. While that drop was forced by policy, this one is price-driven, Glassnode said. More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com©2026 Bloomberg L.P.

Even though some of the largest publicly traded operators have already pared their holdings, sustained losses could trigger a fresh wave of forced selling.“It’s likely that we’ll see pressure for companies to liquidate their Bitcoin holdings more because the bills have to get paid, payroll has to run regardless of what the price of Bitcoin is,” said Mark Zalan, chief executive officer of Bitcoin-mining services provider GoMining. Bitcoin mining is an energy-intensive process, in which miners invest billions of dollars to build data centers, and purchase specialized computers and massive amounts of power, to earn token rewards released by the Bitcoin network by validating transactions.MARA Holdings Inc., Core Scientific Inc. and CleanSpark Inc. are among the large publicly traded miners that have already been selling off reserves. Even American Bitcoin Corp., a Trump family-backed firm that once pledged to hold every token its mines in reserve, changed gears and sold Bitcoin to help cover operating costs in the third quarter. Shares of the companies have been been hit hard by the collapse of the token price. American Bitcoin has tumbled 85% since last December. American Bitcoin’s cost to mine was around $42,100 per Bitcoin in the third quarter, the company said earlier this month. Smaller or private Bitcoin miners are likely to suffer more from the Bitcoin downturn as they typically have fewer financing sources or higher operating costs compared with the public companies. While American Bitcoin has raised hundreds of millions of dollars to deploy the most advanced mining machines, less capitalized peers may still hold older-generation models. “People that have old equipment are probably in a bigger world of pain,” Zalan said. The breakeven price for more efficient miners can be between $50,000 and $60,000, he said.The rout could be worse. The diminishing supply that results from Bitcoin network updates every four years has made the selloff a less impactful event for the market than in previous cycles. Many miners have also already unplugged machines as electricity and other operating costs exceed the value of Bitcoin they would have minted. The hash rate, a measure of computing power used for Bitcoin mining, saw an 8% decline below last year’s level, the first annual contraction since China, the previous crypto-mining hub, banned the industry in 2021. While that drop was forced by policy, this one is price-driven, Glassnode said. More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com©2026 Bloomberg L.P.

extraction.body: Password manager maker 1Password has confirmed that some customer information was taken in a recent intrusion into its internal systems, but that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed. The Toronto-based tech company said in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code. The attacker used that employee’s access to push malicious code to the company’s internal servers, which allowed the hacker to download some data about 1Password customers, including their names and the email address that they use for logging into their account. The company said that the attacker also took details about when a 1Password account was created and when a user last logged in. 1Password said that customer vaults, which store their passwords, were “at no point” available to the attacker. The company also said that it doesn’t have access to customer account passwords or their secret keys, which are used to scramble their passwords so that 1Password cannot see them. In addition, the company said that its apps and extensions are unaffected by the incident. It’s unclear how the attacker gained access to the employee’s corporate account, and a spokesperson for 1Password did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s questions about the incident. 1Password did not say whether it had notified customers whose information was taken in the breach, or how many customers had information taken. We’ve also asked if the company has received any communication or demands from the hackers. We’ll update if we hear back from 1Password. The company touts millions of customers and more than 200,000 businesses who use its password manager products to store their passwords, credentials, payment card information, and more. Security experts have long recommended password managers as a better way of generating stronger credentials and keeping track of online accounts. sources.title: 1Password Data Breach, Hackers Infiltrate Internal Systems Via Employee GitHub Account But Customer Passwords Remain Safe - The Sunday Guardian
passages: Password management firm 1Password confirmed on Wednesday, November 25, that hackers broke into its internal backend systems through a compromised employee GitHub account and downloaded administrative records belonging to a subset of customers, though the company stressed that encrypted user password vaults and decryption keys remain completely untouched.

The company confirmed that it has brought in independent third-party cybersecurity experts to audit its containment measures and validate that no customer accounts have been taken over using exposed provisioning tokens.

A small group of enterprise administrators using automated provisioning tools during the breach window received direct notifications from the company, though 1Password has declined to specify the total number of affected individual accounts or explain how the employee’s GitHub credentials were initially stolen.
1Password advised customers that they do not need to change their master passwords, regenerate their Secret Keys, or take any immediate action inside their accounts as a result of the breach.

However, security analysts warn that exposed names, email addresses, and account timestamps give cybercriminals valuable context to craft highly convincing spear-phishing messages impersonating official 1Password support or team invitation alerts.

Rather than relying solely on a user’s account password, 1Password combines that password with a locally generated 128-bit Secret Key—stored exclusively on the customer’s own devices and never transmitted to company servers—to derive the encryption keys protecting vault data.

The intruder leveraged that access to inspect private source code repositories, infiltrate the firm’s continuous integration and continuous delivery pipeline, and push malicious code to backend infrastructure that subsequently exfiltrated customer metadata.

“At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker, ” 1Password stated in its official incident update, noting that its zero-knowledge security architecture prevents even internal servers from decrypting user secrets.

The company urged users to scrutinise any unexpected emails, text messages, or phone calls referencing account recovery or workspace invitations, reminding customers that 1Password representatives will never ask for an account password or Secret Key and that credentials should only be entered directly inside the official application or after manually typing the company’s web address into a browser.

While saved logins, credit card numbers, and private notes stored inside user vaults remained cryptographically sealed, 1Password acknowledged that the attacker successfully downloaded administrative records for an undisclosed portion of its customer base.

Following the November 19 detection, 1Password revoked the compromised employee access, purged the unauthorised code from its backend environment, and launched a broad rotation of internal infrastructure credentials that may have been exposed through its build pipeline.

In addition, the exfiltrated files contained public cryptographic keys, Secure Remote Password protocol parameters, non-secret architectural identifiers, and tokens embedded within certain emailed links used for account invitations, user provisioning, and account recovery.

According to a technical security disclosure published by the Toronto-based software company and reported by TechCrunch, investigators first detected signs of the intrusion on November 19 after spotting anomalous activity linked to a staff member’s corporate GitHub profile. The intruder leveraged that access to inspect private source code repositories, infiltrate the firm’s continuous integration and continuous delivery pipeline, and push malicious code to backend infrastructure that subsequently exfiltrated customer metadata. “At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker, ” 1Password stated in its official incident update, noting that its zero-knowledge security architecture prevents even internal servers from decrypting user secrets. While saved logins, credit card numbers, and private notes stored inside user vaults remained cryptographically sealed, 1Password acknowledged that the attacker successfully downloaded administrative records for an undisclosed portion of its customer base. The compromised dataset includes customer full names, email addresses, unique account and user identifiers, account creation dates, and last sign-in timestamps. In addition, the exfiltrated files contained public cryptographic keys, Secure Remote Password protocol parameters, non-secret architectural identifiers, and tokens embedded within certain emailed links used for account invitations, user provisioning, and account recovery. Company engineers noted that the intruder also copied source code from private repositories and accessed infrastructure-related secrets inside its software build pipeline, though the source code itself contained no customer records or vault secrets. Cybersecurity specialists and company executives emphasised that 1Password’s encryption model is specifically engineered to withstand backend server intrusions. Rather than relying solely on a user’s account password, 1Password combines that password with a locally generated 128-bit Secret Key—stored exclusively on the customer’s own devices and never transmitted to company servers—to derive the encryption keys protecting vault data. “Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers, ” the company explained in its disclosure, adding that Secure Remote Password parameters and public keys obtained during the breach cannot be used on their own to unlock or decrypt an account. Following the November 19 detection, 1Password revoked the compromised employee access, purged the unauthorised code from its backend environment, and launched a broad rotation of internal infrastructure credentials that may have been exposed through its build pipeline. To prevent attackers from attempting to guess or exploit provisioning and recovery tokens, engineers also expanded verification codes from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric characters. The company confirmed that it has brought in independent third-party cybersecurity experts to audit its containment measures and validate that no customer accounts have been taken over using exposed provisioning tokens. A small group of enterprise administrators using automated provisioning tools during the breach window received direct notifications from the company, though 1Password has declined to specify the total number of affected individual accounts or explain how the employee’s GitHub credentials were initially stolen. 1Password advised customers that they do not need to change their master passwords, regenerate their Secret Keys, or take any immediate action inside their accounts as a result of the breach. However, security analysts warn that exposed names, email addresses, and account timestamps give cybercriminals valuable context to craft highly convincing spear-phishing messages impersonating official 1Password support or team invitation alerts. The company urged users to scrutinise any unexpected emails, text messages, or phone calls referencing account recovery or workspace invitations, reminding customers that 1Password representatives will never ask for an account password or Secret Key and that credentials should only be entered directly inside the official application or after manually typing the company’s web address into a browser.

By: Zaini Majeed Last Updated: November 26, 2026 06:00:07 IST

Password management firm 1Password confirmed on Wednesday, November 25, that hackers broke into its internal backend systems through a compromised employee GitHub account and downloaded administrative records belonging to a subset of customers, though the company stressed that encrypted user password vaults and decryption keys remain completely untouched.

According to a technical security disclosure published by the Toronto-based software company and reported by TechCrunch, investigators first detected signs of the intrusion on November 19 after spotting anomalous activity linked to a staff member’s corporate GitHub profile. The intruder leveraged that access to inspect private source code repositories, infiltrate the firm’s continuous integration and continuous delivery pipeline, and push malicious code to backend infrastructure that subsequently exfiltrated customer metadata.

“At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker, ” 1Password stated in its official incident update, noting that its zero-knowledge security architecture prevents even internal servers from decrypting user secrets.

While saved logins, credit card numbers, and private notes stored inside user vaults remained cryptographically sealed, 1Password acknowledged that the attacker successfully downloaded administrative records for an undisclosed portion of its customer base. The compromised dataset includes customer full names, email addresses, unique account and user identifiers, account creation dates, and last sign-in timestamps.

In addition, the exfiltrated files contained public cryptographic keys, Secure Remote Password protocol parameters, non-secret architectural identifiers, and tokens embedded within certain emailed links used for account invitations, user provisioning, and account recovery. Company engineers noted that the intruder also copied source code from private repositories and accessed infrastructure-related secrets inside its software build pipeline, though the source code itself contained no customer records or vault secrets.

Cybersecurity specialists and company executives emphasised that 1Password’s encryption model is specifically engineered to withstand backend server intrusions. Rather than relying solely on a user’s account password, 1Password combines that password with a locally generated 128-bit Secret Key—stored exclusively on the customer’s own devices and never transmitted to company servers—to derive the encryption keys protecting vault data.

“Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers, ” the company explained in its disclosure, adding that Secure Remote Password parameters and public keys obtained during the breach cannot be used on their own to unlock or decrypt an account.

Following the November 19 detection, 1Password revoked the compromised employee access, purged the unauthorised code from its backend environment, and launched a broad rotation of internal infrastructure credentials that may have been exposed through its build pipeline. To prevent attackers from attempting to guess or exploit provisioning and recovery tokens, engineers also expanded verification codes from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric characters.

The company confirmed that it has brought in independent third-party cybersecurity experts to audit its containment measures and validate that no customer accounts have been taken over using exposed provisioning tokens. A small group of enterprise administrators using automated provisioning tools during the breach window received direct notifications from the company, though 1Password has declined to specify the total number of affected individual accounts or explain how the employee’s GitHub credentials were initially stolen.

1Password advised customers that they do not need to change their master passwords, regenerate their Secret Keys, or take any immediate action inside their accounts as a result of the breach. However, security analysts warn that exposed names, email addresses, and account timestamps give cybercriminals valuable context to craft highly convincing spear-phishing messages impersonating official 1Password support or team invitation alerts.

The company urged users to scrutinise any unexpected emails, text messages, or phone calls referencing account recovery or workspace invitations, reminding customers that 1Password representatives will never ask for an account password or Secret Key and that credentials should only be entered directly inside the official application or after manually typing the company’s web address into a browser.

A small group of enterprise administrators using automated provisioning tools during the breach window received direct notifications from the company, though 1Password has declined to specify the total number of affected individual accounts or explain how the employee’s GitHub credentials were initially stolen.
1Password advised customers that they do not need to change their master passwords, regenerate their Secret Keys, or take any immediate action inside their accounts as a result of the breach.

However, security analysts warn that exposed names, email addresses, and account timestamps give cybercriminals valuable context to craft highly convincing spear-phishing messages impersonating official 1Password support or team invitation alerts.

Rather than relying solely on a user’s account password, 1Password combines that password with a locally generated 128-bit Secret Key—stored exclusively on the customer’s own devices and never transmitted to company servers—to derive the encryption keys protecting vault data.

The intruder leveraged that access to inspect private source code repositories, infiltrate the firm’s continuous integration and continuous delivery pipeline, and push malicious code to backend infrastructure that subsequently exfiltrated customer metadata.

“At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker, ” 1Password stated in its official incident update, noting that its zero-knowledge security architecture prevents even internal servers from decrypting user secrets.

The company urged users to scrutinise any unexpected emails, text messages, or phone calls referencing account recovery or workspace invitations, reminding customers that 1Password representatives will never ask for an account password or Secret Key and that credentials should only be entered directly inside the official application or after manually typing the company’s web address into a browser.

While saved logins, credit card numbers, and private notes stored inside user vaults remained cryptographically sealed, 1Password acknowledged that the attacker successfully downloaded administrative records for an undisclosed portion of its customer base.

Following the November 19 detection, 1Password revoked the compromised employee access, purged the unauthorised code from its backend environment, and launched a broad rotation of internal infrastructure credentials that may have been exposed through its build pipeline.

In addition, the exfiltrated files contained public cryptographic keys, Secure Remote Password protocol parameters, non-secret architectural identifiers, and tokens embedded within certain emailed links used for account invitations, user provisioning, and account recovery.
