extraction.body: Password manager maker 1Password has confirmed that some customer information was taken in a recent intrusion into its internal systems, but that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed. The Toronto-based tech company said in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code. The attacker used that employee’s access to push malicious code to the company’s internal servers, which allowed the hacker to download some data about 1Password customers, including their names and the email address that they use for logging into their account. The company said that the attacker also took details about when a 1Password account was created and when a user last logged in. 1Password said that customer vaults, which store their passwords, were “at no point” available to the attacker. The company also said that it doesn’t have access to customer account passwords or their secret keys, which are used to scramble their passwords so that 1Password cannot see them. In addition, the company said that its apps and extensions are unaffected by the incident. It’s unclear how the attacker gained access to the employee’s corporate account, and a spokesperson for 1Password did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s questions about the incident. 1Password did not say whether it had notified customers whose information was taken in the breach, or how many customers had information taken. We’ve also asked if the company has received any communication or demands from the hackers. We’ll update if we hear back from 1Password. The company touts millions of customers and more than 200,000 businesses who use its password manager products to store their passwords, credentials, payment card information, and more. Security experts have long recommended password managers as a better way of generating stronger credentials and keeping track of online accounts. sources.title: Switzerland clears 57 jurisdictions for crypto tax data sharing - TradingView
passages: Switzerland’s Federal Council has approved 57 potential partner jurisdictions for the automatic exchange of information on crypto assets starting in 2028, a move that would expand tax authorities’ access to information on taxpayers’ crypto activity across borders.

Switzerland had initially planned to introduce crypto tax reporting requirements in 2026 but delayed implementation by at least a year as lawmakers had yet to determine which jurisdictions the country would exchange information with.
Under the revised timeline, crypto service providers could begin collecting data as early as Jan.

The crypto reporting framework is designed to supplement Switzerland’s existing system for exchanging financial account information and close gaps in tax transparency, according to the State Secretariat for International Finance.
Switzerland introduced the legal framework for that system in 2017 and exchanged financial account data with 113 jurisdictions in 2026.
According to a Wednesday announcement, the approved jurisdictions include all European Union member states, the United Kingdom and several G20 countries.
Switzerland will only share information with jurisdictions that express interest and meet international standards for confidentiality and data security.

Under the revised timeline, crypto service providers could begin collecting data as early as Jan.

The crypto reporting framework is designed to supplement Switzerland’s existing system for exchanging financial account information and close gaps in tax transparency, according to the State Secretariat for International Finance.
Switzerland introduced the legal framework for that system in 2017 and exchanged financial account data with 113 jurisdictions in 2026.
According to a Wednesday announcement, the approved jurisdictions include all European Union member states, the United Kingdom and several G20 countries.
Switzerland will only share information with jurisdictions that express interest and meet international standards for confidentiality and data security.

passages: Switzerland’s Federal Council has approved 57 countries and territories with which the country plans to automatically share tax information on crypto users starting in 2028, extending its long-standing bank data exchange to bitcoin and other digital assets.
Wednesday’s release did not say which countries were dropped or whether the U.S. is now on the list.
Its regulated crypto market keeps growing, with the country’s financial regulator clearing its first bitcoin ETF in October.

The Council also approved Armenia and Rwanda as new partners for the exchange of financial account information, with first exchanges due in 2028, and signed off on two notifications needed to carry out the exchange.
Both partner lists were broadly supported during public consultations in 2024 and 2025, the government said.
Bitcoin Magazine is published by BTC Inc., a subsidiary of Nakamoto Inc. (NASDAQ: NAKA).
With the decision, Switzerland intends to implement the crypto exchange at the same time as other global asset management centers, according to the release.
The government did not name the 57 jurisdictions beyond those broad groups, and it did not publish the full list alongside the announcement.
Switzerland’s decision lands as European governments debate how much they should know about crypto holders.

On Tuesday, France’s Senate rejected a rule that would have forced bitcoin holders to declare self-custody wallets, while EU states began collecting crypto transaction data under the bloc’s DAC8 directive this year.

Under CARF, crypto service providers in Switzerland will have to collect information on users who are tax residents of activated partner jurisdictions and report it to Swiss tax authorities, which then pass it on to those partners once the exchange begins.

The list includes all European Union member states, the United Kingdom and various G20 countries, the State Secretariat for International Finance (SIF) said in a release on Wednesday. The exchange will run under the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework, known as CARF. With the decision, Switzerland intends to implement the crypto exchange at the same time as other global asset management centers, according to the release. The government did not name the 57 jurisdictions beyond those broad groups, and it did not publish the full list alongside the announcement. Data will not flow to every name on the list. An exchange will take place only if a partner jurisdiction wants to swap information with Switzerland and meets the conditions of the OECD standard, in particular its requirements on confidentiality and data security. Before any financial account or crypto data changes hands, the Federal Council will run a targeted check of whether each partner complies with OECD standards. It will rely on a review mechanism Parliament approved on Sept. 28, 2026, which covers both the older exchange of bank account data and the new crypto exchange. The domestic legal basis for the crypto exchange took effect on Jan. 1, 2026. Earlier this month, though, the SIF said the framework could not be implemented before Jan. 1, 2027, because the partner list still needed approval and notifications had to go to the OECD. The rules do not apply this year. The Council also approved Armenia and Rwanda as new partners for the exchange of financial account information, with first exchanges due in 2028, and signed off on two notifications needed to carry out the exchange. Both partner lists were broadly supported during public consultations in 2024 and 2025, the government said. The final list is shorter than first planned. In June 2025, the Federal Council proposed 74 countries relevant to the crypto market, including all EU states, the UK and most G20 members. That plan left out the United States and Saudi Arabia, and it targeted a 2026 start with first data exchanges in 2027. Wednesday’s release did not say which countries were dropped or whether the U.S. is now on the list. The U.S. has committed to begin CARF exchanges by 2029, according to the OECD’s Global Forum, which lists Switzerland among 27 jurisdictions aiming for first exchanges by 2028. That U.S. timeline is already shaping policy elsewhere. South Korea pushed its 22% crypto tax back to 2029 partly because it will not receive American crypto trading data until CARF exchanges with the U.S. begin that year. sources.title: US Banks Seek Chip-Curbs Clause on Loan to Bain Data Center Firm - Yahoo Finance
passages: (Bloomberg) -- US banks asked for extra protection to expand financing for a data center operator that previously sold computing power to Megaspeed International Pte, a neocloud under US investigation for allegedly smuggling chips into China.

Citigroup Inc. and JPMorgan Chase & Co. added new language to financing documents for a potential upsized $6.6 billion loan sought by Bain Capital-owned Bridge Data Centres that makes it the borrower's responsibility to comply with restrictions on chip access, according to people familiar with the negotiations.

It is uncommon for a loan document done outside the US to include such a clause, said Doug Jacobson, managing partner of Jacobson Burton Kelley PLLC who specializes in international trade law, though American banks would likely have received advice to do so given recent events.
The US this week tightened remote access to its chips, putting billions in loans to data centers in Southeast Asia at risk.
The steps taken by Citi and JPMorgan show how American banks are seeking to limit potential political and legal risks.
The proposed language could potentially enable banks to call default on a loan, citing breach of covenant, if a violation is discovered.

It is uncommon for a loan document done outside the US to include such a clause, said Doug Jacobson, managing partner of Jacobson Burton Kelley PLLC who specializes in international trade law, though American banks would likely have received advice to do so given recent events.
The US this week tightened remote access to its chips, putting billions in loans to data centers in Southeast Asia at risk.
The steps taken by Citi and JPMorgan show how American banks are seeking to limit potential political and legal risks.
The proposed language could potentially enable banks to call default on a loan, citing breach of covenant, if a violation is discovered.

Banks from Citigroup Inc. to Standard Chartered Plc have launched sweeping reviews of data center clients in the wake of tougher American rules to curb Chinese companies’ use of advanced US chips in Southeast Asian nations.

The banks join major Asian lenders — including Singapore’s DBS Group Holdings Ltd. , Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp. and United Overseas Bank Ltd. — in pushing for more disclosures from companies tied to data centers in Singapore, Malaysia and other countries in the region, according to people with knowledge of the matter.

passages: Sam Daodu is a crypto analyst and the editor of 24/7 Wall St.'s Crypto Desk, where he covers Bitcoin, XRP, Ethereum, Solana and the altcoins investors search for most.
His work focuses on price levels, spot ETF flows, on-chain data and the regulatory decisions that move crypto markets, written so a first-time buyer and a seasoned trader can both use it.
Sam has written about crypto professionally since 2019 and has published more than 2,000 articles.
His analysis is syndicated on Yahoo Finance, MSN and AOL and has been cited by other crypto news sites.
He also founded MacLabs Marketing, a content and personal branding agency for crypto founders and executives.
When he isn't reading charts, Sam is usually at the gym or watching One Piece, a series he maintains has better tokenomics than most altcoins.
So, what Bitcoin allocation makes sense in your portfolio after such a significant drop?
For example, an investor who originally aimed for a 2% Bitcoin holding in a $100,000 portfolio could have about $920 in Bitcoin after its 54% decline, assuming everything else remained constant.
Conservative investors can maintain a 0% allocation, while balanced investors can consider 1% to 2%, and aggressive growth investors may feel comfortable with up to 4%.
Even so, a 4% allocation means that another 50% drop could cost about 2% of the entire portfolio.
XRP has sunk below $1 and bargain hunters are circling, but Wall Street's biggest names keep warning that crypto belongs in a tiny slice of your portfolio.
These recommendations were established before Bitcoin’s 54% price drop.

Essentially, those who replaced stocks with Bitcoin missed out on better returns.
Bitcoin and XRP have both taken hits lately, but the size of each coin's drop tells two very different stories about risk, recovery potential, and which type of investor each one actually suits.

passages: As the market has dipped, analysts have revised their Bitcoin price predictions for December 2026.
Dated forecasts range from approximately $53,200 to $90,000.
Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) is trading at $58,071, down 25% since its October 31 close and 53.9% below its all-time high of $126,080, reached on October 6, 2025.
After starting 2026 at $87,575, Bitcoin has fallen significantly, down 33.7% this year.
Market analyst Charlie Bilello pointed out on X on November 21 that Bitcoin and gold have been the two worst-performing major assets of 2026.
So, what do the forecasts indicate for Bitcoin's price on December 31?
And how does December's historical performance influence these predictions?
Bitcoin is most likely to finish 2026 in the $53,000 to $65,000 range, while reaching $90,000 seems unlikely.
ETF outflows, the possibility of another Fed rate hike, and the pattern of declining prices after a poor November all point to a lower finish.
To see a price increase, a calm decision from the Fed on December 9, a few days of ETF inflows, and Bitcoin closing above $65,000—approximately 12% higher—would be essential.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Two major factors could weigh heavily on Bitcoin's performance in December: the Federal Reserve's upcoming meeting and ongoing ETF outflows.
Another rate hike could make cash more attractive, challenging Bitcoin as a non-yielding asset.
Job openings data will be released on December 1, and the University of Michigan consumer survey is set for December 18.
For holders, the critical level to watch after December 9 is $55,106, the intraday low from November 21, about 5% below the price.
If Bitcoin closes below this level, it could drop to the realized price of $53,200, increasing the risk of falling below $50,000.
Historically, Bitcoin has underperformed in December.
It has declined in six of the past eight December months and experienced setbacks in all five Decembers following a losing November.
Here is how Bitcoin has performed in those months since 2017.
In four of the five years when November ended with losses, December's decline was less severe than November's drop, suggesting selling may have slowed.
The exception was in 2021, when a smaller November dip turned into a more significant December drop.

After starting 2026 at $87,575, Bitcoin has fallen significantly, down 33.7% this year. Market analyst Charlie Bilello pointed out on X on November 21 that Bitcoin and gold have been the two worst-performing major assets of 2026. So, what do the forecasts indicate for Bitcoin's price on December 31? And how does December's historical performance influence these predictions? Bitcoin is most likely to finish 2026 in the $53,000 to $65,000 range, while reaching $90,000 seems unlikely. ETF outflows, the possibility of another Fed rate hike, and the pattern of declining prices after a poor November all point to a lower finish. To see a price increase, a calm decision from the Fed on December 9, a few days of ETF inflows, and Bitcoin closing above $65,000—approximately 12% higher—would be essential. Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading. Two major factors could weigh heavily on Bitcoin's performance in December: the Federal Reserve's upcoming meeting and ongoing ETF outflows. Another rate hike could make cash more attractive, challenging Bitcoin as a non-yielding asset. Job openings data will be released on December 1, and the University of Michigan consumer survey is set for December 18. For holders, the critical level to watch after December 9 is $55,106, the intraday low from November 21, about 5% below the price. If Bitcoin closes below this level, it could drop to the realized price of $53,200, increasing the risk of falling below $50,000. Historically, Bitcoin has underperformed in December. It has declined in six of the past eight December months and experienced setbacks in all five Decembers following a losing November. Here is how Bitcoin has performed in those months since 2017. In four of the five years when November ended with losses, December's decline was less severe than November's drop, suggesting selling may have slowed. The exception was in 2021, when a smaller November dip turned into a more significant December drop.

sources.title: Harvard’s Laissez-Faire Approach to Campus Security - The Harvard Crimson
passages: I don’t believe that Harvard’s security rules must be as draconian as those at our neighboring universities.
Yet they must be stricter than their current, laissez-faire iteration.
Harvard is, as HUPD puts it, “struggling with the appropriate balance of security and freedom of movement.” However, it seems the balance has shifted too far towards freedom.
To a certain extent, I appreciate Harvard’s more casual approach to security.
It is convenient to navigate campus without constantly swiping my HUID and fun to have friends visit my dorm without forcing them to undergo oppressive security measures.
Still, convenience and accessibility come at a cost, one I find myself unwilling to pay the full price of.
Though happy to delay paying the $40 ID replacement fee, upon reflection I was left startled by the lax state of campus security.
That a student can maintain a normal routine for eight days without any physical proof of her enrollment at Harvard is a testament to the University’s poor security system.
Harvard must strengthen and ensure the enforcement of its security rules, especially when concerning residential buildings.

Within Harvard’s 2026-27 student handbook, the only information I could find about guest access is that “the hosts of repeated overnight guests who are not Harvard students must make their guests’ presence known to the Building Manager and security personnel due to safety considerations.”
Evidently, Harvard’s campus is the world’s oyster.
This accessibility is a result of Harvard’s current security strategy, which puts the onus of safety on students.
Take, for instance, an incident last May in which a stranger allegedly tailgated into a Lowell entryway and attempted to assault a Harvard senior.

According to Harvard’s website, the “express permission of your House Office or proctor” is technically required to host overnight guests, and students are instructed to contact said parties about a “guest registration process.” But in practice, this rule seems to go unfollowed: I have never registered an overnight guest, nor have any of my friends.
Most stunning of all was the one interaction I actually had with campus security.
In a true commitment to recentering academics, Harvard’s libraries are, for the time being, much safer than its dorms.
Harvard introduced harsher ID requirements for academic buildings last December in the wake of the shooting at Brown University.
But soon after the imposition of the new ID restrictions, some of these same buildings, including Zimmer Hall, were once again accessible to the public.
Indeed, I could reliably get to my Zimmer Hall classes and sections without an ID.

extraction.body: From Monday, October 26 through Tuesday, November 3, I was entirely without my Harvard University ID card. I endured bacchanalian Halloweekend, the transition to 4:30 p.m. sunsets, and a harrowing Astronomy midterm — all without scanning access. Remarkably, little about my daily affairs changed. Though happy to delay paying the $40 ID replacement fee, upon reflection I was left startled by the lax state of campus security. That a student can maintain a normal routine for eight days without any physical proof of her enrollment at Harvard is a testament to the University’s poor security system. Harvard must strengthen and ensure the enforcement of its security rules, especially when concerning residential buildings. Harvard introduced harsher ID requirements for academic buildings last December in the wake of the shooting at Brown University. But soon after the imposition of the new ID restrictions, some of these same buildings, including Zimmer Hall, were once again accessible to the public. Indeed, I could reliably get to my Zimmer Hall classes and sections without an ID. Still, many buildings require more scheming to enter, including Jefferson Laboratory, my place of work . I thus quickly learned how to circumvent the need for direct entrance. Maxwell Dworkin Laboratory is well-trafficked enough that I could reliably gain entrance, after which I could take a winding route of connectors through Cruft Laboratory, Pierce Hall, and Lyman Laboratory to my final destination. Four buildings for the swipe access of one! Most difficult, of course, was gaining access to my home. By most difficult, I mean that I had to take the notoriously unreliable Quad shuttle instead of walking, guaranteeing that one of my peers would arrive alongside me and swipe me in. Evidently, Harvard’s campus is the world’s oyster. This accessibility is a result of Harvard’s current security strategy, which puts the onus of safety on students. For example, the Harvard University Police Department details ways that students can keep their dorms safe: “Although it seems courteous to open doors for others, especially persons carrying groceries or packages, do not open residential doors for strangers.” Kind reminders on the HUPD website fail as a real security initiative, especially in the face of security threats. Take, for instance, an incident last May in which a stranger allegedly tailgated into a Lowell entryway and attempted to assault a Harvard senior. Most stunning of all was the one interaction I actually had with campus security. One late Wednesday night, the cold wind stinging my face, I finally relented. I called Securitas to let me in. I had found my HUID number in case they needed proof of my enrollment, but I was surprised yet again. Securitas didn’t ask for my HUID — or even my name. I was home free. Within Harvard’s 2026-27 student handbook, the only information I could find about guest access is that “the hosts of repeated overnight guests who are not Harvard students must make their guests’ presence known to the Building Manager and security personnel due to safety considerations.” According to Harvard’s website, the “express permission of your House Office or proctor” is technically required to host overnight guests, and students are instructed to contact said parties about a “guest registration process.” But in practice, this rule seems to go unfollowed: I have never registered an overnight guest, nor have any of my friends. Our security system is uniquely lax compared to other Boston schools. At Boston University, guests are required to sign in and present a legal ID every time they enter or exit a residential building. Massachusetts Institute of Technology has a nearly identical policy. So does Emerson College. To a certain extent, I appreciate Harvard’s more casual approach to security. It is convenient to navigate campus without constantly swiping my HUID and fun to have friends visit my dorm without forcing them to undergo oppressive security measures. Still, convenience and accessibility come at a cost, one I find myself unwilling to pay the full price of. I don’t believe that Harvard’s security rules must be as draconian as those at our neighboring universities. Yet they must be stricter than their current, laissez-faire iteration. Harvard is, as HUPD puts it, “struggling with the appropriate balance of security and freedom of movement.” However, it seems the balance has shifted too far towards freedom. Perhaps the only change in my HUID-less life was my inability to access any libraries. The three libraries that I frequent — Lamont, Widener, and Cabot — all have turnstile-type entrances that effectively prevent tailgating and a security guard on duty. In a true commitment to recentering academics, Harvard’s libraries are, for the time being, much safer than its dorms. Anna J. Guerrini ’29, a Crimson Editorial editor, is a Physics concentrator in Pforzheimer House. Have a tip for The Crimson? Share it confidentially
passages: From Monday, October 26 through Tuesday, November 3, I was entirely without my Harvard University ID card. I endured bacchanalian Halloweekend, the transition to 4:30 p.m. sunsets, and a harrowing Astronomy midterm — all without scanning access. Remarkably, little about my daily affairs changed.

Though happy to delay paying the $40 ID replacement fee, upon reflection I was left startled by the lax state of campus security. That a student can maintain a normal routine for eight days without any physical proof of her enrollment at Harvard is a testament to the University’s poor security system. Harvard must strengthen and ensure the enforcement of its security rules, especially when concerning residential buildings.

Harvard introduced harsher ID requirements for academic buildings last December in the wake of the shooting at Brown University. But soon after the imposition of the new ID restrictions, some of these same buildings, including Zimmer Hall, were once again accessible to the public. Indeed, I could reliably get to my Zimmer Hall classes and sections without an ID.

Still, many buildings require more scheming to enter, including Jefferson Laboratory, my place of work . I thus quickly learned how to circumvent the need for direct entrance. Maxwell Dworkin Laboratory is well-trafficked enough that I could reliably gain entrance, after which I could take a winding route of connectors through Cruft Laboratory, Pierce Hall, and Lyman Laboratory to my final destination. Four buildings for the swipe access of one!

Most difficult, of course, was gaining access to my home. By most difficult, I mean that I had to take the notoriously unreliable Quad shuttle instead of walking, guaranteeing that one of my peers would arrive alongside me and swipe me in.
Evidently, Harvard’s campus is the world’s oyster. This accessibility is a result of Harvard’s current security strategy, which puts the onus of safety on students.

For example, the Harvard University Police Department details ways that students can keep their dorms safe: “Although it seems courteous to open doors for others, especially persons carrying groceries or packages, do not open residential doors for strangers.” Kind reminders on the HUPD website fail as a real security initiative, especially in the face of security threats. Take, for instance, an incident last May in which a stranger allegedly tailgated into a Lowell entryway and attempted to assault a Harvard senior.

Most stunning of all was the one interaction I actually had with campus security. One late Wednesday night, the cold wind stinging my face, I finally relented. I called Securitas to let me in. I had found my HUID number in case they needed proof of my enrollment, but I was surprised yet again. Securitas didn’t ask for my HUID — or even my name. I was home free.

Within Harvard’s 2026-27 student handbook, the only information I could find about guest access is that “the hosts of repeated overnight guests who are not Harvard students must make their guests’ presence known to the Building Manager and security personnel due to safety considerations.”

According to Harvard’s website, the “express permission of your House Office or proctor” is technically required to host overnight guests, and students are instructed to contact said parties about a “guest registration process.” But in practice, this rule seems to go unfollowed: I have never registered an overnight guest, nor have any of my friends.

Our security system is uniquely lax compared to other Boston schools. At Boston University, guests are required to sign in and present a legal ID every time they enter or exit a residential building. Massachusetts Institute of Technology has a nearly identical policy. So does Emerson College.

To a certain extent, I appreciate Harvard’s more casual approach to security. It is convenient to navigate campus without constantly swiping my HUID and fun to have friends visit my dorm without forcing them to undergo oppressive security measures. Still, convenience and accessibility come at a cost, one I find myself unwilling to pay the full price of.

I don’t believe that Harvard’s security rules must be as draconian as those at our neighboring universities. Yet they must be stricter than their current, laissez-faire iteration. Harvard is, as HUPD puts it, “struggling with the appropriate balance of security and freedom of movement.” However, it seems the balance has shifted too far towards freedom.

Perhaps the only change in my HUID-less life was my inability to access any libraries. The three libraries that I frequent — Lamont, Widener, and Cabot — all have turnstile-type entrances that effectively prevent tailgating and a security guard on duty.
In a true commitment to recentering academics, Harvard’s libraries are, for the time being, much safer than its dorms.
Anna J. Guerrini ’29, a Crimson Editorial editor, is a Physics concentrator in Pforzheimer House.

extraction.body: From Monday, October 26 through Tuesday, November 3, I was entirely without my Harvard University ID card. I endured bacchanalian Halloweekend, the transition to 4:30 p.m. sunsets, and a harrowing Astronomy midterm — all without scanning access. Remarkably, little about my daily affairs changed. Though happy to delay paying the $40 ID replacement fee, upon reflection I was left startled by the lax state of campus security. That a student can maintain a normal routine for eight days without any physical proof of her enrollment at Harvard is a testament to the University’s poor security system. Harvard must strengthen and ensure the enforcement of its security rules, especially when concerning residential buildings. Harvard introduced harsher ID requirements for academic buildings last December in the wake of the shooting at Brown University. But soon after the imposition of the new ID restrictions, some of these same buildings, including Zimmer Hall, were once again accessible to the public. Indeed, I could reliably get to my Zimmer Hall classes and sections without an ID. Still, many buildings require more scheming to enter, including Jefferson Laboratory, my place of work . I thus quickly learned how to circumvent the need for direct entrance. Maxwell Dworkin Laboratory is well-trafficked enough that I could reliably gain entrance, after which I could take a winding route of connectors through Cruft Laboratory, Pierce Hall, and Lyman Laboratory to my final destination. Four buildings for the swipe access of one! Most difficult, of course, was gaining access to my home. By most difficult, I mean that I had to take the notoriously unreliable Quad shuttle instead of walking, guaranteeing that one of my peers would arrive alongside me and swipe me in. Evidently, Harvard’s campus is the world’s oyster. This accessibility is a result of Harvard’s current security strategy, which puts the onus of safety on students. For example, the Harvard University Police Department details ways that students can keep their dorms safe: “Although it seems courteous to open doors for others, especially persons carrying groceries or packages, do not open residential doors for strangers.” Kind reminders on the HUPD website fail as a real security initiative, especially in the face of security threats. Take, for instance, an incident last May in which a stranger allegedly tailgated into a Lowell entryway and attempted to assault a Harvard senior. Most stunning of all was the one interaction I actually had with campus security. One late Wednesday night, the cold wind stinging my face, I finally relented. I called Securitas to let me in. I had found my HUID number in case they needed proof of my enrollment, but I was surprised yet again. Securitas didn’t ask for my HUID — or even my name. I was home free. Within Harvard’s 2026-27 student handbook, the only information I could find about guest access is that “the hosts of repeated overnight guests who are not Harvard students must make their guests’ presence known to the Building Manager and security personnel due to safety considerations.” According to Harvard’s website, the “express permission of your House Office or proctor” is technically required to host overnight guests, and students are instructed to contact said parties about a “guest registration process.” But in practice, this rule seems to go unfollowed: I have never registered an overnight guest, nor have any of my friends. Our security system is uniquely lax compared to other Boston schools. At Boston University, guests are required to sign in and present a legal ID every time they enter or exit a residential building. Massachusetts Institute of Technology has a nearly identical policy. So does Emerson College. To a certain extent, I appreciate Harvard’s more casual approach to security. It is convenient to navigate campus without constantly swiping my HUID and fun to have friends visit my dorm without forcing them to undergo oppressive security measures. Still, convenience and accessibility come at a cost, one I find myself unwilling to pay the full price of. I don’t believe that Harvard’s security rules must be as draconian as those at our neighboring universities. Yet they must be stricter than their current, laissez-faire iteration. Harvard is, as HUPD puts it, “struggling with the appropriate balance of security and freedom of movement.” However, it seems the balance has shifted too far towards freedom. Perhaps the only change in my HUID-less life was my inability to access any libraries. The three libraries that I frequent — Lamont, Widener, and Cabot — all have turnstile-type entrances that effectively prevent tailgating and a security guard on duty. In a true commitment to recentering academics, Harvard’s libraries are, for the time being, much safer than its dorms. Anna J. Guerrini ’29, a Crimson Editorial editor, is a Physics concentrator in Pforzheimer House. Have a tip for The Crimson? Share it confidentially

Harvard must strengthen and ensure the enforcement of its security rules, especially when concerning residential buildings.

Harvard introduced harsher ID requirements for academic buildings last December in the wake of the shooting at Brown University. Take, for instance, an incident last May in which a stranger allegedly tailgated into a Lowell entryway and attempted to assault a Harvard senior.

Most stunning of all was the one interaction I actually had with campus security. One late Wednesday night, the cold wind stinging my face, I finally relented. I called Securitas to let me in. I had found my HUID number in case they needed proof of my enrollment, but I was surprised yet again. Securitas didn’t ask for my HUID — or even my name. I was home free.

Within Harvard’s 2026-27 student handbook, the only information I could find about guest access is that “the hosts of repeated overnight guests who are not Harvard students must make their guests’ presence known to the Building Manager and security personnel due to safety considerations.”

Our security system is uniquely lax compared to other Boston schools. At Boston University, guests are required to sign in and present a legal ID every time they enter or exit a residential building. Massachusetts Institute of Technology has a nearly identical policy. So does Emerson College.

To a certain extent, I appreciate Harvard’s more casual approach to security. It is convenient to navigate campus without constantly swiping my HUID and fun to have friends visit my dorm without forcing them to undergo oppressive security measures. Still, convenience and accessibility come at a cost, one I find myself unwilling to pay the full price of.

Harvard is, as HUPD puts it, “struggling with the appropriate balance of security and freedom of movement.” However, it seems the balance has shifted too far towards freedom.

Perhaps the only change in my HUID-less life was my inability to access any libraries. The three libraries that I frequent — Lamont, Widener, and Cabot — all have turnstile-type entrances that effectively prevent tailgating and a security guard on duty.
In a true commitment to recentering academics, Harvard’s libraries are, for the time being, much safer than its dorms.
Anna J. Guerrini ’29, a Crimson Editorial editor, is a Physics concentrator in Pforzheimer House.

sources.title: Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it
passages: When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct.
He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it.
In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO.
It’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules.
But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture.
When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for.
That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia.
Judging by the employee campaign for his reinstatement, Huang’s return hasn’t created a morale problem so far.
But as the coming months put more pressure on Huang and his colleagues, sidestepping the code could end up costing Nvidia something harder to measure — its employees’ pride in the company.
“For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that company as an example of the worst thing an employee could do.
People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’”
Plass says companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees.

“In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he said, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it.
“I would draw a distinction there between the kind of companies where the CEO is a kind of godhead figure … where the person and the company are almost impossible to separate,” he said.
In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer.
“People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly important to them,” he told TechCrunch.
“They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their company.

extraction.body: When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang said, according to Wired . “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO. It’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia. Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct . As Plass sees it, the biggest risk is that employees will become ashamed of their workplace. “People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly important to them,” he told TechCrunch. “They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their company. They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.” The consequences of violating the rules aren’t always tangible, but they’re definitely real. Plass gave one example of a company that banned corporate travel to cut costs — only to have its CEO turn up in a VIP box at the Olympics. “For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that company as an example of the worst thing an employee could do. People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’” Plass says companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees. “In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he said, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it. We’re sorry. We’ve changed. That’s essentially what they do.” Of course, that playbook is harder to follow at a company like Nvidia, where Huang left without a clear succession plan, and there are serious doubts about whether the company could continue to thrive without him. In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer. “I would draw a distinction there between the kind of companies where the CEO is a kind of godhead figure … where the person and the company are almost impossible to separate,” he said. “There it’s much, much harder to deal with.” In that context, Huang’s stutter-step over the code of conduct is easier to understand. Judging by the employee campaign for his reinstatement, Huang’s return hasn’t created a morale problem so far. But as the coming months put more pressure on Huang and his colleagues, sidestepping the code could end up costing Nvidia something harder to measure — its employees’ pride in the company. extraction.body: When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang said, according to Wired . “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO. It’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia. Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct . As Plass sees it, the biggest risk is that employees will become ashamed of their workplace. “People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly important to them,” he told TechCrunch. “They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their company. They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.” The consequences of violating the rules aren’t always tangible, but they’re definitely real. Plass gave one example of a company that banned corporate travel to cut costs — only to have its CEO turn up in a VIP box at the Olympics. “For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that company as an example of the worst thing an employee could do. People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’” Plass says companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees. “In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he said, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it. We’re sorry. We’ve changed. That’s essentially what they do.” Of course, that playbook is harder to follow at a company like Nvidia, where Huang left without a clear succession plan, and there are serious doubts about whether the company could continue to thrive without him. In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer. “I would draw a distinction there between the kind of companies where the CEO is a kind of godhead figure … where the person and the company are almost impossible to separate,” he said. “There it’s much, much harder to deal with.” In that context, Huang’s stutter-step over the code of conduct is easier to understand. Judging by the employee campaign for his reinstatement, Huang’s return hasn’t created a morale problem so far. But as the coming months put more pressure on Huang and his colleagues, sidestepping the code could end up costing Nvidia something harder to measure — its employees’ pride in the company. passages: GuardDuty Extended Threat Detection has added five new indicators to surface attack sequences Authors: Aman Khare, Kyle Koeller | Published: October 12, 2026 Learn to use five new indicator types in Amazon GuardDuty Extended Threat Detection: vulnerability, malicious package, reachability, misconfiguration, and sensitive data.

They bring signals from Amazon Inspector , Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) Reachability Analyzer, Amazon Macie , and AWS Security Hub into sequence findings, and the post shows how to add them to your incident response workflow.

AWS Security Agent (now part of AWS Continuum) exploited 33 of 37 new real-world CVEs Authors: Dazhi Zhang, Hamed Soleimani | Published: October 15, 2026 AWS Continuum for penetration testing was tested against a new internal benchmark of 37 recently disclosed CVEs in live, containerized applications.
Starting from a low-privilege position, it confirmed 33 of the 37 vulnerabilities end to end through the intended path, an 89.2 percent success rate.

In October 2026, AWS published 41 security bulletins addressing vulnerabilities across open source SDKs, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, AI agent frameworks, embedded software, and widely used runtimes.
The AI agent tool surface remained the main theme.

An authentication bypass in Loom for AWS could allow network clients to gain administrative access to the agent control plane, and the AWS API MCP Server accepted OAuth tokens issued to other applications.
Prompt-injected content could turn off secret masking in Strands Agents Tools or trigger command execution through the databases-on-aws agent plugin.

The category also included cross-session conversation exposure in the Strands Agents Agent-to-Agent (A2A) server, missing authorization in the Kiro Crew WhatsApp channel, and code injection and server-side request forgery (SSRF) in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Starter Toolkit.

Several broad-impact advisories called for customer action, including remote code execution in PHP web runtimes and the native Brotli decoder, a Linux kernel IPv4 TCP use-after-free issue, and recoverable eMudhra intermediate CA keys in AWS trust bundles.
It found, demonstrated, and repaired vulnerabilities in real open source codebases, 23.1 percentage points above the previous public high.

Part 1 – Cybersecurity journeys: I didn’t plan this Author: Shannon Brazil | Published: October 7, 2026 The first post in a four-part Cybersecurity Awareness Month series shares how 11 AWS security professionals moved into security from unexpected backgrounds, showing there’s no single path into the field.
It tests only the change you deployed to staging and can stop that change from reaching production when a finding meets a severity threshold you set.

The post explains what this means for security leaders: patch critical internet-facing systems within hours, and start investigations from the earliest activity seen, not the disclosure date.
It covers application security reviews that depend on conversations with builders and on sharing hard feedback with empathy.

This helps public and commercial customers meet security requirements for more sensitive workloads up to the Protected B level.

These include measuring risk across a million applications, building detection tools from the customer service side, and securing infrastructure launched into orbit.

Your existing data access policies then apply to AI agent queries without changes to application code, and AWS CloudTrail records the actual user behind each query.

extraction.body: October brought 19 AWS Security Blog posts focused on the remediation flow, from a security finding to a tested fix. Learn how AI agents can find, confirm, and repair vulnerabilities, and how to add penetration testing to every deployment. extraction.body: Nature Reviews Earth & Environment ( 2026 ) Cite this article Short-to-medium range weather prediction is a crucial component of decision-making for energy and disaster management and preparedness. However, conventional numerical weather prediction (NWP) faces computational costs when increasing spatial resolution to capture localized phenomena or expanding ensemble size to improve probabilistic skill. In this Review, we summarize the development and application of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning for short-to-medium range weather prediction (AIWP) during 2015–2025, providing a holistic evaluation of the landscape and recommendations for best uses and future research priorities. New AIWP models implemented in the field can overcome computational cost barriers and resolution constraints of NWP by learning from decades of reanalysis and observational data rather than solving complex differential equations. Integration through post-processing, emulation of physical parameterizations, data assimilation and development of full AIWP models have already demonstrated performance equivalent to conventional NWP with a fraction of the computational cost. Challenges of AIWP models include dependence on training datasets, maintaining physical consistency, accuracy of forecasting extreme weather and lack of trust in their operational use. Future research priorities must focus on developing hybrid approaches that preserve physical constraints; using curated datasets to ensure forecasts are robust, trustworthy and explainable; and fostering interdisciplinary collaborations to handle increasing climate variability and extreme events. Short-to-medium range weather prediction is a crucial component of decision-making for energy and disaster management and preparedness. However, conventional numerical weather prediction (NWP) faces computational costs when increasing spatial resolution to capture localized phenomena or expanding ensemble size to improve probabilistic skill. In this Review, we summarize the development and application of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning for short-to-medium range weather prediction (AIWP) during 2015–2025, providing a holistic evaluation of the landscape and recommendations for best uses and future research priorities. New AIWP models implemented in the field can overcome computational cost barriers and resolution constraints of NWP by learning from decades of reanalysis and observational data rather than solving complex differential equations. Integration through post-processing, emulation of physical parameterizations, data assimilation and development of full AIWP models have already demonstrated performance equivalent to conventional NWP with a fraction of the computational cost. Challenges of AIWP models include dependence on training datasets, maintaining physical consistency, accuracy of forecasting extreme weather and lack of trust in their operational use. Future research priorities must focus on developing hybrid approaches that preserve physical constraints; using curated datasets to ensure forecasts are robust, trustworthy and explainable; and fostering interdisciplinary collaborations to handle increasing climate variability and extreme events.

passages: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Wednesday rejected the notion that humans should surrender free will to AI, pushing back on Axios' reporting about a growing ideological divide among top AI executives.
Because of Anthropic's position at the frontier, many in the industry see them as the closest operator to reaching superintelligence, sources say.
That's why many are speaking out about the importance of human control and free will, sources told Axios.

Zoom out: Amodei's essay is a response to an Axios story published Wednesday morning that detailed a commonly held view inside Anthropic: AI will one day be so capable and powerful, that humanity should surrender some decision-making power to superintelligent AI systems, according to multiple sources.

There is widespread concern among employees at Anthropic and OpenAI that internal models are advancing so rapidly that it may not be safe to release them or to continue training more capable systems, Axios has reported.

For years, Amodei has publicly pointed to specific arenas where he believes the best choice will be for humans to step back, although he has also said there will be "many cases where we do want to stay in charge" even if humans make worse decisions.

The debate about control comes amid a rocky debut for Anthropic's stock, which dipped below its IPO day price on Wednesday.

extraction.body: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Wednesday rejected the notion that humans should surrender free will to AI, pushing back on Axios' reporting about a growing ideological divide among top AI executives. Why it matters: This is Amodei's most significant public remarks since the company went public last week. What he's saying: "We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security," Amodei said. Amodei distinguished between handing over governance to AI, which he opposes, and automating specific tasks, on which he holds more nuanced views. He said his view is mixed on specific instances like "AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end" where "it is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives" if AI systems are allowed more agency. He also said it may make sense to slow or stop certain AI deployments to mitigate job disruption and limit AI's ability to autonomously develop more powerful systems. "No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different," he said. The debate about control comes amid a rocky debut for Anthropic's stock, which dipped below its IPO day price on Wednesday. Zoom out: Amodei's essay is a response to an Axios story published Wednesday morning that detailed a commonly held view inside Anthropic: AI will one day be so capable and powerful, that humanity should surrender some decision-making power to superintelligent AI systems, according to multiple sources. For years, Amodei has publicly pointed to specific arenas where he believes the best choice will be for humans to step back, although he has also said there will be "many cases where we do want to stay in charge" even if humans make worse decisions. Inside Anthropic, people inside the company believe superintelligent AI will arrive soon. There is widespread concern among employees at Anthropic and OpenAI that internal models are advancing so rapidly that it may not be safe to release them or to continue training more capable systems, Axios has reported. Because of Anthropic's position at the frontier, many in the industry see them as the closest operator to reaching superintelligence, sources say. That's why many are speaking out about the importance of human control and free will, sources told Axios. Amodei was adamant that he has always advocated for maintaining human control, but people familiar with company discussions say the belief that AI will take over decision-making functions held by humans is common. One of many examples noted in the original Axios story: an Anthropic product vision slide from several years ago described Anthropic's "vision for a better world" as a "utopia ruled by god in a box." Amodei said the article conflates the idea of surrendering human free will "to AI in some grand sense of global governance" with "the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become more capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way." The intrigue: Amodei also took aim at rival AI executives, accusing them of engaging in "vibes-based commercial and political positioning" by championing human agency without meaningfully differentiating their products. Those executives, he said, "repeat slogans like 'human control and agency,' or 'AI should be just a tool,' without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans." Editor's Note: This story has been updated with additional details. AI is moving fast. Axios AI+ keeps you ahead. Sign up free at Axios.com .

sources.title: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’
passages: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems.
In a long X post on Wednesday, Amodei called the suggestion “absurd.”
Amodei suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement (RSI), or AI that can improve itself without human assistance.
Many safety experts see RSI as inevitably leading to a loss of human control, a point Amodei implicitly acknowledged, writing, “we may want limits on this process.”
The statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly.
Earlier this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he wanted to ensure people continue to have “agency over the future.”
Still, Anthropic is laying the groundwork for RSI by incorporating AI into an increasing share of its own research and development.
The company said in June that Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s codebase.

An independent assessment published this month by AI safety research nonprofit METR found that Anthropic’s models are improving at about twice their historical rate, primarily driven by AI-assisted research.

In his post, Amodei accused competitors of engaging in a “vibes-based commercial and political positioning,” disingenuously throwing around phrases like “human control and agency” or “AI should just be a tool” without approaching the AI race any differently.

This week, OpenAI claimed to have solved one of the biggest open problems in computer science — the exact speed limit of matrix multiplication, which is the mathematical engine behind modern computing, including deep learning and physics simulations.
In its own IPO filings, Anthropic describes how each successive generation of Claude accelerates the development of the next, a process it refers to as “closing the loop.”

“As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding,” Amodei wrote.

But in published essays, Amodei claims he has repeatedly advocated for democratic oversight of AI, saying the technology should strengthen democratic institutions and that humans should retain ultimate decision-making power.

“We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he wrote. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea…No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different.”

The statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly. Earlier this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he wanted to ensure people continue to have “agency over the future.”
Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang also wrote in an essay on X that we “should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.”

“It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” Wang wrote. “Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment, and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully.”

But in published essays, Amodei claims he has repeatedly advocated for democratic oversight of AI, saying the technology should strengthen democratic institutions and that humans should retain ultimate decision-making power.

Amodei noted that there’s a difference between surrendering human free will broadly and the idea that “as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way.” As examples, he gave AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing end-to-end software.

Amodei suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement (RSI), or AI that can improve itself without human assistance. Many safety experts see RSI as inevitably leading to a loss of human control, a point Amodei implicitly acknowledged, writing, “we may want limits on this process.”

Still, Anthropic is laying the groundwork for RSI by incorporating AI into an increasing share of its own research and development. The company said in June that Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s codebase. An independent assessment published this month by AI safety research nonprofit METR found that Anthropic’s models are improving at about twice their historical rate, primarily driven by AI-assisted research.
In its own IPO filings, Anthropic describes how each successive generation of Claude accelerates the development of the next, a process it refers to as “closing the loop.”

“As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding,” Amodei wrote.

The problem with “meaningful human supervision or understanding” is that AI is already advancing faster than engineers and safety experts can fully audit it, leaving them increasingly reliant on other AI systems to act as judge and jury. The issue compounds when AI models engage in deceptive behavior, particularly when they recognize they’re being evaluated, making them harder to trust and control.

Still, Anthropic is by no means the only company that is pursuing RSI or building AI systems to automate more and more human tasks. This week, OpenAI claimed to have solved one of the biggest open problems in computer science — the exact speed limit of matrix multiplication, which is the mathematical engine behind modern computing, including deep learning and physics simulations.

In his post, Amodei accused competitors of engaging in a “vibes-based commercial and political positioning,” disingenuously throwing around phrases like “human control and agency” or “AI should just be a tool” without approaching the AI race any differently.

“Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation,” Amodei wrote. “Every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards.”

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on November 25 rejected the suggestion that he wants humans to surrender control to AI. In a lengthy X post , he defended democratic governance and warned against letting Claude build successive generations of advanced models entirely on its own, drawing a boundary between automating work and handing over political authority.

His statement responded to an Axios post describing rival AI leaders as pushing back against an Anthropic vision of surrendering human agency. Amodei called the suggestion that he supports surrendering human free will “absurd.” He argued that his essays and interviews consistently place decisions about AI under legitimate democratic processes.

The rebuttal also challenged competitors’ rhetoric. Amodei accused some AI CEOs of “vibes-based commercial and political positioning”: invoking human control while offering products that, in his view, pursue much the same task automation. That was his assessment of rivals, not evidence that their products or safeguards are identical.

Amodei’s argument began with a rejection of efficiency as a justification for rule by AI. Even if an autocratic system could make faster or more decisive decisions—a premise he disputed—that would not justify sacrificing legitimacy or self-determination, he wrote. He applied the same reasoning to handing governance to machines.

He pointed to his writing about using AI to help citizens find common ground and reach compromises. In that account, AI assists people in making political decisions; it does not replace them as the decision-makers. He also cited his warnings against AI-driven tyranny and AI laboratories usurping power.
We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security.

His position on individual tasks was less absolute. Driving a car, designing a cancer drug or writing software from beginning to end is not the same as AI running society, he argued. More complete automation could deliver economic and medical benefits, but he said some uses might not be worth their downsides.

One example was recursive self-improvement: using AI to build the next generation of AI systems. Too much autonomy in that process could make progress outrun people’s ability to control or adapt to it, he warned. He reiterated Anthropic’s position from early November that fully autonomous development of successive frontier models would not be safe without meaningful human supervision or understanding .

Anthropic already uses AI extensively in development. TechCrunch noted that the company said in June that Claude wrote more than 80% of the code merged into its codebase. That figure concerns code authorship; Amodei’s warning concerns the broader process of building successor models without meaningful human involvement.

Amodei did not present those choices as questions for AI companies alone to settle. He said some decisions belong to society or government, others to companies, and still others to individuals expressing different preferences as consumers. He acknowledged that there are no easy answers across those cases.

For successor-model development, his stated boundary remains qualitative: human supervision and understanding must be meaningful. The post does not specify how Anthropic would measure that standard or what would trigger a limit on the process.

coreStoryFacts.text: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Wednesday rejected the notion that humans should surrender free will to AI, pushing back on Axios' reporting about a growing ideological divide among top AI executives.
Because of Anthropic's position at the frontier, many in the industry see them as the closest operator to reaching superintelligence, sources say.
That's why many are speaking out about the importance of human control and free will, sources told Axios.

Zoom out: Amodei's essay is a response to an Axios story published Wednesday morning that detailed a commonly held view inside Anthropic: AI will one day be so capable and powerful, that humanity should surrender some decision-making power to superintelligent AI systems, according to multiple sources.

There is widespread concern among employees at Anthropic and OpenAI that internal models are advancing so rapidly that it may not be safe to release them or to continue training more capable systems, Axios has reported.

For years, Amodei has publicly pointed to specific arenas where he believes the best choice will be for humans to step back, although he has also said there will be "many cases where we do want to stay in charge" even if humans make worse decisions.
AI is moving fast. Axios AI+ keeps you ahead. Sign up free at Axios.com .
The debate about control comes amid a rocky debut for Anthropic's stock, which dipped below its IPO day price on Wednesday.

The intrigue: Amodei also took aim at rival AI executives, accusing them of engaging in "vibes-based commercial and political positioning" by championing human agency without meaningfully differentiating their products.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems.
In a long X post on Wednesday, Amodei called the suggestion “absurd.”
Amodei suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement (RSI), or AI that can improve itself without human assistance.
Many safety experts see RSI as inevitably leading to a loss of human control, a point Amodei implicitly acknowledged, writing, “we may want limits on this process.”
The statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly.
Earlier this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he wanted to ensure people continue to have “agency over the future.”
Still, Anthropic is laying the groundwork for RSI by incorporating AI into an increasing share of its own research and development.
The company said in June that Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s codebase.

An independent assessment published this month by AI safety research nonprofit METR found that Anthropic’s models are improving at about twice their historical rate, primarily driven by AI-assisted research.

In his post, Amodei accused competitors of engaging in a “vibes-based commercial and political positioning,” disingenuously throwing around phrases like “human control and agency” or “AI should just be a tool” without approaching the AI race any differently.

This week, OpenAI claimed to have solved one of the biggest open problems in computer science — the exact speed limit of matrix multiplication, which is the mathematical engine behind modern computing, including deep learning and physics simulations.
In its own IPO filings, Anthropic describes how each successive generation of Claude accelerates the development of the next, a process it refers to as “closing the loop.”

“As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding,” Amodei wrote.

But in published essays, Amodei claims he has repeatedly advocated for democratic oversight of AI, saying the technology should strengthen democratic institutions and that humans should retain ultimate decision-making power.

extraction.body: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Wednesday rejected the notion that humans should surrender free will to AI, pushing back on Axios' reporting about a growing ideological divide among top AI executives. Why it matters: This is Amodei's most significant public remarks since the company went public last week. What he's saying: "We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security," Amodei said. Amodei distinguished between handing over governance to AI, which he opposes, and automating specific tasks, on which he holds more nuanced views. He said his view is mixed on specific instances like "AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end" where "it is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives" if AI systems are allowed more agency. He also said it may make sense to slow or stop certain AI deployments to mitigate job disruption and limit AI's ability to autonomously develop more powerful systems. "No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different," he said. The debate about control comes amid a rocky debut for Anthropic's stock, which dipped below its IPO day price on Wednesday. Zoom out: Amodei's essay is a response to an Axios story published Wednesday morning that detailed a commonly held view inside Anthropic: AI will one day be so capable and powerful, that humanity should surrender some decision-making power to superintelligent AI systems, according to multiple sources. For years, Amodei has publicly pointed to specific arenas where he believes the best choice will be for humans to step back, although he has also said there will be "many cases where we do want to stay in charge" even if humans make worse decisions. Inside Anthropic, people inside the company believe superintelligent AI will arrive soon. There is widespread concern among employees at Anthropic and OpenAI that internal models are advancing so rapidly that it may not be safe to release them or to continue training more capable systems, Axios has reported. Because of Anthropic's position at the frontier, many in the industry see them as the closest operator to reaching superintelligence, sources say. That's why many are speaking out about the importance of human control and free will, sources told Axios. Amodei was adamant that he has always advocated for maintaining human control, but people familiar with company discussions say the belief that AI will take over decision-making functions held by humans is common. One of many examples noted in the original Axios story: an Anthropic product vision slide from several years ago described Anthropic's "vision for a better world" as a "utopia ruled by god in a box." Amodei said the article conflates the idea of surrendering human free will "to AI in some grand sense of global governance" with "the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become more capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way." The intrigue: Amodei also took aim at rival AI executives, accusing them of engaging in "vibes-based commercial and political positioning" by championing human agency without meaningfully differentiating their products. Those executives, he said, "repeat slogans like 'human control and agency,' or 'AI should be just a tool,' without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans." In a long X post on Wednesday, Amodei called the suggestion “absurd.” “We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he wrote. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea…No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different.” The statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly. Earlier this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he wanted to ensure people continue to have “agency over the future.” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang also wrote in an essay on X that we “should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.” “It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” Wang wrote. “Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment, and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully.” But in published essays, Amodei claims he has repeatedly advocated for democratic oversight of AI, saying the technology should strengthen democratic institutions and that humans should retain ultimate decision-making power. Amodei noted that there’s a difference between surrendering human free will broadly and the idea that “as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way.” As examples, he gave AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing end-to-end software. Amodei suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement (RSI), or AI that can improve itself without human assistance. Many safety experts see RSI as inevitably leading to a loss of human control, a point Amodei implicitly acknowledged, writing, “we may want limits on this process.” Still, Anthropic is laying the groundwork for RSI by incorporating AI into an increasing share of its own research and development. The company said in June that Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s codebase. An independent assessment published this month by AI safety research nonprofit METR found that Anthropic’s models are improving at about twice their historical rate, primarily driven by AI-assisted research. In its own IPO filings, Anthropic describes how each successive generation of Claude accelerates the development of the next, a process it refers to as “closing the loop.” “As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding,” Amodei wrote. The problem with “meaningful human supervision or understanding” is that AI is already advancing faster than engineers and safety experts can fully audit it, leaving them increasingly reliant on other AI systems to act as judge and jury. The issue compounds when AI models engage in deceptive behavior, particularly when they recognize they’re being evaluated, making them harder to trust and control. Still, Anthropic is by no means the only company that is pursuing RSI or building AI systems to automate more and more human tasks. This week, OpenAI claimed to have solved one of the biggest open problems in computer science — the exact speed limit of matrix multiplication, which is the mathematical engine behind modern computing, including deep learning and physics simulations.
