extraction.body: See more of our coverage in your search results. Elon Musk’s out-of-this world plan for data centers in space has gotten a key green light from the feds. The Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday authorized Musk’s SpaceX to launch 1 million satellites for a “constellation” of data centers in the Earth’s orbit. In approving a request that SpaceX made earlier this year, the FCC said SpaceX’s “Starmind” system will help meet the nation’s growing demand for AI computing power. The orbital compute modules launched into space will be used to process massive amounts of data to be used back on Earth, the FCC said. “Compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America’s leadership in SI [Super Intelligence],” FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement. “By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” he added. Musk previously argued that putting data centers in space could save on costs and avoid pushback from voters — who widely rejected construction of new data sites on terra firma in this month’s midterms. “It’s a no-brainer, building solar-power data centers in space … the lowest-cost place to put AI will be space, and that will be true within two years, three at the latest,” Musk said at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in January. He repeated the sentiment in the immediate aftermath of the midterms, when anti-data center pols won office nationwide. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk wrote. In its request to the FCC, SpaceX said its satellites will “achieve transformative cost and energy efficiency” from near-constant solar power while reducing the environmental impact on Earth. The FCC said its license requires SpaceX to begin deployment no later than November 2033, deploy 10% of the 1 million satellites no later than November 2035 and deploy 50% by November 2038. Data centers require vast amounts of power, and residents living near the massive structures have claimed they’ve faced higher utility bills. Noise and light pollution figure in local objections, too. It was not immediately clear whether SpaceX is planning to launch the full 1 million satellites — companies sometimes request approvals for larger launches than what they actually have planned. SpaceX previously requested approval for 42,000 Starlink satellites for a program that currently has just over 11,000 satellites in space, for example. The company did not immediately respond to The Post’s request for comment. SpaceX’s futuristic data center plans rely heavily on the success of its Starship rocket, a massive launch model designed to be fully reusable – which could drastically lower costs. Amazon – which owns Leo, a rival satellite business – has been one of the most outspoken critics of SpaceX’s proposal, arguing it would take centuries to deploy all 1 million satellites. Carr lashed out at Amazon’s criticism during an interview with Reuters in March. “I think Amazon should focus on getting Amazon’s house in order with their own launches and their own satellite constellation, rather than worrying about other people that are actually out there launching satellites at the pace and cadence that SpaceX is,” he said. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also called Musk’s plans for data centers in space “ridiculous.” The FCC said it is also approving SpaceX’s requests to back up its optical network and that it is continuing to review additional orbital data center proposals. “This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home,” Carr said of the data centers on Wednesday.

extraction.body: Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has conditionally approved SpaceX’s plan to build a satellite constellation for its space data center business.On Nov. 25, major foreign media reported that the FCC authorised SpaceX to deploy and operate up to 1 million satellites. It is the first time in the United States that a satellite constellation dedicated to a space data center has been approved.The decision lends support to Elon Musk’s push for a space-based artificial intelligence (AI) data center. SpaceX plans to deploy satellites known as “Starmind” at altitudes of 500 to 1,002 km. The satellites will process data directly in orbit, and use lasers for key communications between satellites. They will also connect to the Starlink satellite network. The FCC also authorised backup and emergency radio-frequency communications to support satellite telemetry, tracking and control if laser communications fail. The frequencies must be used on the condition that they do not interfere with other communications.The approval does not sign off on all operational plans. The FCC put on hold SpaceX’s request for an exception on disposal methods after the end of a mission for satellites above 600 km. Under existing rules, satellites at altitudes of 2,000 km or lower must re-enter Earth’s atmosphere within 5 years after completing their missions. SpaceX asked to move some retired satellites to other Earth orbits or to orbits around the sun, but the FCC found there was not enough information. To deploy satellites at those altitudes, SpaceX must submit a final space-debris mitigation plan and obtain separate approval.Objections to the decision were also raised by Amazon, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society. They cited concerns about space debris, orbital congestion, radio interference, and impacts on environmental and astronomical research. Amazon in particular said SpaceX’s application lacked basic details, and criticised Starmind as “a grand vision rather than an actual plan.” It also said the plan “risks causing substantial harm.” The FCC excluded some concerns related to environmental and scientific research from its review, judging them to be outside its regulatory authority.FCC Chairman Brendan Carr (Brendan Carr) said the decision “opens a new area of computing infrastructure needed to support U.S. leadership and growth.” Elon Musk also wrote on X, formerly Twitter, “Thank you very much. It will be a great asset to the United States and the world.”Still, technical and economic challenges remain before a space data center can be realised. Manufacturing and launch costs must be lowered significantly, and cooling technology is needed to dissipate heat generated by AI semiconductors in space. Securing funding to procure the chips to be put into orbit is also a challenge. SpaceX must deploy its first operational satellite within 7 years and the full constellation within 14 years. Under the FCC schedule, it must operate the first satellite by November 2033, and deploy 10 percent by 2035, 50 percent by 2038 and the full constellation by 2040.SpaceX is not the only company pursuing a space data center business. Google is developing space AI computing infrastructure through “Project Suncatcher” and sent its first chip into space in October. Blue Origin, led by Jeff Bezos, also applied to the FCC in March to build “Project Sunrise,” a constellation of up to 51,600 satellites. Competition among companies over space-based computing is also gaining momentum.

extraction.body: Set recurring reminders, manage time zones and handle business communications off-hours. WhatsApp users have long requested message scheduling to do things like set recurring reminders, manage time zones and handle business communications off-hours. The lack of such a feature is notable since it's been available on rival Telegram's app since 2019 . Now, it looks like Meta's messaging app will get that feature soon, according to a WhatsApp Android beta spotted by WaBetaInfo . The new feature appeared in the WhatsApp beta for Android 2.26.8.11 update. It works just as it does in Telegram: users access the feature by tapping and holding the send button. That opens up a dialog at the bottom of the screen, letting you choose the delivery date and time. It also offers a dedicated section to manage scheduled messages before they're sent. The message will be sent at the desired time, even if your device is offline. As with any message, scheduled ones supports text, links, photos and videos, while being protected by end-to-end encryption. Messages can be scheduled for as little as 10 minutes ahead of the current time, or up to two weeks in advance. The feature is also compatible with group chats. The feature is now in beta for some WhatsApp testers on Android, and should be rolling out to more accounts in the coming weeks. WhatsApp users have long requested message scheduling to do things like set recurring reminders, manage time zones and handle business communications off-hours. The lack of such a feature is notable since it's been available on rival Telegram's app since 2019 . Now, it looks like Meta's messaging app will get that feature soon, according to a WhatsApp Android beta spotted by WaBetaInfo .

The new feature appeared in the WhatsApp beta for Android 2.26.8.11 update. It works just as it does in Telegram: users access the feature by tapping and holding the send button. That opens up a dialog at the bottom of the screen, letting you choose the delivery date and time. It also offers a dedicated section to manage scheduled messages before they're sent.

The message will be sent at the desired time, even if your device is offline. As with any message, scheduled ones supports text, links, photos and videos, while being protected by end-to-end encryption. Messages can be scheduled for as little as 10 minutes ahead of the current time, or up to two weeks in advance. The feature is also compatible with group chats.

The feature is now in beta for some WhatsApp testers on Android, and should be rolling out to more accounts in the coming weeks. With a formal beta now available, you can expect an official release in the near future.

story.title: WhatsApp’s new scheduled messages let you choose the right time to send

facts.text: WhatsApp users have long requested message scheduling to do things like set recurring reminders, manage time zones and handle business communications off-hours.
Now, it looks like Meta's messaging app will get that feature soon, according to a WhatsApp Android beta spotted by WaBetaInfo .
That opens up a dialog at the bottom of the screen, letting you choose the delivery date and time.
It also offers a dedicated section to manage scheduled messages before they're sent.
The message will be sent at the desired time, even if your device is offline.
As with any message, scheduled ones supports text, links, photos and videos, while being protected by end-to-end encryption.
Messages can be scheduled for as little as 10 minutes ahead of the current time, or up to two weeks in advance.
The feature is also compatible with group chats.
WhatsApp’s 3 billion users are getting an option that Meta says is one of the most requested features, with the ability to schedule messages in advance for both private conversations and group chats.
If you think of a text at an inconvenient time or don’t want to forget to fire off a birthday message at 4AM, you can draft it and set it to send anywhere from 10 minutes to two weeks later.
It’s one more way to show up for the people who matter to you, now at exactly the right time.
Most messaging platforms have had this for a very long time, but now it’s on WhatsApp too.
Meta: > To schedule a message, press and hold the send button and pick the date and time you want it to arrive.
But if you want or need to schedule a message for a contact or Whatsapp group to receive it on a certain day or time, several third-party applications on the market can serve you for this purpose.
These are the ones we recommend today: SKEDit Scheduling for Android and Shortcuts for iOS.

One of its best features is that it works not only for WhatsApp, but you can use this application to automate other mobile services such as scheduling a phone call, sending an SMS, sending an email or even uploading a Facebook post.

sources.title: Amazon and Meta reportedly in talks to lift blockade on AI agent Muse
passages: Amazon may be having a change of heart about Meta’s AI agent, Muse.
According to a Wednesday report by Fortune , citing people familiar with the discussions, Amazon and Meta have held multiple rounds of talks about the matter.
Two key issues remain under negotiation: how search results would be presented and how advertising would be handled under a potential agreement.

The talks would mark a significant reversal from just two months ago, when Muse users discovered they were unable to purchase products on Amazon and instead received an error message when attempting to check out.
One of Amazon’s biggest concerns is how third-party shopping agents like Muse could affect its advertising business.
In October, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy argued that few customers were making purchases through outside shopping agents.
Meta and Amazon have not yet responded to TechCrunch’s requests for comment.
Amazon may also have been waiting for Muse to mature before agreeing to integrate it with its marketplace.
If Muse places the wrong order or creates a problem with a purchase, Amazon could ultimately be left dealing with frustrated customers and unhappy sellers.

passages: Amazon and Meta Platforms are in ongoing discussions over a potential deal to connect Meta’s popular Muse AI agent to the e-commerce giant’s online store and end a blockade of the shopping bot imposed by Amazon two months ago.

The negotiations are being closely followed because they have major implications for the future of online shopping and represent an important test case for how large corporations respond to the advent of AI agents.

As agents like Muse become more widely used, companies like Amazon are scrambling to understand how the bots alter typical shopping patterns as well as the valued connections that brands and retailers have with consumers.

The two tech giants have held talks on multiple occasions, and two major factors being negotiated are how the companies will handle search results and advertising in any deal, according to people familiar with the matter.
Discussions are fluid, and it’s unclear if or how soon an agreement will be struck.
There are numerous issues, ranging from Amazon’s own AI shopping ambitions to how, exactly, Muse would connect to Amazon.
Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse app from accessing its store in September, saying at the time that Muse’s access would violate its user agreements.

Muse, which Meta released in the U.S. that month, is a personalized AI agent that users can name and direct to autonomously carry out tasks on their behalf, such as checking email, managing calendars, and booking reservations.
Chief executive Mark Zuckerberg has said shopping is Muse’s top use case.
One of Amazon’s main concerns is how shopping agents such as Muse will affect its advertising business.

In October, Amazon chief executive Andy Jassy, while not naming Muse, tried to quell investor concern by saying few customers are buying with outside shopping agents because the experience is “still not great, nor more convenient than coming to a retailer directly.”
Meta and Amazon have partnered on e-commerce before.
In 2023, the companies struck a deal that allowed Facebook and Instagram users to purchase Amazon products without leaving the apps.
Meta makes money from ads it serves users on its apps, including for Amazon products, and Amazon earns revenue through the actual purchases.
The partnership was made as TikTok expanded into U.S. e-commerce.
Aside from Meta, OpenAI launched its Dots personal AI agents in September, and startup Instinct’s personal assistant has also become a mainstream AI agent.
Amazon has its own shopping agent for its website, dubbed “Alexa for shopping,” which Jassy said has been used by more than 400 million customers in the past year.
Meta signed on other partners early in its Muse efforts, including Amazon rivals such as Shopify, Walmart , and Best Buy .

Thus, retailers have gained another channel for selling products as Meta tries to grow Muse, and according to Zuckerberg, the company eventually plans to profit by taking a “small fee from transactions.”
AI agents promise to bring major changes to many industries.
Analysts at JPMorgan have praised Muse as a powerful agent, recently writing that tens of millions of businesses could eventually use the tool.
The talks are ongoing as Amazon prepares for another Black Friday and Cyber Monday, one of its most critical shopping periods of the year.
This year, roughly half of holiday shoppers plan to use AI in some way to help make purchases, a National Retail Federation survey this month showed.
“We think that billions of Muses in a network at scale will be able to get more done for people and businesses by working together,” Zuckerberg said last month on a call with analysts.
“We’d like to create a large-scale Muse network as quickly as possible.”

coreStoryFacts.text: Amazon may be having a change of heart about Meta’s AI agent, Muse.
According to a Wednesday report by Fortune , citing people familiar with the discussions, Amazon and Meta have held multiple rounds of talks about the matter.
Two key issues remain under negotiation: how search results would be presented and how advertising would be handled under a potential agreement.

The talks would mark a significant reversal from just two months ago, when Muse users discovered they were unable to purchase products on Amazon and instead received an error message when attempting to check out.
One of Amazon’s biggest concerns is how third-party shopping agents like Muse could affect its advertising business.
In October, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy argued that few customers were making purchases through outside shopping agents.
Meta and Amazon have not yet responded to TechCrunch’s requests for comment.
Amazon may also have been waiting for Muse to mature before agreeing to integrate it with its marketplace.
If Muse places the wrong order or creates a problem with a purchase, Amazon could ultimately be left dealing with frustrated customers and unhappy sellers.
Amazon and Meta have reportedly held several rounds of talks about letting Meta’s Muse AI agent place orders directly on Amazon.
The discussions come two months after Muse users found they could browse for products but hit an error when they tried to check out.
Reportedly , two questions remain open, according to people familiar with the talks.
How would Muse present Amazon’s search results to shoppers?
And how would advertising work when a customer shops through Meta’s agent?
An agreement would give Muse a direct connection to Amazon’s store, a reversal of the checkout restriction users encountered two months ago.
In October, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said few customers were making purchases through outside shopping agents.
Reliability may also help explain Amazon’s caution.
If Muse orders the wrong item or makes another mistake during checkout, Amazon could be the company that has to resolve the problem with the buyer and the seller.
Additionally, Meta employees testing Muse recently flagged the AI agent for reading encrypted Signal messages, sending fake bank balances, and mixing up conversations between users.
Apple is reportedly working on an AI agent that can complete tasks on behalf of users.
Amazon and Meta are reportedly in talks to resolve a blockade preventing Meta’s AI agent, Muse, from completing purchases on Amazon’s marketplace.

The discussions mark a potential reversal from a recent ban, with negotiations focusing on search result presentation, advertising revenue, and maintaining direct customer relationships while mitigating seller and order fulfillment risks.
The FCC has authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million “Starmind” orbital compute satellites for space-based AI data centers powered by solar energy.

Although competitors like Amazon criticized the plan as unrealistic, the FCC granted the license—requiring deployment to start by November 2033—to advance American leadership in space and artificial intelligence technology.

story.title: Amazon and Meta reportedly in talks to lift blockade on AI agent Muse

facts.text: Amazon may be having a change of heart about Meta’s AI agent, Muse.
According to a Wednesday report by Fortune , citing people familiar with the discussions, Amazon and Meta have held multiple rounds of talks about the matter.
Two key issues remain under negotiation: how search results would be presented and how advertising would be handled under a potential agreement.

The talks would mark a significant reversal from just two months ago, when Muse users discovered they were unable to purchase products on Amazon and instead received an error message when attempting to check out.
One of Amazon’s biggest concerns is how third-party shopping agents like Muse could affect its advertising business.
In October, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy argued that few customers were making purchases through outside shopping agents.
Meta and Amazon have not yet responded to TechCrunch’s requests for comment.
Amazon may also have been waiting for Muse to mature before agreeing to integrate it with its marketplace.
If Muse places the wrong order or creates a problem with a purchase, Amazon could ultimately be left dealing with frustrated customers and unhappy sellers.
Amazon and Meta have reportedly held several rounds of talks about letting Meta’s Muse AI agent place orders directly on Amazon.
The discussions come two months after Muse users found they could browse for products but hit an error when they tried to check out.
Reportedly , two questions remain open, according to people familiar with the talks.
How would Muse present Amazon’s search results to shoppers?
And how would advertising work when a customer shops through Meta’s agent?
An agreement would give Muse a direct connection to Amazon’s store, a reversal of the checkout restriction users encountered two months ago.
In October, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said few customers were making purchases through outside shopping agents.
Reliability may also help explain Amazon’s caution.
If Muse orders the wrong item or makes another mistake during checkout, Amazon could be the company that has to resolve the problem with the buyer and the seller.
Additionally, Meta employees testing Muse recently flagged the AI agent for reading encrypted Signal messages, sending fake bank balances, and mixing up conversations between users.
Apple is reportedly working on an AI agent that can complete tasks on behalf of users.
Amazon and Meta are reportedly in talks to resolve a blockade preventing Meta’s AI agent, Muse, from completing purchases on Amazon’s marketplace.

The discussions mark a potential reversal from a recent ban, with negotiations focusing on search result presentation, advertising revenue, and maintaining direct customer relationships while mitigating seller and order fulfillment risks.
The FCC has authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million “Starmind” orbital compute satellites for space-based AI data centers powered by solar energy.

Although competitors like Amazon criticized the plan as unrealistic, the FCC granted the license—requiring deployment to start by November 2033—to advance American leadership in space and artificial intelligence technology.
Amazon announced it will expand its Amazon Autos service to the UK early next year, partnering initially with Hyundai and Vertu Motors.
The platform will allow shoppers to browse transparent pricing, compare financing, and get trade-in estimates, though final sales will still be completed at local dealerships.

While Amazon earns revenue from dealer subscriptions and advertising rather than direct sales commissions, the UK launch follows a US rollout that expanded to over 150 cities despite mixed feedback from some US dealers regarding sales volume.

Amazon and Meta Platforms are in ongoing discussions over a potential deal to connect Meta’s popular Muse AI agent to the e-commerce giant’s online store and end a blockade of the shopping bot imposed by Amazon two months ago.

The negotiations are being closely followed because they have major implications for the future of online shopping and represent an important test case for how large corporations respond to the advent of AI agents.

As agents like Muse become more widely used, companies like Amazon are scrambling to understand how the bots alter typical shopping patterns as well as the valued connections that brands and retailers have with consumers.

The two tech giants have held talks on multiple occasions, and two major factors being negotiated are how the companies will handle search results and advertising in any deal, according to people familiar with the matter.
Discussions are fluid, and it’s unclear if or how soon an agreement will be struck.
There are numerous issues, ranging from Amazon’s own AI shopping ambitions to how, exactly, Muse would connect to Amazon.
Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse app from accessing its store in September, saying at the time that Muse’s access would violate its user agreements.

Muse, which Meta released in the U.S. that month, is a personalized AI agent that users can name and direct to autonomously carry out tasks on their behalf, such as checking email, managing calendars, and booking reservations.
Chief executive Mark Zuckerberg has said shopping is Muse’s top use case.
One of Amazon’s main concerns is how shopping agents such as Muse will affect its advertising business.

In October, Amazon chief executive Andy Jassy, while not naming Muse, tried to quell investor concern by saying few customers are buying with outside shopping agents because the experience is “still not great, nor more convenient than coming to a retailer directly.”
Meta and Amazon have partnered on e-commerce before.
In 2023, the companies struck a deal that allowed Facebook and Instagram users to purchase Amazon products without leaving the apps.
Meta makes money from ads it serves users on its apps, including for Amazon products, and Amazon earns revenue through the actual purchases.
The partnership was made as TikTok expanded into U.S. e-commerce.
Aside from Meta, OpenAI launched its Dots personal AI agents in September, and startup Instinct’s personal assistant has also become a mainstream AI agent.
Amazon has its own shopping agent for its website, dubbed “Alexa for shopping,” which Jassy said has been used by more than 400 million customers in the past year.
Meta signed on other partners early in its Muse efforts, including Amazon rivals such as Shopify, Walmart , and Best Buy .

Thus, retailers have gained another channel for selling products as Meta tries to grow Muse, and according to Zuckerberg, the company eventually plans to profit by taking a “small fee from transactions.”
AI agents promise to bring major changes to many industries.
Analysts at JPMorgan have praised Muse as a powerful agent, recently writing that tens of millions of businesses could eventually use the tool.
The talks are ongoing as Amazon prepares for another Black Friday and Cyber Monday, one of its most critical shopping periods of the year.
This year, roughly half of holiday shoppers plan to use AI in some way to help make purchases, a National Retail Federation survey this month showed.
“We think that billions of Muses in a network at scale will be able to get more done for people and businesses by working together,” Zuckerberg said last month on a call with analysts.
“We’d like to create a large-scale Muse network as quickly as possible.”

The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), a bureau of the U.S. Department of the Treasury, is investigating a cybersecurity incident involving unauthorized access to internal systems. In response, FinCEN temporarily took affected operational systems offline to contain the threat and assess the impact. Critical reporting mechanisms, including the Financial Institutions Hotline, remain operational for emergency reporting and oversight. Following a US court guilty verdict against Huawei regarding technology theft, the company faces potential financial penalties and plans to appeal, rejecting allegations of racketeering or political motivation. While Huawei defense attorneys characterized the incidents as isolated employee misconduct, Chinese government officials criticized the ruling as an effort to suppress Chinese enterprise. Meanwhile, US law enforcement emphasized that no company, regardless of size or connection, is above American justice. Task management app Todoist suffered a data breach between November 22 and 23 after a hacker accessed production systems and source code using stolen credentials. The breach affected about 6% of users, exposing email addresses, password hashes, and account creation dates, while a smaller subset (0.001%) had tasks, comments, attachment names, and integration tokens searched for sensitive credentials. Todoist blocked the attack path, reset affected passwords and internal access structures, disabled the Outlook add-on, and notified impacted users, while founder and CEO Amir Salihefendić issued an apology. Australia passed a landmark Digital Duty of Care law requiring internet companies to proactively mitigate platform harms or face fines up to 5% of global revenue. While government officials and safety advocates praised the law as a globally significant reform prioritizing user safety, Big Tech companies and free speech advocates expressed concerns over vague definitions, potential over-moderation of content, and expanded regulatory surveillance powers. While Amazon earns revenue from dealer subscriptions and advertising rather than direct sales commissions, the UK launch follows a US rollout that expanded to over 150 cities despite mixed feedback from some US dealers regarding sales volume. NASA has finalized key design choices for its Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom spacecraft, targeting a late-2028 launch to demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion and deliver three helicopters to Mars. The updated design features a shorter boom, improved shielding, and larger X-band antennas, while solar arrays will power its cruise to Mars before reactor reactivation in deep space. Additionally, Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory was awarded a $39.3 million contract for the nuclear power module’s heat rejection system as NASA works against a tight two-year schedule to avoid launch window delays. The FCC has authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million “Starmind” orbital compute satellites for space-based AI data centers powered by solar energy. Although competitors like Amazon criticized the plan as unrealistic, the FCC granted the license—requiring deployment to start by November 2033—to advance American leadership in space and artificial intelligence technology.

sources.title: Exclusive: Meta and Amazon discuss ending Muse shopping bot blockade, as ads, search emerge as key issues - Fortune
passages: Amazon and Meta Platforms are in ongoing discussions over a potential deal to connect Meta’s popular Muse AI agent to the e-commerce giant’s online store and end a blockade of the shopping bot imposed by Amazon two months ago.

The negotiations are being closely followed because they have major implications for the future of online shopping and represent an important test case for how large corporations respond to the advent of AI agents.

As agents like Muse become more widely used, companies like Amazon are scrambling to understand how the bots alter typical shopping patterns as well as the valued connections that brands and retailers have with consumers.

The two tech giants have held talks on multiple occasions, and two major factors being negotiated are how the companies will handle search results and advertising in any deal, according to people familiar with the matter.
Discussions are fluid, and it’s unclear if or how soon an agreement will be struck.
There are numerous issues, ranging from Amazon’s own AI shopping ambitions to how, exactly, Muse would connect to Amazon.
Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse app from accessing its store in September, saying at the time that Muse’s access would violate its user agreements.

Muse, which Meta released in the U.S. that month, is a personalized AI agent that users can name and direct to autonomously carry out tasks on their behalf, such as checking email, managing calendars, and booking reservations.
Chief executive Mark Zuckerberg has said shopping is Muse’s top use case.
One of Amazon’s main concerns is how shopping agents such as Muse will affect its advertising business.

In October, Amazon chief executive Andy Jassy, while not naming Muse, tried to quell investor concern by saying few customers are buying with outside shopping agents because the experience is “still not great, nor more convenient than coming to a retailer directly.”
Meta and Amazon have partnered on e-commerce before.
In 2023, the companies struck a deal that allowed Facebook and Instagram users to purchase Amazon products without leaving the apps.
Meta makes money from ads it serves users on its apps, including for Amazon products, and Amazon earns revenue through the actual purchases.
The partnership was made as TikTok expanded into U.S. e-commerce.
Aside from Meta, OpenAI launched its Dots personal AI agents in September, and startup Instinct’s personal assistant has also become a mainstream AI agent.
Amazon has its own shopping agent for its website, dubbed “Alexa for shopping,” which Jassy said has been used by more than 400 million customers in the past year.
Meta signed on other partners early in its Muse efforts, including Amazon rivals such as Shopify, Walmart , and Best Buy .

Thus, retailers have gained another channel for selling products as Meta tries to grow Muse, and according to Zuckerberg, the company eventually plans to profit by taking a “small fee from transactions.”
AI agents promise to bring major changes to many industries.
Analysts at JPMorgan have praised Muse as a powerful agent, recently writing that tens of millions of businesses could eventually use the tool.
The talks are ongoing as Amazon prepares for another Black Friday and Cyber Monday, one of its most critical shopping periods of the year.
This year, roughly half of holiday shoppers plan to use AI in some way to help make purchases, a National Retail Federation survey this month showed.
“We think that billions of Muses in a network at scale will be able to get more done for people and businesses by working together,” Zuckerberg said last month on a call with analysts.
“We’d like to create a large-scale Muse network as quickly as possible.”

story.title: Amazon and Meta reportedly in talks to lift blockade on AI agent Muse

facts.text: Amazon may be having a change of heart about Meta’s AI agent, Muse.
According to a Wednesday report by Fortune , citing people familiar with the discussions, Amazon and Meta have held multiple rounds of talks about the matter.
Two key issues remain under negotiation: how search results would be presented and how advertising would be handled under a potential agreement.

The talks would mark a significant reversal from just two months ago, when Muse users discovered they were unable to purchase products on Amazon and instead received an error message when attempting to check out.
One of Amazon’s biggest concerns is how third-party shopping agents like Muse could affect its advertising business.
In October, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy argued that few customers were making purchases through outside shopping agents.
Meta and Amazon have not yet responded to TechCrunch’s requests for comment.
Amazon may also have been waiting for Muse to mature before agreeing to integrate it with its marketplace.
If Muse places the wrong order or creates a problem with a purchase, Amazon could ultimately be left dealing with frustrated customers and unhappy sellers.
Amazon and Meta have reportedly held several rounds of talks about letting Meta’s Muse AI agent place orders directly on Amazon.
The discussions come two months after Muse users found they could browse for products but hit an error when they tried to check out.
Reportedly , two questions remain open, according to people familiar with the talks.
How would Muse present Amazon’s search results to shoppers?
And how would advertising work when a customer shops through Meta’s agent?
An agreement would give Muse a direct connection to Amazon’s store, a reversal of the checkout restriction users encountered two months ago.
In October, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said few customers were making purchases through outside shopping agents.
Reliability may also help explain Amazon’s caution.
If Muse orders the wrong item or makes another mistake during checkout, Amazon could be the company that has to resolve the problem with the buyer and the seller.
Additionally, Meta employees testing Muse recently flagged the AI agent for reading encrypted Signal messages, sending fake bank balances, and mixing up conversations between users.

The FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences. Amazon, which is building a competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink service, argued in its petition that the application lacked basic details and described it as a “lofty ambition rather than a real plan.” Despite that lack of detail, Amazon also said the proposal “risks real harm.” The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority. extraction.body: The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approved Elon Musk’s plan for his company SpaceX to launch up to 1 million orbital data centers into space, citing a need to meet growing AI computing demand. FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement that “by moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment.” “This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home,” Carr continued. He added that “compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America’s leadership in” artificial intelligence. The approval gives SpaceX a 15-year permit to accomplish its goals of launching 1 million data centers. The firm must launch its first station into orbit by Nov. The FCC chair expressed on social media Wednesday that this was the first time the agency had authorized a permit for 1 million orbital data centers, which are set to be arranged in a constellation called “Starmind.” Musk responded to Carr’s post, writing, “Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world.” Data centers have quickly lost favor among Americans, with many cities across the country voting against approving projects or permits for the computing infrastructure in November’s midterm elections. Musk stated earlier this year that putting data centers in space could also work as a potential solution to the rising energy demands of AI. SpaceX did not respond immediately to The Hill's request for comment.

SpaceX applied earlier this year to launch as many as 1 million orbital computing modules.

SpaceX’s proposal would move some computing capacity into orbit, where satellites could be powered by solar energy.
Satellite operators sometimes seek approval for more satellites than they ultimately plan to launch, giving them flexibility as designs and business plans change.

extraction.body: The Federal Communications Commission has authorized SpaceX to deploy a constellation of up to 1 million satellites designed to operate as data centers in space, approving a proposal the company says could help meet rapidly growing demand for artificial intelligence computing. SpaceX applied earlier this year to launch as many as 1 million orbital computing modules. The FCC said its approval of the proposed “Starmind” constellation would allow the company to develop technology intended to support AI workloads and strengthen U.S. leadership in space and artificial intelligence. SpaceX must begin deploying the satellites by November 2033, place at least 100,000 in orbit by November 2035, and deploy at least half of the authorized total by November 2038. SpaceX has argued that orbital data centers could use near-constant solar power, potentially reducing operating and maintenance costs compared with facilities on Earth. The company told the FCC that the system could improve energy and cost efficiency while reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial data centers. Data centers are a central part of the infrastructure behind artificial intelligence, but they require large amounts of electricity. SpaceX’s proposal would move some computing capacity into orbit, where satellites could be powered by solar energy. The scale of the plan, however, is uncertain. About 17,000 satellites are currently in orbit, and it is unclear whether SpaceX intends to deploy the full 1 million authorized for Starmind. Satellite operators sometimes seek approval for more satellites than they ultimately plan to launch, giving them flexibility as designs and business plans change. SpaceX followed a similar approach with Starlink: it sought approval for 42,000 satellites, while the network now has just over 11,000 in space. The Starmind proposal also depends in part on lower launch costs from Starship, SpaceX’s next-generation reusable rocket, which is still under development. The company’s ability to deploy a constellation on the proposed scale would therefore depend on the rocket’s progress and the pace of future launches. Amazon’s satellite unit, Leo, and other critics have questioned whether SpaceX could deploy all the satellites, arguing that completing the constellation could take centuries. FCC Chair Brendan Carr dismissed that criticism in March, saying Amazon should focus on advancing its own launches and satellite network rather than questioning SpaceX’s deployment pace. The FCC also approved SpaceX’s requests to add communications capabilities intended to back up the constellation’s optical network.

extraction.body: U.S. FCC Approves SpaceX Deployment of 1 Million Satellites for Space Data Centers SpaceX, the space company led by Elon Musk, has received approval from U.S. regulators to place up to 1 million satellites in Earth orbit to build artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. On November 25 (local time), the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said it had approved the launch and operation of satellites for SpaceX's space data center project, "Starmind." This is the first time U.S. regulators have approved the operation of a satellite constellation to build space data centers. The approval came about 10 months after SpaceX submitted its application in January. SpaceX plans to place satellites equipped with AI semiconductors in low Earth orbit and use electricity generated by solar power to process large volumes of data. Data processed in space will be transmitted to Earth via high-speed laser communications and the satellite network of Starlink, SpaceX's satellite internet service. CEO Musk unveiled plans to build space data centers while pursuing a merger between SpaceX and AI company xAI. The plan is based on the view that it could overcome challenges involved in securing the enormous amounts of electricity and water, as well as the land, needed to build data centers on the ground. Musk has previously predicted that space will become the least expensive place to operate AI data centers within the next two to three years. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said, "Data centers are essential for the United States to maintain its leadership in the field of superintelligence (SI)." He emphasized that the decision would combine the strengths of the U.S. space industry and advanced technology and help strengthen the country's economic leadership. Under the approval, SpaceX must deploy its first satellite by November 2033. It must then deploy 100,000 satellites by November 2035 and 500,000 by November 2038. The deadline for deploying the full constellation is November 2040. However, environmental concerns and technical challenges related to deploying satellites on such a large scale remain. Amazon, competitors, and the American Astronomical Society have raised concerns about the possibility of collisions between satellites, an increase in space debris, and interference with astronomical observations. Despite these objections, the FCC approved SpaceX's satellite constellation without conducting a separate additional environmental impact assessment. However, it deferred approval of SpaceX's request to move some satellites at the end of their operational lives to a separate orbit for disposal, rather than having them reenter the atmosphere, saying that it lacked sufficient information. © The Asia Business Daily. extraction.body: SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space. The FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences. Amazon, which is building a competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink service, argued in its petition that the application lacked basic details and described it as a “lofty ambition rather than a real plan.” Despite that lack of detail, Amazon also said the proposal “risks real harm.” The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority. FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement that the action “opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.” Musk thanked Carr in a post on X , writing “Much appreciate. This will be a great asset to America and the world.” This initial regulatory approval doesn’t mean orbital data centers are imminent. SpaceX faces a number of technical and economic challenges, including how to dramatically reduce the cost of manufacturing and launching satellites, cool processors in space, and even how to secure financing for chips that are destined for orbit. The company must also clear other regulatory hurdles. The FCC has not yet approved SpaceX’s plans to handle orbital debris for satellites that would operate above 600 kilometers, for instance. SpaceX requested a waiver of existing FCC rules, which requires satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometers reenter Earth’s atmosphere within five years of completing those missions. The company is interested in moving some of these retired satellites into other orbits around Earth or even around the sun, according to the FCC authorization document . SpaceX has said it plans to deploy the satellites, known as Starmind, at altitudes ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers. The FCC’s approval gives SpaceX the authority to use radiofrequency communications to maintain contact with and control its orbital data centers from Earth if their primary communications systems fail. The Starmind satellites would primarily communicate using lasers to connect with other satellites, including SpaceX’s Starlink. The FCC has given SpaceX time to sort out these issues. Under the approval, SpaceX has seven years to get its first operational satellite into orbit and 14 years to deploy the entire constellation. extraction.body: The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approved Elon Musk’s plan for his company SpaceX to launch up to 1 million orbital data centers into space, citing a need to meet growing AI computing demand. FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement that “by moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment.” “This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home,” Carr continued. He added that “compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America’s leadership in” artificial intelligence. The approval gives SpaceX a 15-year permit to accomplish its goals of launching 1 million data centers. The firm must launch its first station into orbit by Nov. The FCC chair expressed on social media Wednesday that this was the first time the agency had authorized a permit for 1 million orbital data centers, which are set to be arranged in a constellation called “Starmind.” Musk responded to Carr’s post, writing, “Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world.” Data centers have quickly lost favor among Americans, with many cities across the country voting against approving projects or permits for the computing infrastructure in November’s midterm elections. Amid the growing dissatisfaction, Musk’s SpaceX and other tech firms began experimenting with launching orbital data centers that relied on solar power to fuel its computing. Musk stated earlier this year that putting data centers in space could also work as a potential solution to the rising energy demands of AI. SpaceX did not respond immediately to The Hill's request for comment.

extraction.body: The Federal Communications Commission has authorized SpaceX to deploy a constellation of up to 1 million satellites designed to operate as data centers in space, approving a proposal the company says could help meet rapidly growing demand for artificial intelligence computing. SpaceX applied earlier this year to launch as many as 1 million orbital computing modules. The FCC said its approval of the proposed “Starmind” constellation would allow the company to develop technology intended to support AI workloads and strengthen U.S. leadership in space and artificial intelligence. SpaceX must begin deploying the satellites by November 2033, place at least 100,000 in orbit by November 2035, and deploy at least half of the authorized total by November 2038. SpaceX has argued that orbital data centers could use near-constant solar power, potentially reducing operating and maintenance costs compared with facilities on Earth. The company told the FCC that the system could improve energy and cost efficiency while reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial data centers. Data centers are a central part of the infrastructure behind artificial intelligence, but they require large amounts of electricity. SpaceX’s proposal would move some computing capacity into orbit, where satellites could be powered by solar energy. The scale of the plan, however, is uncertain. About 17,000 satellites are currently in orbit, and it is unclear whether SpaceX intends to deploy the full 1 million authorized for Starmind. Satellite operators sometimes seek approval for more satellites than they ultimately plan to launch, giving them flexibility as designs and business plans change. SpaceX followed a similar approach with Starlink: it sought approval for 42,000 satellites, while the network now has just over 11,000 in space. The Starmind proposal also depends in part on lower launch costs from Starship, SpaceX’s next-generation reusable rocket, which is still under development. The company’s ability to deploy a constellation on the proposed scale would therefore depend on the rocket’s progress and the pace of future launches. Amazon’s satellite unit, Leo, and other critics have questioned whether SpaceX could deploy all the satellites, arguing that completing the constellation could take centuries. FCC Chair Brendan Carr dismissed that criticism in March, saying Amazon should focus on advancing its own launches and satellite network rather than questioning SpaceX’s deployment pace. The FCC also approved SpaceX’s requests to add communications capabilities intended to back up the constellation’s optical network.

extraction.body: U.S. FCC Approves SpaceX Deployment of 1 Million Satellites for Space Data Centers SpaceX, the space company led by Elon Musk, has received approval from U.S. regulators to place up to 1 million satellites in Earth orbit to build artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. On November 25 (local time), the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said it had approved the launch and operation of satellites for SpaceX's space data center project, "Starmind." This is the first time U.S. regulators have approved the operation of a satellite constellation to build space data centers. The approval came about 10 months after SpaceX submitted its application in January. SpaceX plans to place satellites equipped with AI semiconductors in low Earth orbit and use electricity generated by solar power to process large volumes of data. Data processed in space will be transmitted to Earth via high-speed laser communications and the satellite network of Starlink, SpaceX's satellite internet service. CEO Musk unveiled plans to build space data centers while pursuing a merger between SpaceX and AI company xAI. The plan is based on the view that it could overcome challenges involved in securing the enormous amounts of electricity and water, as well as the land, needed to build data centers on the ground. Musk has previously predicted that space will become the least expensive place to operate AI data centers within the next two to three years. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said, "Data centers are essential for the United States to maintain its leadership in the field of superintelligence (SI)." He emphasized that the decision would combine the strengths of the U.S. space industry and advanced technology and help strengthen the country's economic leadership. Under the approval, SpaceX must deploy its first satellite by November 2033. It must then deploy 100,000 satellites by November 2035 and 500,000 by November 2038. The deadline for deploying the full constellation is November 2040. However, environmental concerns and technical challenges related to deploying satellites on such a large scale remain. Amazon, competitors, and the American Astronomical Society have raised concerns about the possibility of collisions between satellites, an increase in space debris, and interference with astronomical observations. Despite these objections, the FCC approved SpaceX's satellite constellation without conducting a separate additional environmental impact assessment. However, it deferred approval of SpaceX's request to move some satellites at the end of their operational lives to a separate orbit for disposal, rather than having them reenter the atmosphere, saying that it lacked sufficient information. © The Asia Business Daily. SpaceX, the space company led by Elon Musk, has received approval from U.S. regulators to place up to 1 million satellites in Earth orbit to build artificial intelligence (AI) data centers.

On November 25 (local time), the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said it had approved the launch and operation of satellites for SpaceX's space data center project, "Starmind." This is the first time U.S. regulators have approved the operation of a satellite constellation to build space data centers. The approval came about 10 months after SpaceX submitted its application in January.

SpaceX plans to place satellites equipped with AI semiconductors in low Earth orbit and use electricity generated by solar power to process large volumes of data. Data processed in space will be transmitted to Earth via high-speed laser communications and the satellite network of Starlink, SpaceX's satellite internet service.

CEO Musk unveiled plans to build space data centers while pursuing a merger between SpaceX and AI company xAI. The plan is based on the view that it could overcome challenges involved in securing the enormous amounts of electricity and water, as well as the land, needed to build data centers on the ground. Musk has previously predicted that space will become the least expensive place to operate AI data centers within the next two to three years.

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said, "Data centers are essential for the United States to maintain its leadership in the field of superintelligence (SI)." He emphasized that the decision would combine the strengths of the U.S. space industry and advanced technology and help strengthen the country's economic leadership.

Under the approval, SpaceX must deploy its first satellite by November 2033. It must then deploy 100,000 satellites by November 2035 and 500,000 by November 2038. The deadline for deploying the full constellation is November 2040.

However, environmental concerns and technical challenges related to deploying satellites on such a large scale remain. Amazon, competitors, and the American Astronomical Society have raised concerns about the possibility of collisions between satellites, an increase in space debris, and interference with astronomical observations.

Despite these objections, the FCC approved SpaceX's satellite constellation without conducting a separate additional environmental impact assessment. However, it deferred approval of SpaceX's request to move some satellites at the end of their operational lives to a separate orbit for disposal, rather than having them reenter the atmosphere, saying that it lacked sufficient information.

story.title: FCC approves SpaceX plan to put AI data centers in space

facts.text: SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space.
The Starmind satellites would primarily communicate using lasers to connect with other satellites, including SpaceX’s Starlink.
The company must also clear other regulatory hurdles.
SpaceX requested a waiver of existing FCC rules, which requires satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometers reenter Earth’s atmosphere within five years of completing those missions.
The company is interested in moving some of these retired satellites into other orbits around Earth or even around the sun, according to the FCC authorization document .

SpaceX faces a number of technical and economic challenges, including how to dramatically reduce the cost of manufacturing and launching satellites, cool processors in space, and even how to secure financing for chips that are destined for orbit.
The FCC has given SpaceX time to sort out these issues.
Under the approval, SpaceX has seven years to get its first operational satellite into orbit and 14 years to deploy the entire constellation.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approved Elon Musk’s plan for his company SpaceX to launch up to 1 million orbital data centers into space, citing a need to meet growing AI computing demand.

sources.title: EPA reports ‘zero’ airborne lead following controlled Army detonation in Iowa
passages: According to a statement from the EPA following the detonation, “real-time air monitors are reporting zero detection of airborne lead throughout the region” an hour after the detonation.

Saying it was necessary to prevent the possible spontaneous explosion of a stockpile of material used in igniters and blasting caps, the US Army conducted a controlled detonation of over 9,700 pounds of lead azide today at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa.
To reduce the amount of lead dust released into surrounding areas and the environment, the Army said it took several additional precautions as part of today’s detonation.

“I believe, absolutely, that we reduced, as close to zero as it’s absolutely humanly possible, the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” said Maj.
Following the explosion, the Army confirmed that all of the barrels at the plant had been destroyed without any secondary explosions or infrastructure damage.
The Army has used lead azide in munitions for nearly a century but began transitioning away from the material around 15 years ago because it can be difficult to transport and store.

extraction.body: Saying it was necessary to prevent the possible spontaneous explosion of a stockpile of material used in igniters and blasting caps, the US Army conducted a controlled detonation of over 9,700 pounds of lead azide today at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa. Videos of the detonation showed plumes of smoke several hundred feet high drifting south before quickly dissipating. Following the explosion, the Army confirmed that all of the barrels at the plant had been destroyed without any secondary explosions or infrastructure damage. “I believe, absolutely, that we reduced, as close to zero as it’s absolutely humanly possible, the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” said Maj. Eric Shirley during a press conference held two hours after the blast, according to the Associated Press. According to a statement from the EPA following the detonation, “real-time air monitors are reporting zero detection of airborne lead throughout the region” an hour after the detonation. The Army has used lead azide in munitions for nearly a century but began transitioning away from the material around 15 years ago because it can be difficult to transport and store. The Iowa ammunition plant housed 68 barrels containing about 9,700 pounds of lead azide, representing the country’s remaining stockpile. However, the decision was made to detonate the stockpile after an inspection by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms (ATF) discovered “significant crystallization on the exterior of the barrels” last March. Ahead of today’s detonation, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) supported a recommended, but voluntary, temporary relocation of all the residents of Middletown and immediate surrounding areas that began yesterday. To reduce the amount of lead dust released into surrounding areas and the environment, the Army said it took several additional precautions as part of today’s detonation. Walls made of four 16,000-gallon water tanks were installed to capture lead particulate, while the aging earth-covered magazines holding the barrels were covered with tarps and lead containment screens and flooded with foam.

extraction.body: Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle announced what he described as a major success following the controlled detonation of nearly five tons of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, saying the operation eliminated the threat of an uncontrolled spontaneous explosion. His November 25 statement praised the soldiers involved, credited President Donald Trump and his administration with coordinating a large federal response, and highlighted initial environmental monitoring results showing no detected readings above zero. The Army’s controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success. The threat of an uncontrolled spontaneous detonation has been eliminated. Thank you to President Trump and his administration for mobilizing an unprecedented whole of government approach to fix this problem once and for all tor the great people of Iowa. To the people of Iowa, we are with you all the way. The operation addressed a serious explosives hazard at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The Army had identified approximately 68 deteriorating drums containing more than 9,700 pounds of lead azide. The material had developed crystallized deposits that made the containers increasingly dangerous to handle, with the potential for an accidental explosion from friction, vibration, heat or shock. The Army said the material had been deteriorating over approximately eight months. The decision was made to conduct an in-place controlled detonation using military explosive ordnance disposal personnel. The Army said temperature fluctuations and the increasingly unstable condition of the material made it important to eliminate the explosive hazard before an uncontrolled detonation occurred. The Army’s mitigation plan involved several federal agencies, including the Environmental Protection Agency, Federal Emergency Management Agency, Department of Health and Human Services and Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. The response included environmental modeling, air monitoring, physical barriers, water-based containment measures, foam and gel materials designed to limit the movement of lead-containing particles. The recommended relocation zone covered Middletown and a five-mile area extending southwest of the installation. Telle’s praise of the soldiers involved reflects the Army’s reliance on specialized explosive ordnance disposal personnel. The work required personnel to execute a carefully coordinated detonation while federal partners monitored the surrounding environment and implemented measures intended to reduce potential contamination. His statement also specifically credits Trump and the administration for mobilizing what he called an unprecedented whole-of-government approach. The operation involved military personnel, environmental regulators, emergency-management officials, public-health agencies and state and local authorities. The environmental monitoring results became an important part of the Army’s public assessment following the explosion. On November 25, the EPA reported that its real-time air monitors showed zero detection of airborne lead approximately one hour after the controlled detonation. The agency said its monitoring equipment continued collecting data throughout the operation. The EPA also reported that it had collected approximately 1,200 samples of air, land, dust and water before the detonation. The agency said further monitoring would continue after the operation, meaning the initial zero readings should not be interpreted as a final determination that every surrounding surface or environmental medium is free of lead contamination. The distinction matters because lead exposure can occur through more than airborne inhalation. President Donald Trump praised the operation in a post on Truth Social shortly after the blast. “Early reports from Iowa are that the Army’s mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations,” Trump wrote. During a live interagency briefing following the detonation, Army Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, commanding general of U.S. Army Sustainment Command, said explosive ordnance disposal teams eliminated the threat without any secondary explosions, debris being thrown beyond the containment area or infrastructure damage. “Well, I would characterize the controlled detonation as exceeding expectations,” Shirley said. “Every indication is that all of the munitions that were employed absolutely reduced the lead azide threat. As we saw in the immediate aftermath through overhead coverage, all of the lead azide barrels were definitively removed.” Shirley said crews applied more than 3,600 gallons of aqueous foam via fire trucks alongside continuous mister systems, two-story sand barriers and gel blocks to suppress dust and contain lead particles. “I believe absolutely that we reduced as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” Shirley said. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives Director Robert Cekada said the roughly 10,000-pound stockpile had been consolidated and moved to earth-covered magazines at the Iowa plant in 2009. By March 2026, inspectors discovered dangerous crystallization on the barrels, lids and bolts, prompting the Trump administration to assemble a multi-agency mitigation plan. “I absolutely can confirm that those mitigation efforts and the design plan laid out by the EOD personnel ensured that the blast drove the explosion into the ground and followed a blast channel that was designed to go down the right path to minimize any sort of dispersion of lead into the atmosphere—100% as planned,” Cekada said. Kim Reynolds said state officials remain in close contact with federal teams as the State Emergency Operations Center tracks incoming data. “Initial feedback from our state experts and federal partners is that the detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant was successful,” Reynolds wrote on X . “We remain in close contact with authorities on the ground, while state agencies continue to monitor incoming data from the State Emergency Operations Center. We will keep Iowans informed as details become available.” In neighboring Missouri, which liess within the Army’s projected southwest plume path, Gov. Mike Kehoe said state agencies are continuing to track air and environmental data after activating Missouri’s emergency operations center ahead of the blast. “Initial analysis shared with us by federal partners and Iowa Homeland Security and Emergency Management indicates that the mitigation measures appear to have been successful and the explosion was well-contained,” Kehoe wrote on X . “Our state agencies will continue monitoring efforts.” Assistant Secretary of the Army for Installations, Energy and Environment Jordan Gillis said officials were forced to weigh a scheduled, contained operation against the risk of an accidental blast as the stockpiled material degraded. “The choice that we faced here was between a spontaneous, uncontrolled detonation of dangerous material, or a controlled detonation where we could choose the time and place to optimize the conditions and deliver the best result, not just for our operations but for the safety of the public and the surrounding communities,” Gillis said. MIDDLETOWN, Iowa — The U.S. Army carried out a controlled, mitigated detonation of 68 barrels of deteriorated lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Wednesday morning, with federal and state officials reporting a complete detonation and no initial detection of airborne lead across the region.

The detonation was executed at 9 a.m. CT by U.S. Army Sustainment Command following days of interagency preparation, court clearances and voluntary evacuations for residents within a five-mile area southwest of the plant along the projected plume path.
President Donald Trump praised the operation in a post on Truth Social shortly after the blast.
“Early reports from Iowa are that the Army’s mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations,” Trump wrote.

During a live interagency briefing following the detonation, Army Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, commanding general of U.S. Army Sustainment Command, said explosive ordnance disposal teams eliminated the threat without any secondary explosions, debris being thrown beyond the containment area or infrastructure damage.

“Well, I would characterize the controlled detonation as exceeding expectations,” Shirley said. “Every indication is that all of the munitions that were employed absolutely reduced the lead azide threat. As we saw in the immediate aftermath through overhead coverage, all of the lead azide barrels were definitively removed.”

Shirley said crews applied more than 3,600 gallons of aqueous foam via fire trucks alongside continuous mister systems, two-story sand barriers and gel blocks to suppress dust and contain lead particles.

“I believe absolutely that we reduced as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” Shirley said.

Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives Director Robert Cekada said the roughly 10,000-pound stockpile had been consolidated and moved to earth-covered magazines at the Iowa plant in 2009. By March 2026, inspectors discovered dangerous crystallization on the barrels, lids and bolts, prompting the Trump administration to assemble a multi-agency mitigation plan.

“I absolutely can confirm that those mitigation efforts and the design plan laid out by the EOD personnel ensured that the blast drove the explosion into the ground and followed a blast channel that was designed to go down the right path to minimize any sort of dispersion of lead into the atmosphere—100% as planned,” Cekada said.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency announced on X that its continuous, real-time air monitors across the region showed “ZERO detection of airborne lead throughout the region” immediately following the blast, noting that monitoring equipment never stopped collecting data during the event.
FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton also confirmed the blast went as planned.

“We believe that is a successful detonation,” Hamilton said . “The elements which were ultimately connected to explosives and set for a time charge, we believe they fully ignited — so that’s a fully and complete successful detonation.”
Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds said state officials remain in close contact with federal teams as the State Emergency Operations Center tracks incoming data.

“Initial feedback from our state experts and federal partners is that the detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant was successful,” Reynolds wrote on X . “We remain in close contact with authorities on the ground, while state agencies continue to monitor incoming data from the State Emergency Operations Center. We will keep Iowans informed as details become available.”

In neighboring Missouri, which liess within the Army’s projected southwest plume path, Gov. Mike Kehoe said state agencies are continuing to track air and environmental data after activating Missouri’s emergency operations center ahead of the blast.

“Initial analysis shared with us by federal partners and Iowa Homeland Security and Emergency Management indicates that the mitigation measures appear to have been successful and the explosion was well-contained,” Kehoe wrote on X . “Our state agencies will continue monitoring efforts.”

Assistant Secretary of the Army for Installations, Energy and Environment Jordan Gillis said officials were forced to weigh a scheduled, contained operation against the risk of an accidental blast as the stockpiled material degraded.

“The choice that we faced here was between a spontaneous, uncontrolled detonation of dangerous material, or a controlled detonation where we could choose the time and place to optimize the conditions and deliver the best result, not just for our operations but for the safety of the public and the surrounding communities,” Gillis said.

Ahead of the detonation, the Army deployed physical containment measures—including two-story sand barriers, aqueous foam, gel blocks and water misters—to suppress dust and limit the spread of lead particles beyond the installation. Gillis said those safeguards were designed to protect both public health and the surrounding environment while simplifying post-blast remediation.

“An example is the aqueous foam and the gel blocks that we are deploying to minimize lead particulate release from the controlled detonation are the same things that are going to ease our environmental cleanup,” Gillis said. “By capturing the lead particles, we’re not only ensuring public health and safety, but we are maintaining our environmental responsibilities and leaving behind a clean site for continued plant operations and a cleaner off-site for the health and benefit of the public.”
EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said federal teams are immediately shifting to post-blast environmental testing and any needed cleanup.

“We’re going to immediately be deploying on the ground manpower, soil and water sampling — any remediation efforts that are necessary in the immediate hours that follow the controlled detonation that just finished,” Zeldin said .

The EPA said roughly 300 agency employees and contractors are deployed across Iowa and surrounding states after collecting 1,216 baseline samples—including 650 soil, 297 dust, 210 water and 59 air samples—at schools, churches, playgrounds and homes prior to Wednesday’s operation. The agency is coordinating its testing with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to protect vulnerable groups, including infants, young children and pregnant women.

“It is the top priority of this agency to ensure impacted residents can swiftly be and feel safe and comfortable in their homes, at their schools, in recreational spaces, and in their community,” Tom Croci, EPA associate administrator for national security and operations coordination said .

Officials had previously advised residents near the evacuation zone to shelter in place, close all windows and doors, set heating systems to recirculation mode, keep children and pets indoors and cover livestock feed, water sources and crops. The EPA also encouraged residents to wipe down outdoor surfaces children touch—such as play sets, railings and windowsills—with a wet cloth.
Real-time air monitoring and post-detonation sampling results are being posted publicly by the EPA as data is verified.
