coreStoryFacts.text: Switzerland’s Federal Council has approved 57 potential partner jurisdictions for the automatic exchange of information on crypto assets starting in 2028, a move that would expand tax authorities’ access to information on taxpayers’ crypto activity across borders.

Switzerland had initially planned to introduce crypto tax reporting requirements in 2026 but delayed implementation by at least a year as lawmakers had yet to determine which jurisdictions the country would exchange information with.
Under the revised timeline, crypto service providers could begin collecting data as early as Jan.

Switzerland introduced the legal framework for that system in 2017 and exchanged financial account data with 113 jurisdictions in 2026.
According to a Wednesday announcement, the approved jurisdictions include all European Union member states, the United Kingdom and several G20 countries.
Switzerland will only share information with jurisdictions that express interest and meet international standards for confidentiality and data security.

facts.text: Switzerland’s Federal Council has approved 57 potential partner jurisdictions for the automatic exchange of information on crypto assets starting in 2028, a move that would expand tax authorities’ access to information on taxpayers’ crypto activity across borders.

Switzerland had initially planned to introduce crypto tax reporting requirements in 2026 but delayed implementation by at least a year as lawmakers had yet to determine which jurisdictions the country would exchange information with.
Under the revised timeline, crypto service providers could begin collecting data as early as Jan.

The crypto reporting framework is designed to supplement Switzerland’s existing system for exchanging financial account information and close gaps in tax transparency, according to the State Secretariat for International Finance.
Switzerland introduced the legal framework for that system in 2017 and exchanged financial account data with 113 jurisdictions in 2026.
According to a Wednesday announcement, the approved jurisdictions include all European Union member states, the United Kingdom and several G20 countries.
Switzerland will only share information with jurisdictions that express interest and meet international standards for confidentiality and data security.

passages: (Bloomberg) -- US banks asked for extra protection to expand financing for a data center operator that previously sold computing power to Megaspeed International Pte, a neocloud under US investigation for allegedly smuggling chips into China.

Citigroup Inc. and JPMorgan Chase & Co. added new language to financing documents for a potential upsized $6.6 billion loan sought by Bain Capital-owned Bridge Data Centres that makes it the borrower's responsibility to comply with restrictions on chip access, according to people familiar with the negotiations.

It is uncommon for a loan document done outside the US to include such a clause, said Doug Jacobson, managing partner of Jacobson Burton Kelley PLLC who specializes in international trade law, though American banks would likely have received advice to do so given recent events.
The US this week tightened remote access to its chips, putting billions in loans to data centers in Southeast Asia at risk.
The steps taken by Citi and JPMorgan show how American banks are seeking to limit potential political and legal risks.
The proposed language could potentially enable banks to call default on a loan, citing breach of covenant, if a violation is discovered.

facts.text: (Bloomberg) -- US banks asked for extra protection to expand financing for a data center operator that previously sold computing power to Megaspeed International Pte, a neocloud under US investigation for allegedly smuggling chips into China.

Citigroup Inc. and JPMorgan Chase & Co. added new language to financing documents for a potential upsized $6.6 billion loan sought by Bain Capital-owned Bridge Data Centres that makes it the borrower's responsibility to comply with restrictions on chip access, according to people familiar with the negotiations.

It is uncommon for a loan document done outside the US to include such a clause, said Doug Jacobson, managing partner of Jacobson Burton Kelley PLLC who specializes in international trade law, though American banks would likely have received advice to do so given recent events.
The US this week tightened remote access to its chips, putting billions in loans to data centers in Southeast Asia at risk.
The steps taken by Citi and JPMorgan show how American banks are seeking to limit potential political and legal risks.
The proposed language could potentially enable banks to call default on a loan, citing breach of covenant, if a violation is discovered.

Banks from Citigroup Inc. to Standard Chartered Plc have launched sweeping reviews of data center clients in the wake of tougher American rules to curb Chinese companies’ use of advanced US chips in Southeast Asian nations.

The banks join major Asian lenders — including Singapore’s DBS Group Holdings Ltd. , Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp. and United Overseas Bank Ltd. — in pushing for more disclosures from companies tied to data centers in Singapore, Malaysia and other countries in the region, according to people with knowledge of the matter.

The language includes requirements to adhere to US export controls and the Bureau of Industry and Security's Entity List, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing a private matter. Banks would want to ensure they are conducting "sufficient due diligence" in confirming all parties will comply with US export controls, he said. The changes were made before news of former Nvidia Corp. leader Jensen Huang's relationship with Megaspeed's founder Alice Huang brought renewed scrutiny to the neocloud, the people said. The decisions came directly from Citi and JPMorgan's head offices in New York, they said. The move followed a US government probe into Megaspeed's ownership structure and whether it smuggled advanced Nvidia AI chips to China in violation of American export restrictions. Sam has written about crypto professionally since 2019 and has published more than 2,000 articles.
His analysis is syndicated on Yahoo Finance, MSN and AOL and has been cited by other crypto news sites.
He also founded MacLabs Marketing, a content and personal branding agency for crypto founders and executives.
When he isn't reading charts, Sam is usually at the gym or watching One Piece, a series he maintains has better tokenomics than most altcoins.
So, what Bitcoin allocation makes sense in your portfolio after such a significant drop?
For example, an investor who originally aimed for a 2% Bitcoin holding in a $100,000 portfolio could have about $920 in Bitcoin after its 54% decline, assuming everything else remained constant.
Conservative investors can maintain a 0% allocation, while balanced investors can consider 1% to 2%, and aggressive growth investors may feel comfortable with up to 4%.
Even so, a 4% allocation means that another 50% drop could cost about 2% of the entire portfolio.
XRP has sunk below $1 and bargain hunters are circling, but Wall Street's biggest names keep warning that crypto belongs in a tiny slice of your portfolio.
These recommendations were established before Bitcoin’s 54% price drop.
This is because Bitcoin’s price fluctuates much more than traditional stocks or bonds, meaning a small portion of Bitcoin can cause larger swings in a portfolio’s overall performance.
Over the past five years , Bitcoin has gained only 7.9%, while the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:SPY ) rose 50% and the Vanguard Total Bond Market ETF ( NASDAQ:BND ) gained just 0.1%.
Essentially, those who replaced stocks with Bitcoin missed out on better returns.
Bitcoin and XRP have both taken hits lately, but the size of each coin's drop tells two very different stories about risk, recovery potential, and which type of investor each one actually suits.
The Wall Street Bitcoin ETF takeover has crossed a defining threshold.

extraction.body: Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) trades at $58,038 as of 13:59 UTC, down 54% from its all-time high of $126,080 reached on October 6, 2025. This sharp decline has raised questions among investors, especially with $4.91 billion withdrawn from U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs over the past 30 days. So, what Bitcoin allocation makes sense in your portfolio after such a significant drop? Both BlackRock ( NYSE:BLK | BLK Price Prediction ) and Morgan Stanley ( NYSE:MS ) offer insightful guidance on Bitcoin allocation. In December 2024 research, BlackRock suggested a modest 1% to 2% allocation for a diversified portfolio, pointing out that exceeding 2% significantly increases risk. This is because Bitcoin’s price fluctuates much more than traditional stocks or bonds, meaning a small portion of Bitcoin can cause larger swings in a portfolio’s overall performance. In October 2025, Morgan Stanley’s investment committee proposed a slightly broader range of 2% to 4% for growth-oriented portfolios but advised a 0% allocation for more conservative ones. These recommendations were established before Bitcoin’s 54% price drop. Over the past five years , Bitcoin has gained only 7.9%, while the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:SPY ) rose 50% and the Vanguard Total Bond Market ETF ( NASDAQ:BND ) gained just 0.1%. Essentially, those who replaced stocks with Bitcoin missed out on better returns. Bitcoin’s volatility showed most in 2026, as it fell a substantial 33.7% while the S&P 500 fund gained 3.2%. This shows how Bitcoin’s unpredictable price swings can hurt overall returns compared to a balanced stock-and-bond strategy. To maintain a desired asset allocation, an investor rebalances the portfolio. This means selling the parts that have grown past their target share and buying more of what has fallen below it. For example, an investor who originally aimed for a 2% Bitcoin holding in a $100,000 portfolio could have about $920 in Bitcoin after its 54% decline, assuming everything else remained constant. To return to the target allocation, that investor might need to invest about $1,060 more. This can be done through a spot ETF like the Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust ETF ( NYSEARCA:BTC ), which holds actual Bitcoin and is available through brokerage accounts. The suggested allocation ranges still apply. Conservative investors can maintain a 0% allocation, while balanced investors can consider 1% to 2%, and aggressive growth investors may feel comfortable with up to 4%. Even so, a 4% allocation means that another 50% drop could cost about 2% of the entire portfolio. Any rebalance into Bitcoin also carries a risk while the selling continues. If ETF outflows persist near the $569.7 million withdrawn on November 23, Bitcoin may continue to face pressure, and money allocated to rebalance could lose value if the price keeps falling. A look at whether the Bitcoin bottom is in tracks the signals for a potential turnaround. Contact [email protected] for any questions or corrections. passages: As the market has dipped, analysts have revised their Bitcoin price predictions for December 2026.
Dated forecasts range from approximately $53,200 to $90,000.
Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) is trading at $58,071, down 25% since its October 31 close and 53.9% below its all-time high of $126,080, reached on October 6, 2025.
After starting 2026 at $87,575, Bitcoin has fallen significantly, down 33.7% this year.
Market analyst Charlie Bilello pointed out on X on November 21 that Bitcoin and gold have been the two worst-performing major assets of 2026.
So, what do the forecasts indicate for Bitcoin's price on December 31?
And how does December's historical performance influence these predictions?
Bitcoin is most likely to finish 2026 in the $53,000 to $65,000 range, while reaching $90,000 seems unlikely.
ETF outflows, the possibility of another Fed rate hike, and the pattern of declining prices after a poor November all point to a lower finish.
To see a price increase, a calm decision from the Fed on December 9, a few days of ETF inflows, and Bitcoin closing above $65,000—approximately 12% higher—would be essential.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Two major factors could weigh heavily on Bitcoin's performance in December: the Federal Reserve's upcoming meeting and ongoing ETF outflows.
Another rate hike could make cash more attractive, challenging Bitcoin as a non-yielding asset.
Job openings data will be released on December 1, and the University of Michigan consumer survey is set for December 18.
For holders, the critical level to watch after December 9 is $55,106, the intraday low from November 21, about 5% below the price.
If Bitcoin closes below this level, it could drop to the realized price of $53,200, increasing the risk of falling below $50,000.
Historically, Bitcoin has underperformed in December.
It has declined in six of the past eight December months and experienced setbacks in all five Decembers following a losing November.
Here is how Bitcoin has performed in those months since 2017.
In four of the five years when November ended with losses, December's decline was less severe than November's drop, suggesting selling may have slowed.
The exception was in 2021, when a smaller November dip turned into a more significant December drop.

Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) is trading at $58,071, down 25% since its October 31 close and 53.9% below its all-time high of $126,080, reached on October 6, 2025.
After starting 2026 at $87,575, Bitcoin has fallen significantly, down 33.7% this year.
Market analyst Charlie Bilello pointed out on X on November 21 that Bitcoin and gold have been the two worst-performing major assets of 2026.
So, what do the forecasts indicate for Bitcoin’s price on December 31?
And how does December’s historical performance influence these predictions?
Sam Daodu is a crypto analyst and the editor of 24/7 Wall St.'s Crypto Desk, where he covers Bitcoin, XRP, Ethereum, Solana and the altcoins investors search for most.
His work focuses on price levels, spot ETF flows, on-chain data and the regulatory decisions that move crypto markets, written so a first-time buyer and a seasoned trader can both use it.
Sam has written about crypto professionally since 2019 and has published more than 2,000 articles.
His analysis is syndicated on Yahoo Finance, MSN and AOL and has been cited by other crypto news sites.
He also founded MacLabs Marketing, a content and personal branding agency for crypto founders and executives.
When he isn't reading charts, Sam is usually at the gym or watching One Piece, a series he maintains has better tokenomics than most altcoins.
Bitcoin is most likely to finish 2026 in the $53,000 to $65,000 range, while reaching $90,000 seems unlikely.
ETF outflows, the possibility of another Fed rate hike, and the pattern of declining prices after a poor November all point to a lower finish.
To see a price increase, a calm decision from the Fed on December 9, a few days of ETF inflows, and Bitcoin closing above $65,000 —approximately 12% higher—would be essential.
Two major factors could weigh heavily on Bitcoin’s performance in December: the Federal Reserve’s upcoming meeting and ongoing ETF outflows.
Another rate hike could make cash more attractive, challenging Bitcoin as a non-yielding asset.
Job openings data will be released on December 1, and the University of Michigan consumer survey is set for December 18.
For holders, the critical level to watch after December 9 is $55,106, the intraday low from November 21, about 5% below the price.
If Bitcoin closes below this level, it could drop to the realized price of $53,200, increasing the risk of falling below $50,000 .
Bitcoin has shed nearly half its value since October's record, and analysts disagree by tens of thousands of dollars on what comes next.
One Fed meeting in December and one stubborn price level may…
Historically, Bitcoin has underperformed in December.
It has declined in six of the past eight December months and experienced setbacks in all five Decembers following a losing November.
Here is how Bitcoin has performed in those months since 2017 .
Data from SoSoValue shows that cumulative net inflows dropped from $57.6 billion on October 29 to $52.0 billion on November 24.
The only inflow days in November came on November 4 ($74.6 million) and November 16 ($8.0 million), highlighting weak buyer interest.
In four of the five years when November ended with losses, December’s decline was less severe than November’s drop, suggesting selling may have slowed.
The exception was in 2021, when a smaller November dip turned into a more significant December drop.
One brutal day of ETF selling has Bitcoin traders on edge, and an AI model has a surprisingly narrow forecast for where the price lands by month end.

passages: I don’t believe that Harvard’s security rules must be as draconian as those at our neighboring universities.
Yet they must be stricter than their current, laissez-faire iteration.
Harvard is, as HUPD puts it, “struggling with the appropriate balance of security and freedom of movement.” However, it seems the balance has shifted too far towards freedom.
To a certain extent, I appreciate Harvard’s more casual approach to security.
It is convenient to navigate campus without constantly swiping my HUID and fun to have friends visit my dorm without forcing them to undergo oppressive security measures.
Still, convenience and accessibility come at a cost, one I find myself unwilling to pay the full price of.
Though happy to delay paying the $40 ID replacement fee, upon reflection I was left startled by the lax state of campus security.
That a student can maintain a normal routine for eight days without any physical proof of her enrollment at Harvard is a testament to the University’s poor security system.
Harvard must strengthen and ensure the enforcement of its security rules, especially when concerning residential buildings.

extraction.body: From Monday, October 26 through Tuesday, November 3, I was entirely without my Harvard University ID card. I endured bacchanalian Halloweekend, the transition to 4:30 p.m. sunsets, and a harrowing Astronomy midterm — all without scanning access. Remarkably, little about my daily affairs changed. Though happy to delay paying the $40 ID replacement fee, upon reflection I was left startled by the lax state of campus security. That a student can maintain a normal routine for eight days without any physical proof of her enrollment at Harvard is a testament to the University’s poor security system. Harvard must strengthen and ensure the enforcement of its security rules, especially when concerning residential buildings. Harvard introduced harsher ID requirements for academic buildings last December in the wake of the shooting at Brown University. But soon after the imposition of the new ID restrictions, some of these same buildings, including Zimmer Hall, were once again accessible to the public. Indeed, I could reliably get to my Zimmer Hall classes and sections without an ID. Still, many buildings require more scheming to enter, including Jefferson Laboratory, my place of work . I thus quickly learned how to circumvent the need for direct entrance. Maxwell Dworkin Laboratory is well-trafficked enough that I could reliably gain entrance, after which I could take a winding route of connectors through Cruft Laboratory, Pierce Hall, and Lyman Laboratory to my final destination. Four buildings for the swipe access of one! Most difficult, of course, was gaining access to my home. By most difficult, I mean that I had to take the notoriously unreliable Quad shuttle instead of walking, guaranteeing that one of my peers would arrive alongside me and swipe me in. Evidently, Harvard’s campus is the world’s oyster. This accessibility is a result of Harvard’s current security strategy, which puts the onus of safety on students. For example, the Harvard University Police Department details ways that students can keep their dorms safe: “Although it seems courteous to open doors for others, especially persons carrying groceries or packages, do not open residential doors for strangers.” Kind reminders on the HUPD website fail as a real security initiative, especially in the face of security threats. Take, for instance, an incident last May in which a stranger allegedly tailgated into a Lowell entryway and attempted to assault a Harvard senior. Most stunning of all was the one interaction I actually had with campus security. One late Wednesday night, the cold wind stinging my face, I finally relented. I called Securitas to let me in. I had found my HUID number in case they needed proof of my enrollment, but I was surprised yet again. Securitas didn’t ask for my HUID — or even my name. I was home free. Within Harvard’s 2026-27 student handbook, the only information I could find about guest access is that “the hosts of repeated overnight guests who are not Harvard students must make their guests’ presence known to the Building Manager and security personnel due to safety considerations.” According to Harvard’s website, the “express permission of your House Office or proctor” is technically required to host overnight guests, and students are instructed to contact said parties about a “guest registration process.” But in practice, this rule seems to go unfollowed: I have never registered an overnight guest, nor have any of my friends. Our security system is uniquely lax compared to other Boston schools. At Boston University, guests are required to sign in and present a legal ID every time they enter or exit a residential building. Massachusetts Institute of Technology has a nearly identical policy. So does Emerson College. To a certain extent, I appreciate Harvard’s more casual approach to security. It is convenient to navigate campus without constantly swiping my HUID and fun to have friends visit my dorm without forcing them to undergo oppressive security measures. Still, convenience and accessibility come at a cost, one I find myself unwilling to pay the full price of. I don’t believe that Harvard’s security rules must be as draconian as those at our neighboring universities. Yet they must be stricter than their current, laissez-faire iteration. Harvard is, as HUPD puts it, “struggling with the appropriate balance of security and freedom of movement.” However, it seems the balance has shifted too far towards freedom. Perhaps the only change in my HUID-less life was my inability to access any libraries. The three libraries that I frequent — Lamont, Widener, and Cabot — all have turnstile-type entrances that effectively prevent tailgating and a security guard on duty. In a true commitment to recentering academics, Harvard’s libraries are, for the time being, much safer than its dorms. Anna J. Guerrini ’29, a Crimson Editorial editor, is a Physics concentrator in Pforzheimer House. Have a tip for The Crimson? Share it confidentially
passages: From Monday, October 26 through Tuesday, November 3, I was entirely without my Harvard University ID card. I endured bacchanalian Halloweekend, the transition to 4:30 p.m. sunsets, and a harrowing Astronomy midterm — all without scanning access. Remarkably, little about my daily affairs changed.

Though happy to delay paying the $40 ID replacement fee, upon reflection I was left startled by the lax state of campus security. That a student can maintain a normal routine for eight days without any physical proof of her enrollment at Harvard is a testament to the University’s poor security system. Harvard must strengthen and ensure the enforcement of its security rules, especially when concerning residential buildings.

Harvard introduced harsher ID requirements for academic buildings last December in the wake of the shooting at Brown University. But soon after the imposition of the new ID restrictions, some of these same buildings, including Zimmer Hall, were once again accessible to the public. Indeed, I could reliably get to my Zimmer Hall classes and sections without an ID.

Still, many buildings require more scheming to enter, including Jefferson Laboratory, my place of work . I thus quickly learned how to circumvent the need for direct entrance. Maxwell Dworkin Laboratory is well-trafficked enough that I could reliably gain entrance, after which I could take a winding route of connectors through Cruft Laboratory, Pierce Hall, and Lyman Laboratory to my final destination. Four buildings for the swipe access of one!

Most difficult, of course, was gaining access to my home. By most difficult, I mean that I had to take the notoriously unreliable Quad shuttle instead of walking, guaranteeing that one of my peers would arrive alongside me and swipe me in.
Evidently, Harvard’s campus is the world’s oyster. This accessibility is a result of Harvard’s current security strategy, which puts the onus of safety on students.

For example, the Harvard University Police Department details ways that students can keep their dorms safe: “Although it seems courteous to open doors for others, especially persons carrying groceries or packages, do not open residential doors for strangers.” Kind reminders on the HUPD website fail as a real security initiative, especially in the face of security threats. Take, for instance, an incident last May in which a stranger allegedly tailgated into a Lowell entryway and attempted to assault a Harvard senior.

Most stunning of all was the one interaction I actually had with campus security. One late Wednesday night, the cold wind stinging my face, I finally relented. I called Securitas to let me in. I had found my HUID number in case they needed proof of my enrollment, but I was surprised yet again. Securitas didn’t ask for my HUID — or even my name. I was home free.

Within Harvard’s 2026-27 student handbook, the only information I could find about guest access is that “the hosts of repeated overnight guests who are not Harvard students must make their guests’ presence known to the Building Manager and security personnel due to safety considerations.”

According to Harvard’s website, the “express permission of your House Office or proctor” is technically required to host overnight guests, and students are instructed to contact said parties about a “guest registration process.” But in practice, this rule seems to go unfollowed: I have never registered an overnight guest, nor have any of my friends.

Our security system is uniquely lax compared to other Boston schools. At Boston University, guests are required to sign in and present a legal ID every time they enter or exit a residential building. Massachusetts Institute of Technology has a nearly identical policy. So does Emerson College.

To a certain extent, I appreciate Harvard’s more casual approach to security. It is convenient to navigate campus without constantly swiping my HUID and fun to have friends visit my dorm without forcing them to undergo oppressive security measures. Still, convenience and accessibility come at a cost, one I find myself unwilling to pay the full price of.

I don’t believe that Harvard’s security rules must be as draconian as those at our neighboring universities. Yet they must be stricter than their current, laissez-faire iteration. Harvard is, as HUPD puts it, “struggling with the appropriate balance of security and freedom of movement.” However, it seems the balance has shifted too far towards freedom.

Perhaps the only change in my HUID-less life was my inability to access any libraries. The three libraries that I frequent — Lamont, Widener, and Cabot — all have turnstile-type entrances that effectively prevent tailgating and a security guard on duty.
In a true commitment to recentering academics, Harvard’s libraries are, for the time being, much safer than its dorms.
Anna J. Guerrini ’29, a Crimson Editorial editor, is a Physics concentrator in Pforzheimer House.

Though happy to delay paying the $40 ID replacement fee, upon reflection I was left startled by the lax state of campus security. That a student can maintain a normal routine for eight days without any physical proof of her enrollment at Harvard is a testament to the University’s poor security system. Harvard must strengthen and ensure the enforcement of its security rules, especially when concerning residential buildings. Harvard introduced harsher ID requirements for academic buildings last December in the wake of the shooting at Brown University. But soon after the imposition of the new ID restrictions, some of these same buildings, including Zimmer Hall, were once again accessible to the public. Indeed, I could reliably get to my Zimmer Hall classes and sections without an ID. Still, many buildings require more scheming to enter, including Jefferson Laboratory, my place of work . I thus quickly learned how to circumvent the need for direct entrance. Maxwell Dworkin Laboratory is well-trafficked enough that I could reliably gain entrance, after which I could take a winding route of connectors through Cruft Laboratory, Pierce Hall, and Lyman Laboratory to my final destination. Four buildings for the swipe access of one! Most difficult, of course, was gaining access to my home. By most difficult, I mean that I had to take the notoriously unreliable Quad shuttle instead of walking, guaranteeing that one of my peers would arrive alongside me and swipe me in. Evidently, Harvard’s campus is the world’s oyster. This accessibility is a result of Harvard’s current security strategy, which puts the onus of safety on students. For example, the Harvard University Police Department details ways that students can keep their dorms safe: “Although it seems courteous to open doors for others, especially persons carrying groceries or packages, do not open residential doors for strangers.” Kind reminders on the HUPD website fail as a real security initiative, especially in the face of security threats. Take, for instance, an incident last May in which a stranger allegedly tailgated into a Lowell entryway and attempted to assault a Harvard senior. Most stunning of all was the one interaction I actually had with campus security. One late Wednesday night, the cold wind stinging my face, I finally relented. I called Securitas to let me in. I had found my HUID number in case they needed proof of my enrollment, but I was surprised yet again. Securitas didn’t ask for my HUID — or even my name. I was home free. Within Harvard’s 2026-27 student handbook, the only information I could find about guest access is that “the hosts of repeated overnight guests who are not Harvard students must make their guests’ presence known to the Building Manager and security personnel due to safety considerations.” According to Harvard’s website, the “express permission of your House Office or proctor” is technically required to host overnight guests, and students are instructed to contact said parties about a “guest registration process.” But in practice, this rule seems to go unfollowed: I have never registered an overnight guest, nor have any of my friends. Our security system is uniquely lax compared to other Boston schools. At Boston University, guests are required to sign in and present a legal ID every time they enter or exit a residential building. Massachusetts Institute of Technology has a nearly identical policy. So does Emerson College. To a certain extent, I appreciate Harvard’s more casual approach to security. It is convenient to navigate campus without constantly swiping my HUID and fun to have friends visit my dorm without forcing them to undergo oppressive security measures. Still, convenience and accessibility come at a cost, one I find myself unwilling to pay the full price of. I don’t believe that Harvard’s security rules must be as draconian as those at our neighboring universities. Yet they must be stricter than their current, laissez-faire iteration. Harvard is, as HUPD puts it, “struggling with the appropriate balance of security and freedom of movement.” However, it seems the balance has shifted too far towards freedom. Perhaps the only change in my HUID-less life was my inability to access any libraries. The three libraries that I frequent — Lamont, Widener, and Cabot — all have turnstile-type entrances that effectively prevent tailgating and a security guard on duty. In a true commitment to recentering academics, Harvard’s libraries are, for the time being, much safer than its dorms. Anna J. Guerrini ’29, a Crimson Editorial editor, is a Physics concentrator in Pforzheimer House. Have a tip for The Crimson? Share it confidentially
passages: From Monday, October 26 through Tuesday, November 3, I was entirely without my Harvard University ID card. I endured bacchanalian Halloweekend, the transition to 4:30 p.m. sunsets, and a harrowing Astronomy midterm — all without scanning access. Remarkably, little about my daily affairs changed.

Though happy to delay paying the $40 ID replacement fee, upon reflection I was left startled by the lax state of campus security. That a student can maintain a normal routine for eight days without any physical proof of her enrollment at Harvard is a testament to the University’s poor security system. Harvard must strengthen and ensure the enforcement of its security rules, especially when concerning residential buildings.

Harvard introduced harsher ID requirements for academic buildings last December in the wake of the shooting at Brown University. But soon after the imposition of the new ID restrictions, some of these same buildings, including Zimmer Hall, were once again accessible to the public. Indeed, I could reliably get to my Zimmer Hall classes and sections without an ID.

Still, many buildings require more scheming to enter, including Jefferson Laboratory, my place of work . I thus quickly learned how to circumvent the need for direct entrance. Maxwell Dworkin Laboratory is well-trafficked enough that I could reliably gain entrance, after which I could take a winding route of connectors through Cruft Laboratory, Pierce Hall, and Lyman Laboratory to my final destination. Four buildings for the swipe access of one!

Most difficult, of course, was gaining access to my home. By most difficult, I mean that I had to take the notoriously unreliable Quad shuttle instead of walking, guaranteeing that one of my peers would arrive alongside me and swipe me in.
Evidently, Harvard’s campus is the world’s oyster. This accessibility is a result of Harvard’s current security strategy, which puts the onus of safety on students.

For example, the Harvard University Police Department details ways that students can keep their dorms safe: “Although it seems courteous to open doors for others, especially persons carrying groceries or packages, do not open residential doors for strangers.” Kind reminders on the HUPD website fail as a real security initiative, especially in the face of security threats. Take, for instance, an incident last May in which a stranger allegedly tailgated into a Lowell entryway and attempted to assault a Harvard senior.

Most stunning of all was the one interaction I actually had with campus security. One late Wednesday night, the cold wind stinging my face, I finally relented. I called Securitas to let me in. I had found my HUID number in case they needed proof of my enrollment, but I was surprised yet again. Securitas didn’t ask for my HUID — or even my name. I was home free.

Within Harvard’s 2026-27 student handbook, the only information I could find about guest access is that “the hosts of repeated overnight guests who are not Harvard students must make their guests’ presence known to the Building Manager and security personnel due to safety considerations.”

According to Harvard’s website, the “express permission of your House Office or proctor” is technically required to host overnight guests, and students are instructed to contact said parties about a “guest registration process.” But in practice, this rule seems to go unfollowed: I have never registered an overnight guest, nor have any of my friends.

Our security system is uniquely lax compared to other Boston schools. At Boston University, guests are required to sign in and present a legal ID every time they enter or exit a residential building. Massachusetts Institute of Technology has a nearly identical policy. So does Emerson College.

To a certain extent, I appreciate Harvard’s more casual approach to security. It is convenient to navigate campus without constantly swiping my HUID and fun to have friends visit my dorm without forcing them to undergo oppressive security measures. Still, convenience and accessibility come at a cost, one I find myself unwilling to pay the full price of.

I don’t believe that Harvard’s security rules must be as draconian as those at our neighboring universities. Yet they must be stricter than their current, laissez-faire iteration. Harvard is, as HUPD puts it, “struggling with the appropriate balance of security and freedom of movement.” However, it seems the balance has shifted too far towards freedom.

Perhaps the only change in my HUID-less life was my inability to access any libraries. The three libraries that I frequent — Lamont, Widener, and Cabot — all have turnstile-type entrances that effectively prevent tailgating and a security guard on duty.
In a true commitment to recentering academics, Harvard’s libraries are, for the time being, much safer than its dorms.
Anna J. Guerrini ’29, a Crimson Editorial editor, is a Physics concentrator in Pforzheimer House.

sources.title: Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it
passages: When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct.
He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it.
In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO.
It’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules.
But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture.
When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for.
That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia.
Judging by the employee campaign for his reinstatement, Huang’s return hasn’t created a morale problem so far.
But as the coming months put more pressure on Huang and his colleagues, sidestepping the code could end up costing Nvidia something harder to measure — its employees’ pride in the company.
“For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that company as an example of the worst thing an employee could do.
People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’”
Plass says companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees.

“In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he said, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it.
“I would draw a distinction there between the kind of companies where the CEO is a kind of godhead figure … where the person and the company are almost impossible to separate,” he said.
In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer.
“People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly important to them,” he told TechCrunch.
“They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their company.

extraction.body: When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang said, according to Wired . “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO. It’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia. Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct . As Plass sees it, the biggest risk is that employees will become ashamed of their workplace. “People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly important to them,” he told TechCrunch. “They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their company. They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.” The consequences of violating the rules aren’t always tangible, but they’re definitely real. Plass gave one example of a company that banned corporate travel to cut costs — only to have its CEO turn up in a VIP box at the Olympics. “For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that company as an example of the worst thing an employee could do. People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’” Plass says companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees. “In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he said, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it. We’re sorry. We’ve changed. That’s essentially what they do.” Of course, that playbook is harder to follow at a company like Nvidia, where Huang left without a clear succession plan, and there are serious doubts about whether the company could continue to thrive without him. In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer. “I would draw a distinction there between the kind of companies where the CEO is a kind of godhead figure … where the person and the company are almost impossible to separate,” he said. “There it’s much, much harder to deal with.” In that context, Huang’s stutter-step over the code of conduct is easier to understand. Judging by the employee campaign for his reinstatement, Huang’s return hasn’t created a morale problem so far. But as the coming months put more pressure on Huang and his colleagues, sidestepping the code could end up costing Nvidia something harder to measure — its employees’ pride in the company. extraction.body: When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang said, according to Wired . “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO. It’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia. Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct . As Plass sees it, the biggest risk is that employees will become ashamed of their workplace. “People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly important to them,” he told TechCrunch. “They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their company. They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.” The consequences of violating the rules aren’t always tangible, but they’re definitely real. Plass gave one example of a company that banned corporate travel to cut costs — only to have its CEO turn up in a VIP box at the Olympics. “For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that company as an example of the worst thing an employee could do. People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’” Plass says companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees. “In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he said, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it. We’re sorry. We’ve changed. That’s essentially what they do.” Of course, that playbook is harder to follow at a company like Nvidia, where Huang left without a clear succession plan, and there are serious doubts about whether the company could continue to thrive without him. In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer. “I would draw a distinction there between the kind of companies where the CEO is a kind of godhead figure … where the person and the company are almost impossible to separate,” he said. “There it’s much, much harder to deal with.” In that context, Huang’s stutter-step over the code of conduct is easier to understand. Judging by the employee campaign for his reinstatement, Huang’s return hasn’t created a morale problem so far. But as the coming months put more pressure on Huang and his colleagues, sidestepping the code could end up costing Nvidia something harder to measure — its employees’ pride in the company. passages: GuardDuty Extended Threat Detection has added five new indicators to surface attack sequences Authors: Aman Khare, Kyle Koeller | Published: October 12, 2026 Learn to use five new indicator types in Amazon GuardDuty Extended Threat Detection: vulnerability, malicious package, reachability, misconfiguration, and sensitive data.

They bring signals from Amazon Inspector , Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) Reachability Analyzer, Amazon Macie , and AWS Security Hub into sequence findings, and the post shows how to add them to your incident response workflow.

AWS Security Agent (now part of AWS Continuum) exploited 33 of 37 new real-world CVEs Authors: Dazhi Zhang, Hamed Soleimani | Published: October 15, 2026 AWS Continuum for penetration testing was tested against a new internal benchmark of 37 recently disclosed CVEs in live, containerized applications.
Starting from a low-privilege position, it confirmed 33 of the 37 vulnerabilities end to end through the intended path, an 89.2 percent success rate.

In October 2026, AWS published 41 security bulletins addressing vulnerabilities across open source SDKs, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, AI agent frameworks, embedded software, and widely used runtimes.
The AI agent tool surface remained the main theme.

An authentication bypass in Loom for AWS could allow network clients to gain administrative access to the agent control plane, and the AWS API MCP Server accepted OAuth tokens issued to other applications.
Prompt-injected content could turn off secret masking in Strands Agents Tools or trigger command execution through the databases-on-aws agent plugin.

The category also included cross-session conversation exposure in the Strands Agents Agent-to-Agent (A2A) server, missing authorization in the Kiro Crew WhatsApp channel, and code injection and server-side request forgery (SSRF) in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Starter Toolkit.

Several broad-impact advisories called for customer action, including remote code execution in PHP web runtimes and the native Brotli decoder, a Linux kernel IPv4 TCP use-after-free issue, and recoverable eMudhra intermediate CA keys in AWS trust bundles.
It found, demonstrated, and repaired vulnerabilities in real open source codebases, 23.1 percentage points above the previous public high.

Part 1 – Cybersecurity journeys: I didn’t plan this Author: Shannon Brazil | Published: October 7, 2026 The first post in a four-part Cybersecurity Awareness Month series shares how 11 AWS security professionals moved into security from unexpected backgrounds, showing there’s no single path into the field.
It tests only the change you deployed to staging and can stop that change from reaching production when a finding meets a severity threshold you set.
The post includes an example for GitHub Actions.

Amazon Threat Intelligence identifies PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure in MadPot Author: CJ Moses | Published: October 21, 2026 Amazon Threat Intelligence detected activity targeting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) on its MadPot sensors four days before public disclosure.
The post explains what this means for security leaders: patch critical internet-facing systems within hours, and start investigations from the earliest activity seen, not the disclosure date.
It covers application security reviews that depend on conversations with builders and on sharing hard feedback with empathy.

AWS becomes first CSP in Canada to complete the Cloud High profile assessment with 172 services and features in scope Author: Naranjan Goklani | Published: October 27, 2026 AWS completed the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (CCCS) Cloud High (PBHH) security assessment, with 172 services and features assessed in the Canada (Central) and Canada West (Calgary) AWS Regions.
This helps public and commercial customers meet security requirements for more sensitive workloads up to the Protected B level.
The summary assessment is available in AWS Artifact .
Part 2 – Cybersecurity journeys: What even is this job?
These include measuring risk across a million applications, building detection tools from the customer service side, and securing infrastructure launched into orbit.

Identity-aware AI data agents with AWS Lake Formation and Trusted Identity Propagation Authors: Thiyagarajan Mani, Mihir Borkar, Philippe Duplessis-Guindon, Umang Khambhalikar | Published: October 6, 2026 Learn to pass each user’s identity through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to AWS Lake Formation using trusted identity propagation.
Your existing data access policies then apply to AI agent queries without changes to application code, and AWS CloudTrail records the actual user behind each query.
This helps you move from static credentials to short-lived workload identities.
A GitHub repository walks you through deploying the reference architecture.
Amazon Route 53 Resolver shares the IP addresses it returns for each domain name with AWS Network Firewall , which checks new outbound connections against them.
You can then filter non-web traffic such as SSH and SFTP by domain name and validate Server Name Indication (SNI) in TLS traffic without turning on TLS inspection.
The architecture works with your own scanners and models.
The result is vulnerability triage that gives the same findings each time it runs.
Only approved ML-DSA parameter sets can then be used with AWS KMS across your environment.
October brought 19 AWS Security Blog posts focused on the remediation flow, from a security finding to a tested fix.
The post covers the new migration from Active Directory to an external identity provider or the Identity Center directory, which keeps your users, groups, memberships, and assignments in place.
Workloads running outside AWS can then get temporary credentials using X.509 certificates, each with its own identity and set of permissions.
The post also covers guidance for end-of-life PHP versions and a related issue, CVE-2026-115560.

extraction.body: October brought 19 AWS Security Blog posts focused on the remediation flow, from a security finding to a tested fix. Learn how AI agents can find, confirm, and repair vulnerabilities, and how to add penetration testing to every deployment. You’ll also find guidance on extending existing access controls to AI agents with trusted identity propagation and preparing your signing workflows for post-quantum cryptography. The PHP2Shell posts show why patch timelines for internet-facing systems are now measured in hours, and how AWS WAF can help reduce risk while you upgrade. Other posts cover identity source changes in AWS IAM Identity Center , workload identity outside AWS, and domain-based filtering in AWS Network Firewall . AWS Continuum sets a new standard in autonomous code security Authors: Alexander Greaves-Tunnell, Neha Rungta | Published: October 5, 2026 AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities achieved an 89.0 percent end-to-end success rate on the CyberGym-E2E benchmark. However, conventional numerical weather prediction (NWP) faces computational costs when increasing spatial resolution to capture localized phenomena or expanding ensemble size to improve probabilistic skill. In this Review, we summarize the development and application of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning for short-to-medium range weather prediction (AIWP) during 2015–2025, providing a holistic evaluation of the landscape and recommendations for best uses and future research priorities. New AIWP models implemented in the field can overcome computational cost barriers and resolution constraints of NWP by learning from decades of reanalysis and observational data rather than solving complex differential equations. Integration through post-processing, emulation of physical parameterizations, data assimilation and development of full AIWP models have already demonstrated performance equivalent to conventional NWP with a fraction of the computational cost. Challenges of AIWP models include dependence on training datasets, maintaining physical consistency, accuracy of forecasting extreme weather and lack of trust in their operational use. Future research priorities must focus on developing hybrid approaches that preserve physical constraints; using curated datasets to ensure forecasts are robust, trustworthy and explainable; and fostering interdisciplinary collaborations to handle increasing climate variability and extreme events. Short-to-medium range weather prediction is a crucial component of decision-making for energy and disaster management and preparedness. However, conventional numerical weather prediction (NWP) faces computational costs when increasing spatial resolution to capture localized phenomena or expanding ensemble size to improve probabilistic skill. In this Review, we summarize the development and application of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning for short-to-medium range weather prediction (AIWP) during 2015–2025, providing a holistic evaluation of the landscape and recommendations for best uses and future research priorities. New AIWP models implemented in the field can overcome computational cost barriers and resolution constraints of NWP by learning from decades of reanalysis and observational data rather than solving complex differential equations. Integration through post-processing, emulation of physical parameterizations, data assimilation and development of full AIWP models have already demonstrated performance equivalent to conventional NWP with a fraction of the computational cost. Challenges of AIWP models include dependence on training datasets, maintaining physical consistency, accuracy of forecasting extreme weather and lack of trust in their operational use. Future research priorities must focus on developing hybrid approaches that preserve physical constraints; using curated datasets to ensure forecasts are robust, trustworthy and explainable; and fostering interdisciplinary collaborations to handle increasing climate variability and extreme events.

Short-to-medium range weather prediction is a crucial component of decision-making for energy and disaster management and preparedness. However, conventional numerical weather prediction (NWP) faces computational costs when increasing spatial resolution to capture localized phenomena or expanding ensemble size to improve probabilistic skill. In this Review, we summarize the development and application of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning for short-to-medium range weather prediction (AIWP) during 2015–2025, providing a holistic evaluation of the landscape and recommendations for best uses and future research priorities. New AIWP models implemented in the field can overcome computational cost barriers and resolution constraints of NWP by learning from decades of reanalysis and observational data rather than solving complex differential equations. Integration through post-processing, emulation of physical parameterizations, data assimilation and development of full AIWP models have already demonstrated performance equivalent to conventional NWP with a fraction of the computational cost. Challenges of AIWP models include dependence on training datasets, maintaining physical consistency, accuracy of forecasting extreme weather and lack of trust in their operational use. Future research priorities must focus on developing hybrid approaches that preserve physical constraints; using curated datasets to ensure forecasts are robust, trustworthy and explainable; and fostering interdisciplinary collaborations to handle increasing climate variability and extreme events.
